Politics
The world this week
Politics
Nov 5th 2026
The Democratic Party won a landslide in
America’s midterm elections
, gaining majorities in both houses of Congress. In the Senate the party captured seven seats, giving it at least 54 (although Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi are too close to call). Democrats took control of the House of Representatives with the biggest popular-vote margin since 1976.
Donald Trump tried to distance himself from the defeat, claiming that the Republican Party “would have won in a landslide” had he been on the ballot. But Americans were angry at the president’s war in Iran, which has pushed up prices, and corruption. Republicans turned to infighting. J.D. Vance, the vice-president, offered his diagnosis: “The reason we lost is the war.”
The Democrats gained Senate seats in Republican strongholds.
James Talarico
became the first Democratic senator elected in Texas in 38 years, beating the Republican candidate, Ken Paxton, by 12 points.
Adam Hamilton
took the party’s first seat in Kansas since 1932. Annie Andrews won in South Carolina, which had voted for Mr Trump by 18 points in 2024. The Democrats regained support among Hispanic voters, who had swung sharply towards Mr Trump in 2024. This helped negate Republican gerrymandering in House districts in the South.
A day before the election American forces bombed Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The Iranian island hosts several military bases. American officials described the strikes as “defensive”. Mr Trump said that he is not planning to restart the war in Iran, even as he hinted that American forces are ready to launch strikes on the country.
Mr Trump said that America would stop providing around $4bn a year in aid to Israel at the end of 2026. The funding is not due to expire until 2028. Mr Trump said Democrats had used his administration’s support for Israel as a “bad talking-point” during the midterms. Binyamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, has repeatedly said that he wants to wean Israel off American aid.
Joshua Wong, a pro-democracy activist in Hong Kong, was sentenced to ten years in jail. Mr Wong was already serving a shorter sentence under the territory’s national-security law. Meanwhile John Lee, Hong Kong’s leader, apologised after an inquiry exposed regulatory failures and corruption behind a fire in a housing estate last year. The blaze killed 168 people.
Indonesia deployed 20,000 troops to Jakarta, the capital, after the authorities accused several people of snooping on the communications of Prabowo Subianto, the president. Mr Prabowo’s chief of staff and two senior police officers were arrested. An ally of Mr Prabowo said the wiretapping scandal could amount to an attempt to overthrow the government.
Japan’s government created the
National Disaster Management Agency
, which will oversee its preparation and response to calamities such as earthquakes, tsunamis and volcanic eruptions. The agency, which has roughly 350 staff, will co-ordinate between different departments.
Early results in South Africa’s local elections pointed to a bad outcome for the African National Congress. The once-hegemonic party was on course to win about 32% of the vote, its lowest-ever share in a nationwide election. The second-largest party, the Democratic Alliance, was set to win the most votes in Johannesburg, the commercial capital. Whether its candidate, Helen Zille, becomes mayor will depend on coalition talks.
America said it would exclude South Africa and Rwanda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) from next year. The law, passed in 2000, allowed them to export certain goods to America duty-free. The Trump administration is annoyed about South Africa’s refusal to change race-based laws and Rwanda’s warmongering in the Democratic Republic of Congo. But since just a fraction of their exports to America were covered by AGOA, the economic impact will be limited.
King Charles
attended the Commonwealth Summit in Antigua & Barbuda, alongside Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham. Some Caribbean leaders and activists demanded an apology and reparations for Britain’s role in the slave trade. Mr Burnham said he was
open to discussing a formal apology
, but ruled out paying reparations directly.
Donald Tusk, Poland’s prime minister, defended his efforts to overhaul the country’s
Constitutional Tribunal
. On October 30th judges appointed by Mr Tusk’s government took their seats on the court. Karol Nawrocki, the nationalist president, had refused to swear them in. One of the new judges suspended the court’s president, an ally of Mr Nawrocki’s Law and Justice (PiS) party. Mr Tusk said the move was necessary to restore the rule of law, which was undermined by PiS when it was in power in 2015-23. PiS accused Mr Tusk of a “coup”.
Bulgaria elected Iliana Yotova as its first female president. Ms Yotova describes herself as a “president of peace” and favours negotiations with Russia to end the war in Ukraine. Bulgaria’s presidency is a largely ceremonial role. But the election cements Bulgaria’s Russia-friendly tilt under its prime minister, Rumen Radev.
Dozens of supermarkets in Europe lost food after hackers meddled with the temperature settings of their fridges and freezers. Millions of euros’ worth of food was spoiled. Danfoss, a Danish company whose systems were targeted in the cyber-attacks, urged shopkeepers to update their software. Nobody has claimed responsibility for the attacks, though similar incidents earlier this year were linked to pro-Russian hackers.
Alexander Dobrindt, Germany’s interior minister, said there would be “severe penalties” after riots in Frankfurt. More than 100 police officers were injured. The violence followed protests against education-spending cuts and high living costs. Mr Dobrindt blamed “violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from migrant communities”.
Britain and the European Union agreed to a draft deal to remove border checks on food and agricultural goods. The agreement is a boon to British farmers, whose exports to the EU have fallen by a third since Britain left the bloc. It is one of several “mini-deals” (over students, electricity trading and other issues) that the two sides hope to seal before a summit on November 20th.

epub_11.text:
Business
The world this week
| Business
Business
Nov 5th 2026
American stock markets rose a little following the Democrats’
landslide victory
in the midterms. The S&P 500, an index of big American companies, rose by 1.6% the day after the vote, while the tech-heavy NASDAQ rose by nearly 1.5%. Health-care and renewable-energy stocks rallied. Bond yields fell slightly and the dollar weakened.
Some artificial-intelligence stocks fell amid worries that local Democratic lawmakers
could curtail
the construction of data centres. Share prices of Nvidia, the world’s most valuable chipmaker, fell by more than 3%. Those of CoreWeave, a data-centre operator, fell by around 10%. Companies owned by Elon Musk, a big Republican Party donor, took a beating. Shares in SpaceX, his rocketry-cum-AI firm, fell by nearly 4%.
Brent crude, the global oil-price benchmark, fell by 8% to around $95 a barrel—its lowest level since September. Prices had risen in recent weeks over fears that Donald Trump might resume the war with Iran, causing fresh disruption to oil supplies from the Gulf. But after the Republicans’ poor showing in the midterms, traders are betting that the president may be reluctant to restart the unpopular war.
Anthropic committed to spending $895bn on AI infrastructure and computing power, according to a regulatory filing ahead of its planned IPO. The model-maker reported revenues of almost $17bn in the third quarter, up from $1.4bn in the same period a year ago. But computing costs led to operating losses of $567m. Its IPO will be one of the largest ever.
Apple reported its first quarterly results since John Ternus, its new boss, took over in September. The tech giant’s revenue reached $114bn, an increase of 12% year on year. But Mr Ternus warned of a sharp rise in the cost of memory chips, which would squeeze its margins. Shares in the firm briefly fell.
Hackers stole some $6.3bn-worth of tokens from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange. The firm worked with other companies to freeze $3bn-worth of crypto. It promised to cover all losses. TRM Labs, a blockchain-intelligence company, said it suspected that North Korean hackers were responsible. Bitcoin fell by around 5% following the attack, though it has since recovered to its earlier level of around $80,000.
Inflation in the euro zone rose to 4% year on year in October, the highest level since 2023. Energy prices, which have been pushed higher by the war in the Middle East, rose by nearly 21%, driving the increase. Core inflation, which excludes energy and food, was 2.5%. The European Central Bank is now expected to raise its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, to 2.75%, in December.
America’s economy grew at an annualised rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, the fastest expansion in a year and above economists’ predictions. The personal-consumption-expenditures price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation, came in at 3.6% year on year in September.
South Korea’s exports reached $115bn in October, up 94% from a year earlier. Semiconductors performed especially well, as AI firms gobbled up the memory chips produced by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. South Korea has exported $930bn-worth of goods in 2026 so far, putting it within reach of $1trn for a single year.
Chinese stocks found a floor this week after entering a bear market in October. The country’s market regulators announced a rescue plan to support stock buybacks and help investors access collateral for equity purchases. Officials have also quietly paused initial public offerings. China’s markets have been a global outlier this year. The CSI 300 is down by 13%, while most other markets have risen.
Saudi Aramco, the world’s biggest oil company,
reported profits of $31.2bn
in the third quarter, up 9% from a year earlier. High oil prices caused by the Iran war have created a windfall for oil firms. Saudi Arabia’s state oil concern has been more  exposed than many. Attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have disrupted its exports and Yemeni rebels have bombed its facilities. But last month the firm managed to supply around 7m barrels of oil a day, roughly the same as before the war.
Fox News revealed that viewership had fallen by 27% ahead of the midterms. Last October an average of 2.3m people tuned in to the news channel during prime time. This year 1.7m did. Lachlan Murdoch, the cable-television network’s boss, blamed “viewer fatigue”. Mr Trump said Fox owed its poor ratings to “spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats”.

epub_14.title: Donald Trump’s humiliation offers America an opportunity
epub_14.text:
Donald Trump’s humiliation offers America an opportunity
Leaders
| Our cover
Donald Trump’s humiliation offers America an opportunity
Voters demand a new way of doing things in Washington. Let them have it
Nov 5th 2026
SURFERS CALL it the washing machine. When a giant wave throws you off your board and plunges you underwater, you lose all sense of where you are. That is what befell Donald Trump and his party on November 3rd, as they were slammed by tens of millions of American voters. They have still to grasp just how much their country has changed.
Already it is clear this was not a normal midterm swing against a sitting president, but the biggest wave-election since the aftermath of Watergate more than 50 years ago. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, flipping seats deep into once-safe red waters, from South Carolina to Texas.
The coming days will spell out two further lessons. One is that this is not just a triumph for Democrats, but also for American democracy. Voters cannot be taken for granted. If they are angry, they will turn against parties they have long supported. The other lesson, which follows from this, is that both parties now need to find a new way of doing politics—one that spends less time riling up their constituents and more getting things done on their behalf.
The wave has swept across America. With some races still uncalled, the Democrats have 54 Senate seats (including two independents) and around 260 in the House, up from 47 and 214. They are set to win the popular vote for the House by 13 points. They have also taken at least five more governors’ mansions. Kansas has its first Democratic senator since the New Deal. In
Texas
Democrats won their first Senate seat in almost 40 years and kicked out a three-term governor.
It turns out that voters do not much like a president who is elected on a promise to lower prices and stay out of wars, but who then goes on to launch a tariff crusade and attack Iran—thereby driving up prices. And they hate it if that president’s relentless self-glorification and enrichment of his family and friends mocks their own hardship. In Mr Trump’s America, Gallup finds, nine in ten adults complain that corruption in their government is widespread—about as many as in Nigeria.
The vote was thus a verdict on the president. But politicians from both parties should also reflect on voters’ rejection of the ugly mechanics of modern partisanship. Republicans gerrymandered seats, but failed to make gains. Elon Musk, a multi-billionaire, poured more than $150m into a race in Texas, but his candidate was trounced. Republican candidates stoked fears over Muslims and transgender people, and lost. One in Ohio backed an ad in which a mother damned his opponent: her own abused daughter. It sealed his defeat.
The message from this is clear and it is hopeful. It has often seemed as if polarisation was stronger than the electoral feedback that ensures democratic accountability. Not this time. Voters demanded that politicians put the nation’s prosperity above the grubby pursuit of power. Just before the election, polls say, 80% of Americans called for “substantial change” or “complete and total upheaval” in how America is run.
Voters have done their job. Politicians must now do theirs. The immediate task falls to the Republicans. When Mr Trump took control of the party, he ditched its values. Most old-guard Republican politicians were either forced out of office or traded their principles for political survival. With their call for change, voters have given Republicans a second chance. Some may stick with the president, risking further drubbings in future elections. Braver souls will breathe new life into their party, even if that courts Mr Trump’s vengeance. He is more feared than loved. They may discover that, once the old king’s power begins to ebb, it drains away surprisingly fast.
Plenty could go wrong—including with Democrats flushed by success. Their party is only a bit more popular than Mr Trump. Their campaign succeeded by pairing a promise to lower costs with one to crack down on corruption and incompetence. Both are vital, but the balance will be hard to strike.
If Democrats ignore the rot, they will only deepen voters’ cynicism and despair at the federal government in Washington. But if subpoenas and impeachments consume all of their efforts and they fail to improve people’s lives, voters will feel that they have been hoodwinked once again. A running fight with the administration will also make it harder to pass legislation that would, say, restore funding for health care.
Above it all will loom the legacy-obsessed figure of Mr Trump. Some hold out hope that he will spend the rest of his presidency pottering about the White House, gilding golf balls and opining on granite. That underestimates the president’s capacity, for good and ill.
At home Mr Trump may focus on pardoning his friends and punishing his enemies. With only two years left, he and his cronies and ideologues may try to wring what more they can from their time in power, be that through lucrative state-supported mining ventures or more deportations.
The president also retains enormous authority over foreign policy. He may yet pursue further strikes on Iran, try to bully Ukraine into a bad deal with Russia, or
invade Cuba
. As the White House’s more talented staff eye the exits, a depleted executive branch may find itself even more subject to the president’s whims. It will be ill-prepared for a crisis.
There is a glimmer of a possibility, however, that politicians will take their responsibility seriously. Republicans in Congress may consider working with Democrats, and vice versa (imagine that). They could pursue egregious corruption or even impeach the administration’s most reckless cabinet members, including Pete Hegseth, the secretary of war. They could develop rules for artificial intelligence that guard against disastrous outcomes without crippling innovation.
Mr Trump is not a man who enjoys being left out. He may judge that he could improve his legacy by working with Congress, rather than trampling on it. That is not the likeliest scenario, we admit. But, as the voters have shown, politicians who ignore them risk ending up in very deep water.

epub_15.title: El Salvador’s gangbuster tries his luck in Haiti
epub_15.text:
El Salvador’s gangbuster tries his luck in Haiti
Leaders
| Cool dictator, hellish hotspot
El Salvador’s gangbuster tries his luck in Haiti
The status quo is so dire Nayib Bukele might improve it. But the risks are huge
Nov 5th 2026
Few places on Earth are as miserable as Haiti. The last elected president was tortured and shot dead in his home in 2021. Since then, gangs brandishing military-grade weapons have wrought havoc.
They have taken over large swathes of territory in and around the capital, setting up roadblocks, terrorising residents and extorting “taxes” from them. At least 16,000 people, mostly civilians, have been killed, and over 1.5m displaced. Life expectancy is the shortest in the Americas. Ill-funded UN-backed forces sent to quell the violence have struggled. A UN “Gang Suppression Force” was approved in September last year, but only about 2,000 of the 5,500 soldiers it was promised have arrived, and they rarely venture out from their base.
Things are so bad that it is tempting to welcome almost any determined outsider who wants to impose order. Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s president, has just sent over 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers to Haiti. His contingent outnumbers the UN’s forces. Mr Bukele is a brutal strongman but widely admired in the Americas for his crime-busting. Other countries have pledged logistical support for his intervention, including Colombia and the Dominican Republic, which shares an island with Haiti. President Donald Trump, who wants to see the region’s gangs smashed, appears to have
given Mr Bukele the nod
.
Mr Bukele says his aim is to recover four Salvadoran air-force technicians who were working in the UN’s Gang Suppression Force when they vanished (and were perhaps killed) in an ambush last month. But 2,000 troops does not sound like a mere rescue mission. More probably, he wants to burnish his reputation, by showing that his record of suppressing gangs at home in El Salvador can be extended abroad. Mr Bukele once bragged that he was strong enough to fix Haiti. In social-media posts he boasts he can “finish off” its gangs.
Foreign military interventions have a mixed record in Haiti. Previous UN efforts failed to calm the mayhem and sometimes added to it. A big worry about Mr Bukele’s mission is that its aims are unclear. Will the Salvadorans kill some gangsters and leave quickly, or occupy parts of the country? Will they work with other foreign forces and the local army and police? Today’s picture is confused, including not only the UN and the Haitian security services but also Vectus Global, a private military firm run by Erik Prince, an American with links to Trumpworld, who was hired by Haiti’s government to fight the gangs with drones. The UN frets that its role is being usurped.
Mr Bukele is wrong if he imagines Haitian gangs are like their less scary counterparts in El Salvador. Back home Mr Bukele brought down the murder rate by locking up hordes of young men, almost 2% of the total population, without due process. (Trials, if they happen, are of hundreds of suspects at once.) By tossing aside the rulebook while also quietly negotiating with gang bosses, he made his country safer with remarkably little bloodshed: only four police officers died in the first 14 months of his crackdown. Haiti, by contrast, is more like a warzone. Gangs are stronger, the state is weaker and prisons are notorious for escapes. Victory here would be more akin to winning a civil war.
Mr Bukele may end up doing some good in Haiti, especially if he persuades others to send more peacekeepers. But he needs to make clear whether his soldiers will work with the UN or do their own thing. The UN could help with vetting and training, and discourage abuses against civilians. Yet Mr Bukele may prefer his own gloves-off approach. His opacity is troubling. He should spell out his intentions—and remember that it is easier to start a fight than to end one.

epub_16.title: The world must act to stop a cyber-disaster
epub_16.text:
The world must act to stop a cyber-disaster
Leaders
| Give the good guys guns
The world must act to stop a cyber-disaster
Governments should make sure defenders have better models than attackers do
Nov 5th 2026
It was meant to be “cyber-security awareness month”. Experts now call it “Black October”. In recent weeks the normal flow of computer hacks and bugs that engineers must constantly stem has become a torrent. The cause is artificial intelligence, which has turbocharged cyber malfeasance. Open-source AI models have empowered attackers to work with inhuman efficiency, competence and persistence. As a result, years’ worth of critical flaws have been exposed in days.
Those flaws range from shocking to ridiculous. Engineers have rushed to fix a flaw in PHP, a widely used programming language, that let attackers take over any computer using it. Freezers in supermarkets across Europe powered down on the instructions of cyber-criminals. And a crucial internet security certificate was revealed to have a private key of “4”, when it should have been a hundred digits long. Nobody knows what bugs might have been found and exploited in private.
These events have been sobering for the many commentators, including this newspaper, who hoped that the disruption to cyber-security from ai would be short-lived, and that the technology itself would help those who defend digital systems more than it would empower crooks. Those hopes are being dashed. Instead, the digital infrastructure on which modern life depends looks increasingly vulnerable to ai. Urgent action is needed to defend it.
Why are defenders struggling? The first reason is that many of them do not have the most advanced tools. In April Anthropic, a leading model-maker, launched “Project Glasswing”, an invitation-only club with access to the full cyber capabilities of its frontier models. It originally intended to broaden the membership widely. A similar programme from OpenAI was launched with a promise to democratise access to its tools.
However, access to powerful AI has become a geopolitical issue. Both of the model-makers now need sign-off from America’s federal government before admitting new members to their clubs, so expanding them has become a painful political process. In the meantime those outside the gates must defend themselves with the same open-source tools that
are powering the attacks
. Some are stuck in a no-man’s land: unable to access American tech, but also scared of using Chinese alternatives.
The second problem is that when AI is used benignly it creates a friendly-fire problem. The moment that a “patch” for a newly identified vulnerability is released, hackers’ AI models can examine it. This may reveal exactly what the weakness was and how to exploit it in systems that have not yet been fixed. If defenders are really unlucky—as they were with php—the patch may leak before it is released for defenders to use to fix their code. Attackers can then operate against still-defenceless systems.
A final issue is that attackers can exploit prosaic vulnerabilities faster and on a greater scale (see Business section). Cyber-security is not just about having strong systems available in theory, but avoiding laxity in practice. Unfortunately, AI has made human carelessness easier to exploit without making computer users any wiser. An internet-connected fridge running outdated software or using a default password has been a security hazard for decades. Only now, however, have attackers found it so easy to automate the search for and exploitation of weak points, running thousands of attacks in parallel.
Companies and governments must act decisively against these threats. Generating an imbalance in cyber-weaponry is crucial. With equal firepower, defenders rely on a narrow natural advantage: they must find and patch only single vulnerabilities—isolated problems which might in theory help create a breach. Attackers typically need to know of a whole chain of those vulnerabilities in order to breach a system.
Now that AI-powered attacks are proliferating, this advantage is too narrow. Defenders need a bigger armoury. America’s government should take a more permissive attitude to membership of cyber-defence programmes, or at least approve new joiners faster. It would also be better if attackers’ capabilities were pushed further behind the frontier. China’s government has recognised the folly of distributing potent cyber-weapons to all, and is requiring labs to limit the destructive potential of newly released systems.
Organisations that are not yet using AI constantly to find and close security holes have fallen behind the curve and must catch up. Some entities need more help. In America efforts like Texas’s “Project Watershed 250” are funnelling resources to providers of infrastructure to help with the basics. Those efforts should be expanded. In time, the software industry may be able to verify some code formally, thereby proving that it is unhackable, much as a mathematician proves a theorem.
Commerce, infrastructure and human relationships have come to rely on the assumption that the internet is secure. A sudden loss of cyber-security would therefore pose a grave threat to society. Cyber-security awareness has risen over the past month. Action must follow.

epub_17.title: Patients are acting more like consumers. Good
epub_17.text:
Patients are acting more like consumers. Good
Leaders
| Markets maketh medicine
Patients are acting more like consumers. Good
Health care cannot be an ordinary market. But it could be much more like one
Nov 5th 2026
The person who uses a product usually chooses it and pays for it. The great exception is health care. Most of the time insurers (public or private) decide what is covered; doctors decide what is prescribed and patients take what they are given. The result is markets riddled with inefficiency, and nowhere more so than in America, the world’s biggest. This year Americans are expected to spend about $6trn on health, nearly a fifth of their country’s GDP. Yet for all that money, about one adult in ten could not get an appointment when they needed one last year, and more than a quarter put off or skipped care because of the cost.
No wonder patients are taking matters into their own hands. They pepper chatbots with questions such as how to decode a blood test or prepare for an appointment; every week more than 300m people ask ChatGPT about health, says OpenAI, its creator. The market for tests that patients order themselves has grown to be worth about $4bn a year in America, double its size in 2021, reckons Morgan Stanley, a bank. And drugmakers have started selling directly to patients. Eli Lilly, an American pharmaceutical giant, now fills about half of new prescriptions for its obesity jab in America this way, bypassing insurers. All three developments are good news.
One reason is that patient-led markets bring lower prices. Take drugs. In America their true cost is obscured by a tangle of middlemen and insurers, who negotiate secret discounts from inflated list prices. When patients pay directly, prices are transparent and drugmakers must compete. New obesity drugs are a good example. Novo, a Danish drugmaker, launched Wegovy in 2021 at a list price of about $1,350 a month. That led to a price war with Lilly, and competition from cheap copies. Both firms now sell their jabs direct to patients for as little as $300-350 a month. The same logic works for older products. Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company, an online pharmacy founded by a billionaire, buys generics from their makers and sells them at cost plus a 15% mark-up. One study found that patients with employer-provided insurance who pay over $15 for a prescription could buy it more cheaply from Cost Plus nearly 80% of the time.
When patients pay, firms also come up with new ways to sell to them. “Direct primary care”, where medical practices ditch insurers and charge patients a monthly fee instead, has grown by nearly a fifth per year since 2022, to more than 3,600 practices in America. Others, such as Amazon’s One Medical, treat common ailments on a pay-per-visit basis. Drugmakers are looking at treatments that consumers will pay for, even if insurers will not. Novo is eyeing treatments for hair loss, addiction and menopause, conditions that big pharma long dismissed as unworthy of serious research. Even fighting off ageing
now attracts money
.
Most profound of all is the erosion of the original source of market power: a doctor’s hold on medical knowledge. In 1963 Kenneth Arrow, an economist, said that health care could not work like an ordinary market partly because the information a doctor possesses is “necessarily very much greater than that of the patient, or at least so it is believed by both parties”. Technology has since narrowed that gap. Chatbots, though hardly infallible, translate medical jargon into plain English and set out the treatment options for a condition. Increasingly they work with patients’ own data, too.
Consumer-led health care carries dangers. The first is quackery. Websites and influencers peddle peptides and supplements that promise bigger muscles, better skin or a longer life. Many do nothing and some do harm. Regulators should make sure sellers do not lie about their products. Access matters, too. Nearly all consumer health care is paid for out of pocket, so for now it mostly serves the well-off. However, most innovations start out as luxuries and get cheaper.
No one will shop for doctors from the back of an ambulance. Complex and emergency care will stay with doctors, hospitals and insurers. But in the routine parts of medicine, patients can and should be treated as customers. A bloated, paternalistic industry has kept them waiting long enough.

epub_18.title: England’s new ban on kinky porn will misfire
epub_18.text:
England’s new ban on kinky porn will misfire
Leaders
| Repeal the porn laws
England’s new ban on kinky porn will misfire
Bans make moralists feel good, but will not work as planned
Nov 5th 2026
Pornography depicting strangulation, suffocation, incest and actors pretending to be underage will be banned in England and Wales from November 6th. Few will publicly mourn the loss of videos with titles such as “Choking gets her off”. But free expression means nothing if it does not apply to that which is objectionable.
The government argues that porn is causing real harm, by teaching young people that dangerous practices are not merely normal during sex but expected. It notes with shock a sharp rise in “choking”. In America, Australia and Britain roughly half of sexually active 18- to 35-year-olds report having experienced this; a generation ago it was so niche that pollsters did not bother to ask about it. Mostly it is young men choking young women; sometimes, alarmingly, without prior consent.
For many worried parents, that ends the argument. But reality is muddier than the simple morality tale told by anti-porn campaigners. “Choking” refers to a range of acts, including light pressure on the neck, that some consenting adults find pleasurable. Evidence that porn is what made it so widespread is
weak
. Young people hear about sex from a variety of sources, including their peers. Under-18s in Britain are already barred from accessing porn sites, but tech-savvy ones have found ways round the age-verification system—and will find ways round the new ban, too.
The idea that the young can be prevented from hearing about kinks is implausible. Some of the acts whose depiction the government is forbidding are so popular that they appear in pop lyrics. Doja Cat, an American rapper with more than 50m monthly listeners on Spotify, offers lyrics such as: “Spank me, slap me, choke me.”
Restrictions on free speech should be rare, narrow and clearly defined. No one doubts that governments should ban child pornography, and that this ban should be vigorously enforced. But in general people should be allowed to film acts that are legal, even if many voters find them repulsive.
Britain’s new law fails the test. It is both broad and unhelpfully vague. The government has not defined the acts that will be illegal to depict. Instead it expects courts to decide on a case-by-case basis. But Britain’s overburdened state will find it hard to police the many difficult-to-judge edge cases that will emerge. In an industry enamoured with terms like “mummy” and “daddy”, how will judges be able to decide what constitutes a depiction of incest? What about whether a hand on a consenting adult’s neck constitutes strangulation? Or when fellatio crosses the line into suffocation? Courts have many more important things to do than to debate such matters, including hearing cases of actual sexual assault.
Since possession of banned content is punishable by up to two years in prison, the new rules will also dilute what it means to be a sex offender. Such an important label loses value when it can be applied both to paedophiles and those harbouring a stepmum fantasy.
Rather than trying ineffectually to prevent the young from learning about risky acts, governments should be ensuring that they are taught about safety, consent and how to talk frankly to prospective partners about what the other person does and does not want. Sex education in most countries is dismal. In Britain it is better, but still has room for improvement. If children do not learn about sex and relationships from reliable sources, they will depend on unreliable ones.
Pornography is an unpopular thing to defend. But Britain has become too willing to ban anything pearl-clutchers dislike, from plastic straws to noisy protests. A ban on kinky porn may please moralists, but it should alarm anyone who cares about freedom of speech or government overreach.

epub_20.title: LLMs v palaeontology
epub_20.text:
LLMs v palaeontology
Letters
| A selection of correspondence
LLMs v palaeontology
Also this week, publications, film critics, preparing for emergencies, London traditions, accounting
Nov 5th 2026
Letters are welcome via email to
letters@economist.com
F
ind out more
about how we process your letter
I work for an AI lab as a scientist and read your piece on how
AI companies are not merely providing a tool for discovery but choosing to wield it themselves
(“A scientific revolution”, October 17th). My field of palaeontology uses large language models to investigate the evolution of fossils by mining the formal descriptions of species from literature that often extends back to the 18th century. How fossils are formally described (their taxonomy) is key to their identification and use.
The trouble is that LLMs are not good at understanding very old literature and how terminology, measurement and concepts of species and evolution have changed over two centuries. This means an enormous amount of work for human scientists in cleaning the data before the LLM can be put to work. It’s the same for other descriptive, observational sciences like botany and zoology, where written descriptions and evidence are a big part of the accumulated knowledge of humanity codified in legacy scientific literature.
The truth is that the low hanging fruit of AI, the high-quality data already in number form, collected recently in genomics and physics, is easy, but human elbow grease is what will lubricate the older sciences.
Mike StephensonVisiting professor in palaeontologyNanjing University
“Stop the slop” (October 17th) reports that
roughly 90% of papers submitted to “predatory journals” are AI-generated
. However, you characterise these journals simply as being “where authors pay for publication”. There is a brief but critical distinction. Publication fees are neither exclusive to predatory outlets nor inherent to open-access publishing. Many reputable subscription and open-access journals, including those published by non-profit learned societies such as the Federation of European Biochemical Societies, charge legitimate processing or page fees to cover operational costs and support the scientific community.
The defining issue is not that authors pay, but whether rigorous peer review and high-quality editorial oversight are provided in return.
Dietmar MansteinEditorFEBS LettersHanover, Germany
“
Are film critics as snooty and out of touch as people think?
”, you ask (October 24th).  You confuse subjective opinion with objective fact. Neither ten nor 1,000 subjective opinions that agree with one another add up to one objective judgment. So when you say we should “pity the reviewer” who dismissed “Citizen Kane” as “well-intentioned, muddled, amateurish” you tacitly assume that an objective review is possible, implying that any review that does not conform to expert opinion is wrong. Naturally, the great and good in every field like to think their judgments are more informed or even just better than those of hoi polloi. What they have to say may well be more informative and interesting than Kev’s waffle down the pub. But at the end of the day their remarks are just as subjective.
As for “Citizen Kane”, context is everything, especially considering what other films were being made more than 80 years ago. I could never see what all the fuss was about.
Patrick PowellSt Breward, Cornwall
Thank you for drawing attention to
Britain’s preparedness for major emergencies and conflict
(“Dad’s Army returns”, October 17th). However, the image you presented of a large, uniformed civil-aid corps undermines the principle of a whole-society approach. Berets, ranks and bands may appeal to some volunteers, but they reinforce a notion of civil defence as an eccentric, quasi-military pursuit.
Moreover, building preparedness around a centrally directed corps reproduces the very dependencies that a resilient society must be able to withstand. Major, cascading emergencies, such as natural hazards, infrastructure failures or armed attacks, disrupt communications, transport, leadership and logistics. An organisation dependent on those systems will struggle precisely when it is most needed.
Whole-society resilience starts with different questions. What can continue to function when organised assistance is unavailable? Can households meet their essential needs without immediate outside help? Can neighbours support one another? This approach  recognises the strengths already present in communities. Practical skills, professional expertise and local knowledge exist far beyond the organisations formally designated to respond. Adults who are able to do so should be encouraged and equipped to take responsibility for themselves and those around them.
Dr Frank LongGeneral secretaryInstitute of Civil Protection and Emergency ManagementCamberley, Surrey
Here at All Hallows by the Tower (the oldest church in the City of London dating from 675AD) we have our share of
the “lovely nonsense” of traditions
(“Standing on ceremony”, October 17th). One dates from 1380 and involves paying an annual fine of one red rose to the Lord or Lady Mayor on a velvet cushion. On Ascension Day we  “beat the bounds” of the parish to demonstrate where our boundaries lie. Given that we proudly stand next to the Tower of London this involves a ceremonial skirmish with the resplendently dressed, and splendidly armed, Beefeaters. As the sides meet, much bellowing, roaring and stick waving ensues, typically in front of many bemused tourists. But no blood is spilt and both sides retire with honours. Nonsense? Absolutely not. It’s a reminder that the Church of England gives everyone in its land a place to worship, be baptised, married or buried. Lovely? Absolutely.
Reverend Nicol KinradeVicar of All Hallows by the TowerLondon
Schumpeter (October 17th) did an excellent job of describing
the convoluted financial reporting of AI firms
. It reminded me of Charlie Munger, a former vice-chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, who dismissed EBITDA as “bullshit earnings”. If he were alive today, he might well create a more suitable label, like “totally made-up bullshit earnings”.
Scott SimmonsHighlands Ranch, Colorado

epub_22.title: Divided government in America will mean more spending, not less
epub_22.text:
Divided government in America will mean more spending, not less
By Invitation
| Vote, splurge
Divided government in America will mean more spending, not less
But Democrats will struggle to unwind the president’s agenda, writes Tomas Philipson
Nov 5th 2026
THE RESULT of America’s midterm elections occurred under two sets of conflicting facts: by many conventional measures the economy is performing above average, yet Americans remain deeply dissatisfied with their economic circumstances, displaying attitudes in surveys more typical of those during a recession.
And America is far from being in that predicament. Real GDP grew at a healthy 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second. Unemployment and layoffs are low and the roaring expansion in investment, partly thanks to an AI sector free from excessive regulation, offers reasons for optimism about future productivity. Yet the University of Michigan’s consumer-sentiment index stood at just 48.0 in October, down from 53.6 a year earlier. Its index of current economic conditions was even lower, at 46.7. Such readings have in the past been associated with severe economic stress.
The election results may be explained in part by a continued—and generally faster-than-expected—rise in the prices of food, gasoline, housing and much else. Many households with rising nominal wages have endured real wage declines this year.
Democrats naturally took full advantage of public anxiety over affordability during the election campaign. They omitted to mention that much of the rise in prices happened on Joe Biden’s watch. The unadjusted CPI-U consumer-price index jumped by 21.4% during his four years in office, compared with 6.1% during the first 20 months of Donald Trump’s second term.
The economic statistics are not wrong, and households are not imagining their bills. They are looking at different dimensions of economic activity and prosperity. Until real wage growth makes the cumulative inflation shock less painful, Americans may continue to feel economically insecure even as the aggregate economy expands. Ordinary voters do not experience the economy as a quarterly GDP rate or a stock index. They experience it through how much their paycheques can buy and, as this election illustrated, that purchasing power is not always synchronised with the aggregate statistics.
Voters mostly blame the Iran war and tariffs for persistent inflation. The irony of this election is that these are the two policies the new Democratic Congress will find hardest to reverse.
Start with the Iran war. The president began it in February without congressional authorisation. A resolution to curb his war powers would need support from two-thirds of both chambers to survive his veto, and Democrats are well short of that. And much as the new Congress may wish to choke off funding for what it sees as military adventurism, few members would vote to defund troops already in the field.
It is a similar story with tariffs. After an adverse ruling by the Supreme Court in February, the administration reissued the duties under another statute, limited to 150 days unless Congress extends the term. The administration then moved them to a more permanent “Section 301” footing. Democrats can ask for, or trade, exemptions for particular countries or goods, but any broader reversal would be vetoed by the president.
Other parts of the White House agenda will survive the election as well. Chief among them is Mr Trump’s welcome deregulatory programme. An executive order signed in January 2025 told agencies to retire ten rules for every new one. Its impact has been impressive: in the 2025 fiscal year, the White House regulatory office counted 646 deregulatory actions against five new rules, with claimed savings of $212bn.
Much of the deregulation drive is baked in for this Congress. It is true that federal-agency rules issued towards the very end of any given Congress can be overturned by the subsequent one using the Congressional Review Act “lookback” mechanism. However, the administration will probably aim to finish its major rules through notice-and-comment rulemaking well before 2028, meaning that fewer of them will be reversible.
The election’s fiscal impact is less clear. If recent history is a guide, the new divided government will agree to spend more, not less. Since 2013, whenever a president has lacked full control of Congress or needed opposition votes in the Senate, the budget deal that followed has raised spending on both parties’ priorities at once. Republicans got more for defence, Democrats more for domestic programmes. In a classic logroll, each side voted for the other’s spending to secure its own. The 2013 and 2015 deals kept “parity”, with equal increases for defence and non-defence spending. In 2018 Senate Republicans counted it a win that defence rose more than domestic spending, but they still conceded $131bn more for domestic programmes over two years.
This recent history cuts against a long-held view that divided government acts as a brake on spending. For instance, William Niskanen of the Cato Institute, a think-tank, found that, from Dwight Eisenhower to Bill Clinton, real federal spending grew more slowly when the two parties split control of Washington.
The horse-trading of the past decade and a half points in a different direction. Each of the deals came under split control, or when the minority’s Senate votes were needed, and each raised spending above the limits Congress had set for itself. On the annual budget, in short, divided governments have become a way for each side to buy the other’s agreement with additional spending. Added to which, this is a White House that likes to make deals. Only an optimist could expect growth in government debt, and the associated risk of higher interest rates, to be lessened by the new gridlock.
■
Tomas J. Philipson was acting chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers during President Donald Trump’s first term.

epub_23.title: Markets are pushing electrification. Governments must push harder
epub_23.text:
Markets are pushing electrification. Governments must push harder
By Invitation
| Charge!
Markets are pushing electrification. Governments must push harder
The transformation can’t be left to market forces alone, writes Murat Kurum, president of COP31
Nov 5th 2026
FOR 30 YEARS global climate talks have focused on what’s feeding power systems. The defining battles of the annual COP UN climate summits have been between wind turbines and chimney stacks; solar panels and pipelines. How we use that power to electrify buildings, transport and industry has been largely ignored, despite these sectors producing almost half of emissions.
Like a northern European city this summer, electrification is now getting its day in the sun. An opportunity has opened up as the economics have shifted. Energy prices are rising sharply, cost-of-living pressures are biting and green-technology costs are plummeting. Preliminary data indicate markets are moving this year as more electric tech is shifting off the shelves.
Campaigners often insist the economic case for green technology is clear. But hopes that market forces alone will solve the energy transition are misplaced. Even with building momentum, existing trends indicate electrification is expanding too slowly—from meeting 23% of the world’s final energy consumption today to 29% by 2035. This is not the 35% that the science says will keep climate goals within reach. State intervention is still needed, urgently.
The Paris agreement of 2015 legally required countries to submit regular climate plans. These plans have been the main mechanism for driving climate policy. However, in the latest round of plans electrification was largely absent.
Too often, electrification targets are merely implicit within headline emission-reduction goals. Think of it like neglecting to produce an AI strategy because you already have a headline growth target. Statements of government commitment, bespoke policy frameworks and incentive structures are all essential to sending important market signals.
Since the start of the conflict in the Gulf, 25 countries have announced new policies to support greater electrification. That is a start, but not enough. Specifically, they must focus on reducing the payback periods of investing in electric tech and guaranteeing the infrastructure to make it work.
Rarely is electric tech cheaper upfront. For consumers, the economic case rests on higher efficiency and lower running costs. Electric vehicles use 70-80% less energy and can save between $200 and $1,500 per year. But too often, it still takes too long to pay back the initial premium.
The relative cost of electricity compared to fossil fuels is critical. The European Commission recently found that once electricity costs more than 2.5 times as much as natural gas, the case for households to switch to heat pumps weakens sharply. Policymakers can intervene by reforming the tapestries of taxes and subsidies on different energy sources. In some developed countries, taxes make up 30% of the cost of residential electricity, and most EU countries tax electricity more than natural gas. Reforms need balancing against fiscal and socioeconomic needs, but the overall imperative to rebalance in favour of electricity remains.
To reduce upfront costs, governments have long deployed a mixture of direct subsidies, preferential tax rates and social-support schemes. Türkiye’s rapid adoption of electric vehicles has been driven by reductions in value-added tax that lower sticker prices at the dealership.
Multilateral development banks and other development-finance institutions can also use grant-based and concessional capital along with loan guarantees to lower the cost of capital. This is particularly important for developing countries, which face far higher borrowing costs that are holding back investment.
But these incentives cost money. In a fiscally constrained world, electrification must fight harder for a share of a shrinking pie. Nevertheless, as the inherent risks of energy import dependency come more sharply into view, governments should be ready to review the case for more aggressive support. This year 95 countries have introduced emergency price caps, subsidies or fuel-levy cuts to support consumers. Public money might be better spent subsidising the equipment needed to reduce exposure to volatile global markets.
Governments must also give consumers confidence that once they have bought their electric appliance, they will be able to run it. Otherwise, they will not risk the investment. However, 730m people lack electricity, and millions more have only unreliable access. Even in rich countries, low investment in grids is a constraint. There is simply no transition without transmission. Around $1trn is needed each year for grids and storage between now and 2030. Permitting times need to be shortened. Outdated policy and regulatory frameworks that are based on old fuel sources rather than renewables need reform.
So how to kick-start progress? As chair of COP31, Türkiye is making electrification the golden thread, or copper wire, connecting all our efforts. We have proposed a global “35-by-35” target—35% electrification by 2035—to focus minds and enable us to track progress. Türkiye is also leading by example and will publish its national energy plan at COP as part of our efforts to reduce spending on energy imports from 2.1% of GDP to 0.7% by 2050.
Everyone will have their own pathway. Broadly speaking, developed countries will favour electric cars, heat pumps, low-level industrial heating and AI-driven grid optimisation. Developing countries will focus more on electric bikes, cooking-stoves and industrial motors, which require expanding basic electricity access. They will also need more support from international donors.
Overall, we cannot leave electrification to market forces alone. They will not fully deliver the potential for energy security, affordability and emission reductions. We need a partnership where governments enable the private sector to throw its full weight behind electrification. Türkiye will use the summit to press everyone to show what more they can do. In the end, success will be measured in cleaner air, lower global temperatures and communities no longer at the mercy of violently convulsing global energy markets. The International Energy Agency shows that the 35-by-35 target could save $500bn each year in avoided fuel imports. Markets have started this journey. Governments need to finish it.
■
Murat Kurum is Turkey’s environment minister and president of the COP31 climate-change conference.

epub_25.title: What will a lame-duck Donald Trump get up to overseas?
epub_25.text:
What will a lame-duck Donald Trump get up to overseas?
Briefing
| After the midterms
What will a lame-duck Donald Trump get up to overseas?
Embattled at home, the president will look abroad. That is worrying for the world, but it is not clear what he can achieve—for good or ill
Nov 5th 2026
DOUG SOSNIK, a former adviser to Bill Clinton, recalls the president’s frenetic agenda during his final stretch in the White House. “We talked about the schedule and how many more trips we could do—do you mind doing an 18-hour day?” Mr Clinton was a man in a hurry. “I’ve only got a year left in office,” he observed. “I’ve got the rest of my life to sleep.”
The same clock now ticks for Donald Trump. He has been the defining protagonist of the past decade in American politics. But on November 3rd he became only the second term-limited president, after George W. Bush in 2006, to fight his final midterm election in control of both chambers of Congress and to lose both, shocking Mr Trump himself. “Wow,” he told the New York Times upon learning of his party’s loss in South Carolina, a former MAGA stronghold. “That’s amazing.”
In his final two years in office, Mr Trump will be embattled at home as he confronts his political mortality. Congress, which Mr Trump had rendered largely irrelevant while under Republican control, will swamp his administration with hearings and subpoenas on corruption and abuse of power. (“Lawyer up,” one congressman advised on X.) It will dare him to veto popular policies such as restoring health-care funding. Democrats will try to stop his vanity pursuits in the capital, too: his grand ballroom and his triumphal arch. But the area where he will continue to have the greatest, most unrestrained impact is overseas, where he will turn for monsters to slay and legacies to leave.
Mr Trump’s foreign policy—from Venezuela to Greenland to Iran—has been radical and hyperactive. Now it could become more so. Mr Trump has unfinished business in Iran and Cuba that could drag America deeper into the Middle East and Latin America. His flirtation with great-power carve-ups, including summitry with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, could herald a darker world order—and difficulties for Ukraine. His quixotic courtship of Kim Jong Un, North Korea’s leader, could upturn American nuclear policy. All this will unfold as AI wizardry spirals towards artificial general intelligence, throwing up diplomatic and national-security challenges that will fall to Mr Trump to manage.
All this would be concerning enough for the world under a president who had a gift for diplomacy, a Herculean work ethic and a normal attention span. Mr Trump not only will have to do without those qualities, but he will also probably lose experienced staff who could help in a crisis—another feature of lame-duck periods. The president’s adventures abroad over the next two years promise to be chaotic and unpredictable, if not necessarily fruitful.
Mr Trump will not be unique in searching for solace abroad as the end comes into sight. The Economist has analysed presidential travel records going back to Harry Truman. They show that presidents are typically much more active overseas in the last two years of their second terms (see chart). Mr Bush spent 50 days abroad in 2008, twice his previous annual average. After losing the 2006 midterms, he ordered a surge of military forces in Iraq against bitter opposition in Congress in the hope of salvaging a war that had gone badly awry. Barack Obama doubled his travel between the final two years of his first and second terms. His sweeping nuclear deal with Iran came the year after his own bruising in the 2014 midterms. “Presidents by the end of their term are frustrated with the various constraints on them,” says Yuval Levin of the American Enterprise Institute, a think-tank, who served in the Bush administration. “And foreign policy is where there are fewest constraints.”
Mr Trump, like an impresario who changes the act when the audience grows weary, is drawn to foreign-policy manoeuvres that confound his critics and, in his mind, demonstrate his strength. Mr Trump has long boasted of his diplomatic prowess, famously claiming that he would end the Ukraine war in a day—and, at a midterms rally on November 1st, that he would have won the Vietnam war in a week. Mr Trump’s evident failure to win the war at hand, with Iran, therefore rankles with him. The two sides continue to skirmish, with America conducting what it described as “defensive” air strikes on November 2nd.
Until recently Mr Trump was leaning towards his third attack on Iran in 18 months (see map), in concert with Israel, to force it to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and limit its nuclear programme. That would trigger Iranian retaliation against Gulf energy facilities, consuming Mr Trump’s attention for months to come. On October 28th Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator, said that he had received an intelligence briefing on America’s war plans. “I will just say this—their plan is insane,” said Mr Murphy, noting that public reporting had pointed to the targeting of civilian infrastructure. “It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law.” (Three days later Mr Murphy went to hospital after suffering a stroke.) A person familiar with the planning says that Mr Trump was considering whether to strike Iranian oil tankers in Asia.
In recent days other sources say that Mr Trump has put these plans on ice, telling Binyamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, that America will not back an Israeli attack. Israeli forces, which were ready for a strike, have paused their preparations.
Mr Trump will face opposition to fresh strikes from multiple sources. One is J.D. Vance, his vice-president—and a probable candidate for president in 2028—who, in a post on X on November 4th, explicitly blamed the midterms drubbing on the war and said voters wanted a different relationship with Israel. Another is Congress. Such is the scale of the blue wave and so detested is the war—on a par with the Vietnam war—that Democrats might withhold funding (and risk being accused of undermining the troops in the field). Even if Mr Trump chooses to escalate, America is unlikely to have the munitions, air-defence interceptors or political stomach for another protracted campaign. Mr Trump’s aim is presumably to secure a deal that allows him to emerge from the fracas with the appearance of an honourable peace. Iran’s leadership, conscious of Mr Trump’s political frailty, is unlikely to fold easily.
If Iran is the first test of Mr Trump’s diplomatic agenda, Ukraine is likely to be the second. Here the president’s vengeful instincts present dangers. Mr Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukraine for the war, criticised the country’s strikes on Russian oil refineries and belittled Volodymyr Zelensky, its president. So far American intelligence-sharing with Ukraine and arms sales via Europe have survived. When American negotiators unveiled a half-baked 28-point peace plan, in November 2025, Mr Trump’s secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and European allies intervened to prune its worst parts. At each juncture, Mr Trump has stepped back from the breach of a complete abandonment of Ukraine and a definitive turn towards Russia.
Mr Trump may direct his ire once again at Mr Zelensky, should he conclude—wrongly—that Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries were primarily responsible for the fuel-price shock that helped doom Republicans at the polls. In 2020 Mr Trump responded furiously after believing that China had misled him over the spread of covid-19. A similar sense of betrayal could translate into a more aggressive pressure campaign against Mr Zelensky personally and Ukraine as a whole, with the aim of forcing Ukraine’s capitulation.
An early glimpse of Mr Trump’s post-midterms mood may come on November 18th-19th, when he and Mr Putin visit Shenzhen, China, for an international summit hosted by Mr Xi. America’s European allies fret that Ukraine will be on the menu. In recent months, Mr Trump has made concession after concession to Russia, cutting a deal to buy diesel and waiving sanctions in return for the release of an American prisoner, in part to lure Mr Putin to the negotiating table. Mr Putin may conclude that he will never again enjoy as pliant a partner as Mr Trump. But the Russian leader also believes that time is on his side, and that European support for Ukraine will ebb away. What is more, Democrats in Congress can be expected to hinder or block efforts by Mr Trump to give Mr Putin more ground on Ukraine—especially any deal that reeks of corruption.
The president may quickly lose interest (not for the first time) in the quagmire of Ukraine and turn his attention to another developing hot spot in his own hemisphere: Cuba. Since taking office, Mr Trump has squeezed Cuba’s dictatorship economically, causing power cuts, food shortages and a collapse of health care on the island. In January 2026 the president decapitated Venezuela’s government by abducting Nicolás Maduro, its leader. He is thought to be tempted by a similar model of light-touch regime change in Cuba.
America’s economic warfare is intended both to weaken the regime and split the country’s elite, potentially throwing up partners who might work with America, much as Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s acting leader, abandoned Mr Maduro. Mr Trump has made little secret of his goal. “We’ll take ​care of Cuba on our way back from Iran,” he boasted on the campaign trail in October. That month Mr Rubio, a Cuban-American hawk, urged disaffected Cubans to work with the CIA: “To those who seek to ​create positive change in Cuba—now is the time.”
Mr Trump longs to be a president who achieves what his predecessors did not. He would relish being the leader who reversed the Cuban communist victory of 1959. But he is not a man for details. In Venezuela he has largely left the country’s dictatorship in place, swapping its leaders and cutting grubby deals to secure its oil for American firms. A fudge like that would be far harder to pull off in Cuba, notes a person with knowledge of the administration’s debates, because Cuba’s diaspora—which is older and more established than Venezuela’s—would make its wrath felt.
It would arguably help Mr Trump’s chances of success in his foreign-policy endeavours if he had experienced staffers around him. But an exodus may be under way. Mr Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, has quietly been exploring jobs in the private sector. (He may skip the 2028 presidential race, hoping for more favourable conditions in 2032.) Mr Rubio’s departure would shift the balance of the administration, potentially leaving John Ratcliffe, the director of the CIA, as the most influential hawk in the cabinet.
The president may also lose his favourite man at the Pentagon. Many Democrats want to impeach Pete Hegseth, the pugnacious and divisive secretary of war. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely Democratic Speaker of the House, has not ruled it out.
Democrats may demand Mr Hegseth’s ousting as the price of passing an $87.6bn supplemental bill including $67bn for the Department of War, which is in a deep financial hole. Presidents often seek scapegoats after an electoral pummelling. Mr Bush dumped Donald Rumsfeld, his defence secretary, after his midterm loss in 2006; Mr Trump sacked Jeff Sessions, his then attorney-general, after his party’s defeat in the House in 2018.
Yet Mr Trump is more likely to respond with defiance than with contrition. There is speculation that Mr Hegseth could be shunted into the job of national security adviser or possibly appointed to the Senate seat for Tennessee that is to be vacated in January by Marsha Blackburn, who has been elected the state’s governor. There, some note, he would enjoy a degree of protection from Democratic probes—including those into his deadly strikes on boats thought to be carrying drugs.
Even if Mr Hegseth survives, Mr Trump’s coterie of advisers has already begun to thin out. The national security council has been largely gutted, resulting in ad hoc and haphazard decision-making. Experts have been fired en masse, resulting in poor preparation for meetings and negotiations. Policy can swing on the whim of individuals or small groups, as Elon Musk, the founder of SpaceX and a former adviser to Mr Trump, showed when his firm appeared to cut off vital satellite communications to Ukraine during a row in October. Some of Mr Trump’s envoys, both official and unofficial, blend diplomacy with the pursuit of lucrative business deals.
Mr Trump will also find it ever harder to gain the Senate’s assent for new cabinet secretaries and other appointees, leaving officials in acting roles for long stretches. Susie Wiles, the president’s chief of staff, who is widely viewed as a stabilising force in the White House, may depart after serving for longer than any of Mr Trump’s first-term consiglieri. The ultra-nationalist agenda pushed by Stephen Miller, Ms Wiles’s deputy, has proved to be an electoral liability. The quality of staff tends to fall during an administration, observes Mr Sosnik: “You see a thinning of the herd, with the people coming in…generally a peg or two below the people that they replace.”
That leaves an increasingly isolated, embattled Mr Trump looking for ways to shore up his legacy in the only way he knows: entirely ad hoc. It is not unusual for lame-duck presidents to roam the globe in search of lasting achievements in their final days. But history shows it is hard going.
Woodrow Wilson spent six months at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919 and returned to sell the League of Nations to the American public—an effort that failed spectacularly when the Senate spurned the treaty. Dwight Eisenhower’s superpower summit with the Soviet Union fell apart after a U2 spy plane was shot down. In 1968, after he decided not to seek re-election, Lyndon Johnson tried to secure a settlement of the Vietnam war, to no avail. In his last year in office Mr Clinton came close to visiting Pyongyang and tried, but failed, to forge a lasting peace deal between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
Some have fared better. Richard Nixon and Ronald Reagan signed major arms-control agreements in their final years (as did Johnson). Mr Obama normalised ties with Cuba and painstakingly negotiated the Iran nuclear deal (scuttled by Mr Trump). And Mr Trump himself, in the last part of his first term, went on a foreign-policy blitz, meeting Mr Kim three times, signing a peace deal with the Taliban and brokering the Abraham accords which normalised relations between Israel and several Gulf Arab and north African states.
A lame-duck Mr Trump does not seem well-positioned to strike lasting, historic deals. But he will try. He wants to meet Mr Kim yet again to pick up where he left off in his first term. He is keen on a three-way meeting with Mr Putin and Mr Xi at the summit in Shenzhen. That is ostensibly also to discuss nuclear arms control (a topic China has no interest in broaching while its arsenal is below parity with America and Russia). Eventually he may again try to broker a peace in Ukraine.
The prospects for substantive diplomacy seem bleak. The risk is that Mr Trump agrees to shoddy deals that serve as sticking plasters, allowing him to claim he is worthy of a peace prize. (Mr Vance too may encourage such pacts to promote his own peacemaking bona fides to future voters.) That could store up serious problems for Mr Trump’s successor, just as happened in 2020: Mr Trump’s pact with the Taliban contributed to the collapse of the Afghan government and Joe Biden’s chaotic withdrawal the following year.
Mr Trump’s lame-duck status will also make it harder for him to strike lasting deals in the first place. Friends and foes will adjust how they interact with the president, notes Sam Charap of the RAND Corporation, a think-tank, mindful that his political authority will ebb away. The extent of Democratic gains on November 3rd suggests that the party is in a strong position to win the presidency in 2028. Many late-term deals, such as Mr Obama’s nuclear agreement with Iran and opening to Cuba, rest on weak legislative footing and are easily undone by successors. Ukraine, in particular, might try to wait out Mr Trump in the hope of a successor, in 2029, who would look more favourably on the country. Indeed, it will now be hard for Republicans to recapture the Senate—which must approve international treaties—until 2032, beyond Mr Trump’s tenure.
It is possible that Mr Trump’s fundamental unseriousness will work in the world’s favour. It takes work to achieve diplomatic breakthroughs. Mr Trump’s lack of follow-through might end up leaving a status quo world to the next president. Perhaps he will be drawn more to his domestic preoccupations: carving his name into Washington’s granite, securing his family’s post-presidency business interests and doling out pardons. But it is also possible that his impetuous nature will put the world at risk in a crisis, a black swan that tests a president’s wisdom and patience. Consider an AI-enabled cyber crisis or a Chinese blockade of Taiwan, or something worse. For two years, the world will be holding its breath.

epub_27.title: Japan prepares for its next natural disaster
epub_27.text:
Japan prepares for its next natural disaster
Asia
| The next big one
Japan prepares for its next natural disaster
Its new agency has plenty to do before a catastrophe strikes
Nov 5th 2026
AMONG THE countries most prone to natural disasters, Japan has a habit of spawning new bureaucracies. Yet, despite in recent years launching agencies for digital technology and for children and families, its governments have consistently batted away a more obvious idea: to set up a disaster agency. That changed on November 2nd. At the new body’s launch, Hosono Goshi, its freshly appointed minister, stood before a backdrop with a colourful logo resembling the character for “prevent” in bosai, or disaster prevention. He vowed to make Japan “the world’s most disaster-prepared nation”, ready for calamities “on the scale of a national crisis”.
Sitting at the junction of four tectonic plates (see map), Japan suffers around a fifth of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6 or greater. The earthquake and tsunami in 2011 in Tohoku in the north-east of the main island of Honshu, which triggered a nuclear meltdown, are strong memories. In 2024 the Noto peninsula was devastated by a magnitude 7.6 earthquake, and another powerful one struck Kumamoto this summer. Torrential rains and floods, intensified by climate change, pose a growing threat, too.
Yet even these calamities may be dwarfed by what lies ahead, says Kawata Yoshiaki, a disaster-management expert at Kansai University who advised the government about the agency. Seismologists warn of two catastrophic earthquakes; their statistical model suggests a 70% chance of a magnitude 7 or higher quake directly hitting the Tokyo metropolitan area in the next 30 years. Over the same period another feared megaquake along the Nankai Trough off Japan’s Pacific coast has a 60-90% probability. In the worst case, such a quake could kill nearly 300,000 people, force 12.3m to evacuate and cause ¥292trn ($1.8trn) in economic losses, equivalent to more than 40% of Japan’s annual GDP. Mr Kawata expects long blackouts and broken supply chains that would leave vast numbers short of food.
Japan is already a global leader in disaster preparedness, especially in hardware such as earthquake-resistant buildings and early-warning systems. With the new agency, the government hopes to streamline its software and put more resources towards preparing for the bigger and more complex disasters that may lie ahead. Until now, responsibility for disaster management has been distributed across different ministries and levels of government. The prime minister oversaw such efforts with support from a small unit in the Cabinet Office, staffed by officials seconded from other ministries, who rotate out every few years. Ueshima Yasuhiro of Japan Platform, a network of aid groups, likens the government’s previous approach to “putting on a Band-Aid” whenever disaster strikes, rather than treating underlying risks. The new agency, with around 350 staff, aims to boost preparedness by building up institutional knowledge about dealing with a range of potential disasters.
Creating a single centralised body should help address one of the Japanese system’s biggest weaknesses: a notoriously siloed bureaucracy that struggles to co-ordinate across institutions. Consider hospitals, says Mr Kawata, pointing out that they could lose power during a big Tokyo earthquake, putting many thousands of patients at risk; planning evacuations would involve the health ministry. The fisheries agency, meanwhile, could help fishing communities protect themselves against tsunamis. While Mr Hosono will handle day-to-day operations, Takaichi Sanae, the prime minister, will officially head the agency, which will also have powers to make suggestions to other ministries.
Climate change and more extreme weather are demanding vigilance towards less familiar threats. Tokyo experienced 37 consecutive days of rain until the beginning of October this year, the longest stretch since records began in 1886. In nearby Chiba, record rains wreaked havoc in August, followed by a flood weeks later. Waki Yuichiro, a 52-year-old resident, whose house was flooded and car ruined, says he had prepared for earthquakes, “but I never imagined flooding would affect us…In the future, we have to prepare for the unexpected—anything can happen.” Tanaka Yasuo, a volunteer who visits Chiba to repair air-conditioners damaged by the flooding—essential appliances during Japan’s sweltering summer—says that in the past he used to have time to rest between disasters; now they come so frequently that “I can barely take a break”.
Japan’s demography, with its large number of old people, makes it vulnerable in other ways. One growing concern is saigai kanrenshi, or disaster-related deaths: people who survive the initial catastrophe but later die from prolonged stress or deteriorating health during evacuation. After an earthquake in Kumamoto in 2016, such deaths accounted for more than 80% of the toll. In Noto, too, they made up 70% of deaths. Poor conditions in evacuation centres, where survivors still often sleep on crowded gymnasium floors and without adequate sanitation or nutritious food, can make things worse. Such evacuation centres have hardly improved over the years. Ishiba Shigeru, a former prime minister who championed the disaster agency, blames a culture that prizes perseverance and “idealises disaster survivors who endure hardship”. Sugano Taku of Osaka Metropolitan University points out that  municipalities with inadequate resources are being left to handle them on their own; the new agency is supposed to offer them guidance and support.
But it is just one part of Japan’s approach to disasters, which rests on three principles: kojo, government assistance; kyojo, mutual help; and jijo, self-help. In Kumamoto, Fujino Tatsuo and other volunteers clambered onto damaged roofs, removing heavy kawara, traditional Japanese tiles that could fall in another earthquake. Nearby, Miyabara Yukimi’s home had collapsed, though her whole family miraculously crawled out of the rubble. She and her husband spent weeks sleeping in a lorry before volunteers helped them build a makeshift shelter. “It feels like we lost everything—but we still have to make the first step,” says Ms Miyabara.
On its first day the new disaster agency kicked off by issuing an “emergency request” urging local governments to strengthen disaster preparations and citizens to take precautions themselves. Mr Hosono stressed that jijo remained essential. “We cannot achieve this by relying on the government alone,” he said of his ambition to make Japan even more of an example to the rest of the world in disaster preparedness. He advised citizens to secure furniture against earthquakes and stockpile at least three days’ worth of food and water—preferably, enough for a week.
