epub_28.title: Dead Starlink terminals in Myanmar are getting people killed
epub_28.text:
Dead Starlink terminals in Myanmar are getting people killed
Asia
| Weak signal
Dead Starlink terminals in Myanmar are getting people killed
Has Elon Musk taken another war zone offline?
Nov 5th 2026
UNDER BRITISH rule, Burma boasted the largest tungsten mine in the world at Maw Chi, near the border with Thailand. Decades of war and misrule have  slashed the mine’s output. But labourers working in small teams at Maw Chi still dig up the metal before sending it on to Thailand and global markets to make aeroplanes, missiles and semiconductors. That has made Maw Chi a prize in the war between the military junta which seized power in Myanmar in 2021 and rebels opposing it.
Two years ago rebels captured Maw Chi and started to put its revenue stream towards their war effort. The junta responded with occasional air strikes on the mine. Rebels countered by creating an ingenious early-warning system using Starlink, the space-based internet service that is run by SpaceX. When the junta  launched an attack aircraft, a spotter near the airfield would alert civilians at the mine site to take shelter. But on September 1st that warning system failed. A jet bombed the mine at Maw Chi without any alert, says a local rebel commander, killing five and injuring six. One of the Starlink terminals used for the early-warning system had been cut off, leaving the miners in the dark.
Starlink has become essential in parts of Myanmar riven by conflict or governed by rebels. The junta has turned off cellular services in many of these areas, leaving rebel armies and humanitarian organisations reliant on connections to SpaceX’s satellites in low-earth orbit. The democratic government-in-exile uses Starlink to remotely run schools and hospitals in liberated areas, where too large a physical footprint would attract attention from the junta’s air force. In these places Starlink is ubiquitous even though, on paper, the service is not available in Myanmar. Terminals are procured elsewhere and brought into the country illegally. Until recently, SpaceX has tended to turn a benevolent blind eye towards their use.
The episode at Maw Chi was not an isolated incident. Rebels, aid workers and teachers say that some Starlink terminals across Myanmar have been shut down by SpaceX since July. Many others are still up and running, they say, and it is not clear how the company has decided which to cut off. SpaceX has not offered any public explanation, but it has told some aid workers in Myanmar that, under pressure from the American government, it is trying to cut off scam centres based in the country that rely on its services to carry out their transnational frauds. A State Department spokesman says that it is working with private firms and their financiers to combat scam centres, while “preserving access” for those using the technology for “legitimate purposes”. Rumours of a “whitelist” maintained by the State Department have been swirling among aid groups, but no one seems to know what they need to do to be added to it.
For reasons that remain murky, SpaceX had recently throttled Starlink connections in Ukraine, reportedly after talks between Elon Musk, its founder, and President Donald Trump. Its motives in Myanmar are also obscure. Analysts have seen no signs of drones using Starlink in Myanmar, where rebels are on shoestring budgets. New terminals smuggled into Myanmar could cost as much as $8,500 each, say aid workers. That is far too pricey for the poorly funded rebels to simply strap one to a drone made to explode on impact.
But the terminals have been invaluable in letting democratic forces offer services in areas they control. Hospitals under the National Unity Government (NUG), the pro-democracy government-in-exile, use it to consult specialists abroad. And students across Myanmar use it to attend NUG schools remotely. As terminals go dead, students are dropping out. The head teacher at an NUG school says that of 270 students who started the year there, 40 have stopped attending.
Perhaps the most vital use of Starlink has been in early-warning systems like the one at Maw Chi. In a curious twist, some of these systems, say former American officials, were secretly set up by USAID in 2024. Even before Mr Musk put the aid agency through the wood-chipper last year, SpaceX had doubts about this. “They had lots of questions about the legal implications of allowing their terminals to be used in Myanmar,” says a former American official who was involved. In particular, they say, SpaceX was wary of  letting its terminals be used for lethal purposes. Shutting them down is also proving lethal.

epub_29.title: The fight for the soul of the Australian right
epub_29.text:
The fight for the soul of the Australian right
Asia
| Hanson v Hastie
The fight for the soul of the Australian right
Can a special-forces veteran stop the rise of Pauline Hanson?
Nov 5th 2026
Senator pauline hanson swaggered into Secret Harbour on October 30th like a general inspecting troops in newly conquered territory. It was her first visit since One Nation, her ragtag populist party, won a by-election in the coastal town. The race for a seat in the Western Australia state parliament was the latest in an “orange wave” of wins for One Nation in elections this year. But Secret Harbour is special: the town sits inside the federal constituency of one of Ms Hanson’s most formidable opponents, the special-forces veteran and Liberal Party frontbencher Andrew Hastie.
Once dismissed as a gadfly, Ms Hanson is now a real force. In January One Nation overtook the Liberals in the polls and still has a lead. It is neck-and-neck with the governing Labor Party. It still lacks much of the scaffolding of a national organisation, but Ms Hanson has shown that she can turn voter anger at the major parties into seats. So her party has a real shot at replacing the Liberals as the official opposition at the next election in 2028, and an outside one at forming the next government.
The election in February of Angus Taylor as the Liberals’ new leader has not boosted the party’s fortunes. Mr Taylor, attacked by Ms Hanson as a “smarmy management consultant”, has mostly avoided confrontation with her. But Mr Hastie has taken her on directly. Some Liberals argue that, against her, he would be a stronger leader than Mr Taylor. “It was obvious that the better choice would have been Hastie,” says Malcolm Turnbull, a former prime minister and Liberal leader. “I’m sure he’ll lead the Liberal Party some day—if he doesn’t lose his seat.”
That Mr Hastie might face two such different futures is largely a consequence of one decision that he made: to testify against a fellow soldier accused of war crimes. That has led to an emotional debate on the right, one which Ms Hanson has been eager to use to her advantage. “I was subpoenaed, and then under oath required to tell the truth,” Mr Hastie tells The Economist. “Would you rather me be in contempt of court and lie?”
Wildly divergent answers to that question have this year been tearing the Australian right apart. Mr Hastie is now under attack from Ms Hanson and her powerful allies like Gina Rinehart, a mining magnate, and Kerry Stokes, a media baron, some of them once supporters of the Liberals. In July Ms Hanson published a video calling Mr Hastie a “traitor” and encouraging Liberals to abandon him. The strategy seems to be working. Tony Abbott, the president of the Liberal party and another former prime minister, has distanced himself from Mr Hastie. They are trying, he says, “to destroy me personally”. But the stakes for the Australian right are far higher than that.
The veteran of the elite Special Air Service regiment is an unlikely hate figure for the populist right. Mr Hastie has led a push over the past year to drag the Liberal Party to the right on issues that animate populists. His call for lower net migration is now party policy. He is against women in combat. Like many populists, he bemoans the demise of Australian manufacturing, arguing for a more active industrial policy. But he parts ways with them when it comes to the rule of law.
Mr Hastie links his stand against war crimes to his Christianity. He testified against a fellow soldier, he tells supporters, under an oath before God. He is more open about his faith than most Australian politicians: “I learned more about politics and leadership watching my father [a Presbyterian minister] at church than anywhere else.” But “I am not a Christian nationalist.” By contrast, Ms Hanson has called Australia a Christian country, yet dodged questions about her own beliefs.
The lessons from his father’s church sometimes point in unexpected directions. Mr Hastie opposes abortion and gay marriage, but rejects Ms Hanson’s call for a “monocultural” Australia. Worse yet, in his view, are her fans’ calls for racial criteria for immigrants. He recalls his father’s church in Ashfield, then one of Sydney’s most diverse suburbs, which held services in several Asian languages because “everyone is made in God’s image”. Immigrants, he says, should be chosen for their values and skills rather than their ethnicity.
That same philosophy has allowed Mr Hastie to make friends across the aisle. Take Senator Penny Wong, the foreign minister and a Labor stalwart. Ms Wong, gay and born in Malaysia, might seem an unlikely partner. But the two worked well together when Mr Hastie was a backbencher and Ms Wong was in opposition. “It’s always been clear to me…that he is one of the few on his side who believes there is a national interest above partisanship,” says Ms Wong. “While Andrew isn’t really where modern Australia is, he understands that you can’t out-Pauline Pauline.”
That hints at a potential way through for Mr Hastie. Once known as the Liberal Party’s rising right-winger, his fight with One Nation is broadening his appeal. He has no plans to give up his conservative bona fides, but he is seeking out new allies. Within his own party, once-critical moderate grandees like Mr Turnbull now offer cautious praise. At a fundraiser last month 80% of participants were new donors. And he has become a more frequent guest on public television and radio shows, whose viewers tend to skew centre-left. That could leave him in a stronger position to lead the Liberal Party in the future.
But first he must see off Ms Hanson’s campaign to brand him among the conservative base as a traitor. He still looks to be under siege. The home-affairs minister has cited unspecified threats in advising police to upgrade security at his home and office. “It’s a bit unnerving,” Mr Hastie says. “But I’m a Christian. I pray about these things, and I’m at peace about it.”

epub_30.title: Cheap data is great for Indians but not for India’s reputation
epub_30.text:
Cheap data is great for Indians but not for India’s reputation
Asia
| Ashoka
Cheap data is great for Indians but not for India’s reputation
The internet brings out the worst in everyone
Nov 5th 2026
“BITCH LASAGNA” is the name of a song by PewDiePie. It is also a two-word social history of the relationship between India and the internet. For five years Mr Pie, a Swede whose real name is irrelevant, was the owner-operator of YouTube’s most popular channel. In early 2019, after several months of back-and-forth, he was decisively overtaken by T-Series, a Bollywood studio.
In the run-up to his defeat the Swedish streamer posted what his fans described as a “diss”, or insult, track and what anyone else would consider to be bordering on bigotry. Its lyrics include references to open defecation, ridicule of Indian languages and a meme about “bobs or vegana” (don’t ask). The song’s title alludes to a Facebook Messenger screenshot of an Indian man requesting unclothed self-portraits from a woman and, on being ignored, hurling the presumably auto-corrected epithet at her. The internet really does bring out the worst in everyone.
Mr Pie’s battle with T-Series marked a hinge point in India’s internet adoption. In 2016 Mukesh Ambani, an industrialist who inherited a petrochemical company, took literally the maxim that “data is the new oil” and launched
Jio
, a mobile network with rock-bottom prices and generous data allowances. Almost overnight the share of India’s population covered by a modern mobile-broadband network jumped from 4% to 74%. A price war followed. Internet users doubled in just three years from a sixth of India’s people when Jio launched to a third when T-Series triumphed, rising to over two-thirds today. A billion Indians use the internet, or three for every American.
Not satisfied with bringing Indians online, Jio, which in October went public in one of the country’s largest listings, also gives them something to do once they get there. Its streaming service, Hotstar, has more than 450m monthly users, well ahead of Netflix or Amazon’s Prime Video. But neither Jio nor anyone else has managed to build a social space Indians prefer to Western ones. Indians are the largest nationality on YouTube, Instagram and Facebook and a significant minority on X, Reddit and Snapchat. Their influx onto these platforms has not been great for India’s image in the world.
“Bitch Lasagna”, though tasteless, reflects a common stereotype online of Indian men as forever propositioning women on social media. The idea of India as an unsanitary place, too, is depressingly common. And Indians have of late acquired a reputation as fierce nationalists with thin skins and foul mouths. As one viral post on X put it, “Never invade Russia in winter. Never attack India by Twitter.”
Some of the criticism is overblown. Crude men and noisy nationalists exist everywhere, but the sheer scale of the Indian contingent makes them more noticeable. Some of it is the result of India’s openness. Because Indians use the same platforms and often post in English, the country’s flaws are more visible than those of other countries.
And some of it may well be cynical. Social-media algorithms prioritise content that elicits strong reactions. YouTube travel videos that portray India as filthy and dysfunctional often attract millions of views. Instagram has lately been flooded with AI-generated videos showing street-food vendors cooking in appallingly unhygienic conditions. Ragebaiting Indians can be a sound commercial strategy, as the 300m-plus views of “Bitch Lasagna” demonstrated.
All of which obscures just how fun and indeed funny India’s internet can be. Influencers and YouTubers make material for all tastes. Social-media memes are the currency of youth slang and infiltrate the mainstream, too. This year’s “
cockroach
” youth protests started life as an online joke. It is only a matter of time before India’s popular culture starts breaking through more widely. Some of it already has. A dance move in a Telugu song called “Naatu Naatu” went viral in 2022 and later won an Oscar. Early this year an extended joke by Azeem Banatwalla, a stand-up comedian, resonated globally. As more culture crosses over, India’s image online will change too.
Until then, India’s reputation provides fodder for content. Mr Banatwalla’s gag was a list of all the traffic violations you can commit in Mumbai for the price of a speeding fine in Norway. Somnath Padhy, another comic, has a routine riffing on how “there are one billion websites in the world [and] I think Indians have commented on all of them.” And Reddit has a community dedicated to “the chaos unleashed by cheap internet”. It is called “Jio was a mistake”.

epub_32.title: With an eye on America, China is beefing up its AI-controlled labs
epub_32.text:
With an eye on America, China is beefing up its AI-controlled labs
China
| No hands on deck
With an eye on America, China is beefing up its AI-controlled labs
By automating scientific research it hopes to strengthen its industrial muscle
Nov 5th 2026
In a laboratory in Shenzhen, a city in southern China, hundreds of mechanical limbs dance alongside each other in search of scientific discoveries. Few humans are involved. Instead the machines are directed by artificial intelligence. An AI model devises a hypothesis, instructs robots to test it and records the results to improve its next experiment. The autonomous facility, which is owned by a drug-discovery firm called XtalPi, runs around the clock to discover new medicines. During a visit early this year, China’s prime minister, Li Qiang, gushed that
innovation like this
was “the key to winning the future”.
If China is to win, the loser would presumably be America. Both countries are competing to build and apply AI technologies as fast as possible. Scientific discovery may be the most important arena for this race: inventions can improve lives as well as boost a country’s economic and military power. In March China’s new five-year plan called for faster exploration of
AI-driven ways of doing science
as part of a broader push to “seize the commanding heights in the industrial application of AI”.
As often in industry, the government is heavily involved. It is building what it calls an AI-for-science “stack” by linking the specialised datasets, models and computing power that are needed by firms to run autonomous labs. Experts hope these “self-driving” facilities will make research faster, cheaper and far more productive. China’s labs are unlikely, for now, to produce big scientific breakthroughs. But they could supercharge Chinese manufacturing. Officials say they will reduce dependence on Western technology. They also hope these efforts will give China an edge in the AI race. America should pay attention.
Stacks like this have two layers. The first is the brains. In April the Chinese Academy of Sciences launched a platform, often dubbed an “AI scientist”, that is available to hundreds of universities and laboratories in China. It is called ScienceOne (the Chinese name is Panshi, meaning “Bedrock”) and resembles a chatbot. It includes models, or agents, trained on academic reports and non-text data, such as waveforms used to measure seismic vibrations. They can perform hundreds of tasks, like working out the sequences of amino acids in proteins, state media say. China’s scientific models still tend to lag behind America’s. But a researcher at the University of Hong Kong who uses ScienceOne praises its bundle of scientific datasets, AI agents and computing power. “I don’t see anything like it in the US,” he says.
The second layer is the brawn. Advances in applied science need hands-on experiments. Robotised labs have existed for decades, but they require humans to analyse data and refine experiments. AI models can take over the drudgery. They can learn from the results in real time and continuously tweak their approach. Last year XtalPi used its autonomous lab in the discovery of a molecule that could be used for treating a form of stomach cancer that grows in scattered clusters of cells. The firm generated millions of possible molecules and whittled them down to hundreds of candidates before testing the remaining ones on lab-grown tissue, using robots.
China is watching America closely. It stepped up its stack-building after President Donald Trump unveiled a similar plan late last year: the “Genesis Mission”. This also involves the government-led creation of AI platforms to test scientific hypotheses and automate experiments. Many AI researchers believe that labs full of non-human AI scientists could one day churn out everything from cancer cures to hitherto intractable proofs in physics. “This is one area where Chinese policymakers see eye-to-eye with the American AI labs,” says Kyle Chan of the Brookings Institution, an American think-tank.
Both countries have good reasons to involve the state. AI scientists need to be trained on large sets of data such as weather patterns and the results of past experiments. Governments, through national laboratories, are often the biggest keepers of such data. They are also well-placed to provide researchers with access to advanced computing power.
But there are differences between automated labs in America and China. In America they have been showered with venture capital: about $1bn of it last year. Recipients have mainly been startups offering speculative, eye-catching research, such as in the creation of room-temperature superconductors. Dreaming big helps them raise money, says Charles Yang, formerly of Renaissance Philanthropy, a charity that helps donors fund scientific research. In China, firms with automated labs are usually less ambitious. They like research that can quickly generate profit.
China’s use of AI in scientific research is often factory-like. XtalPi’s labs “work 24/7 and the basic cost [once they are up and running] is electricity,” says Shi Xuekun, one of the firm’s managers. The company now serves 17 of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies. China’s biomedical industry is growing fast: last year about half of all drugs licensed globally, by value, were from China, according to Goldman Sachs, a bank—up from 21% in 2024. Smart labs are likely to account for a growing share. In March Eli Lilly secured rights to develop and sell potential drugs from Insilico Medicine, a Hong Kong-listed firm that uses automated labs. The deal could be worth up to $2.75bn.
Makers of industrial materials are also likely to benefit. China is a powerhouse in materials science, publishing four times as many papers in the field as America, according to Nature, a journal. In April researchers at City University of Hong Kong showed how an automated lab could design and test molecules for light-absorbing solar cells. Robots could make the cells just as well as humans, and with far more consistency in their output. At present the average human researcher in a lab might produce one or two new cell-prototypes daily. In a joint venture with JinkoSolar, an industry titan, XtalPi says that it is building an automated facility that will test 1,000 a day.
AI experts differ over the steps needed to create “artificial general intelligence” (AGI)—in essence, AI on steroids. Some of China’s AI stars including Zhou Bowen, the boss of Shanghai AI Lab, a government-backed institute, believe models must first master sciences, and that automated labs will help them do so. Mr Shi hopes that’s right: smarter models could predict the results of the experiments they design, he says. Forget humans. He may then need fewer robots, too.
■
Subscribers can sign up to

China and Taiwan are fighting over Sun Yat-sen

China and Taiwan are fighting over Sun Yat-sen
The 160th birthday of the nationalist revolutionary will be unusually fraught
Nov 5th 2026
On both sides of the Taiwan Strait, there are many roads, districts and schools named after the father of modern China: Sun Yat-sen, the country’s first president after a republican revolution in 1911. Ten years ago, when President Xi Jinping urged “all Chinese who revere Mr Sun Yat-sen” to unite, the fight over his legacy was not so fierce. Now, ahead of the 160th anniversary of his birth on November 12th, cross-strait relations are far more tense. Sun has become a political lightning rod.
Across China, the government has been whipping up Sun mania. Exhibitions, concerts and seminars praise Sun’s devotion to “revitalising” a poor and weak China. Mr Xi is expected to address a decennial Sun-themed pow-wow in Beijing. Of Sun’s “Three Principles of the People” (nationalism, democracy and welfare), Mr Xi stresses the first. He invokes Sun’s concept of national unity to promote his own aim of unifying Taiwan with the mainland. At the 150th anniversary of Sun’s birthday, Mr Xi vowed to “continue to fight for the revitalisation of China”.
Taiwanese officials are pushing back. This year they warned the island’s people not to attend China’s commemorations. In October the government’s Mainland Affairs Council said it would not allow serving or former officials to join the gathering in Beijing (in 2016 about 30 retired Taiwanese generals took part in the corresponding celebration of Sun’s birthday). “What are Taiwanese officials afraid of?” People’s Daily, the Chinese Communist Party’s main mouthpiece, asked in a recent column. They are “terrified” that more Taiwanese will realise their “future development lies in a strong motherland”, it fumed.
But there is another tension: inside Taiwan. The ruling Democratic Progressive Party is not nearly as pro-Sun as the opposition Kuomintang (KMT). Sun, after all, founded the KMT in 1912 (the party fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing a civil war with the Communists). Earlier this year, China criticised Taiwan’s plan to remove politicians, including Sun, from banknotes as an attempt to “erase Chinese national identity”. There is sympathy for that view in the KMT. Much less so among young Taiwanese—while China’s calls for “national reunification” have been growing louder, many have been leaving Sun’s orbit.

Hit podcasts reveal the angst of China’s youth
China
Hit podcasts reveal the angst of China’s youth
The government is getting twitchy about their growing popularity
Nov 5th 2026
In 2007 David Brooks, an American columnist, suggested that the period from adolescence to adulthood should be called the “odyssey years”, alluding to the hazards of the voyage described in
Homer’s epic poem
. This year the term’s Chinese translation, aodesai shiqi, has turned viral online in China. Young people use it to describe the torments they face on life’s journey including securing a job, finding a partner and getting on the housing ladder. State media, forever striving to sound upbeat, offer little guidance. Instead, growing numbers are turning to an independent and remarkably feisty forum: podcasts.
On his hit show, “Qingdao Kuaima”, Fu Yu offers words of comfort. “The odyssey years can transform the trivial, trial-and-error nature of life into a heroic, epic-like trajectory of personal growth,” the 34-year-old tells his half-million listeners.  It was reassuring to hear him explain why young people are insecure, a fan commented.
After a slow start, China’s podcast industry has boomed in recent years. It is still small compared with America’s, but it is tapping into huge demand from angst-ridden youngsters. Enthusiasts call 2020 “year zero”. That was when China’s first big podcast app, Xiaoyuzhou, or “Little Universe”, was launched. It made finding and hosting shows much easier. Now more than one in ten people in China, about 150m, tune into podcasts on Xiaoyuzhou, Himalaya and other Chinese apps, reckons the Chinese Podcast Association, an industry group. Users of Xiaoyuzhou listen for an average of 80 minutes per day; more than 80% are aged between 18 and 35.
Though few podcasts are state-run, they still have to heed censors’ guidelines. In public, no one may question the Communist Party’s rule. But podcasts are changing the media landscape by providing room for more open discussion. State media shun mention of the love lives of gay and lesbian people; social media sometimes scrub references to the topic. Podcasts offer more freedom. They don’t have to use coded language or euphemisms, says Huang Yalan of Jinan University. The government is suspicious of feminism, but many hosts are proudly feminist and eagerly discuss women’s rights.
The slow-burn style of many podcasts gives them protection. Fifteen-second videos on platforms such as Douyin (as TikTok is known in China) are more likely to run afoul of censors because they need to make a striking point to attract viewers. People with the patience to listen to an hour-long show are unlikely to report transgressions, says Yi Yang, who co-founded JustPod, China’s largest podcast-production firm.
In 2025 the most listened-to genre on Xiaoyuzhou was personal growth. Liu Hongxing, a data analyst in Beijing, likes a podcast of this type called “Self-Evolution Theory”, which is the app’s third-most-popular. She says it has introduced her to the idea of living the way she wants to. Previously young people thought self-improvement was about becoming cleverer, says Mr Yang. Recently it has become more about meditating, receiving therapy and learning to understand that life’s problems are not all one’s own fault.
The longer length of podcasts creates room for reflection, whereas short videos tend to oversimplify and stoke anger, says Mr Fu, the podcaster. “Young people...are experiencing anxiety, confusion and pain,” he says. But he refuses to join those who grumble about the privileges enjoyed by the older generation, who have spent much of their adulthood in years of staggering economic growth. Armed with a sociology PhD, he aims to help young people understand the forces behind their problems, such as finding a stable job or—for those who want to opt out of the rat race—deciding where to retreat.
Blake Chen, the 33-year-old founder of a media company in Guangzhou, a southern city, says his generation has never been able to find its place. He believes the gap between young people and their parents is vast—much larger than that between their parents and grandparents. So the young seek guidance from peers. A popular podcast made by Mr Chen’s firm discusses topics such as how to manage inter-generational conflict and whether to marry. Some hit podcasts are hosted by older professionals. Qian Jing, a professor, invites young people to call in with their woes, exuding authority as she tells them how to cope with burnout and find meaning in life. Zhang Chun, a psychological counsellor, describes her own podcast, which is also in the top 50, as collective therapy.
In a leafy district of eastern Beijing, Daxiao Café’s free recording studio has hosted more than 200 podcasts about everything from psychology and women’s health to running and books. Few presenters aim to make money (and few do): they simply enjoy airing views and connecting with others. But this may change—brands are eyeing opportunities. Giada, a luxury fashion firm, launched Xiaoyuzhou’s top podcast called “Flower on the Rock”, which features interviews with women. The host is Chen Luyu, often described as China’s Oprah Winfrey.
As podcasts expand their reach, however, censors will pay more attention. Some apps already use artificial intelligence to screen content. In August regulators called for “red lines” to be drawn around podcast content and said it should uphold “mainstream values”. One show sometimes posts short clips on Xiaoyuzhou saying an episode cannot be uploaded for “technical reasons”—meaning, presumably, problems with censors. But it tells listeners how to find the podcast elsewhere.

epub_35.title: A new path to political power in China runs through state firms
epub_35.text:
A new path to political power in China runs through state firms
China
| Chaguan
A new path to political power in China runs through state firms
China Inc has become a breeding ground for up-and-coming officials
Nov 5th 2026
In much of the world the age of 55 is when an official might start to contemplate life after work. In the rarefied air of China’s elite politics, it is roughly when careers get interesting: quinquagenarians are the sprightly young things who are just beginning to break into the upper echelons. After a reshuffle that ended last week, eight of China’s 31 provinces now have governors born in 1970 or later. None of these leaders, mind you, is so green as to have been born since 1973.
It is worth looking at them more closely. Not because any will run China soon (if ever, given Xi Jinping’s grip), but because, as top performers of their cohort, they reveal traits that the Communist Party values in its leaders today. A common feature is extensive experience in state-owned companies.
Six of the eight governors from this youngish group rose through various appendages of China Inc. Liu Jie, now in Zhejiang province, worked for 16 years at a steel company. Guo Ningning, a rising star in Fujian, toiled for 24 years in state banks. Xie Weijiang, currently in Hunan, spent 23 years in the power sector. Of the three 1970s-born ministers in Beijing, two also worked in state-owned firms. Altogether, nearly three-quarters of the government’s highest-ranking whippersnappers today are graduates of China Inc. It is starting to look like Government Sachs, with Chinese characteristics. One such characteristic, to be clear, is that the revolving door really only turns from state firms to the government, not the other way. And the corporate types still have to wait in line: the eight governors born in the 1970s all serve under provincial party secretaries born in the 1960s.
Rising through state firms is a change from how officials previously climbed the greasy pole. The classic path was to pay your local dues, starting in a county, becoming a small-town mayor and so on until reaching a provincial perch. Another was to get fast-tracked through the Communist Youth League. A third was the technocratic channel, especially for engineers: they might go from working on a dam to the industrial ministry and then to higher leadership. Each had drawbacks. The local route could be parochial for a global superpower. The youth league came to be seen as an arrogant faction—not least by Mr Xi as he consolidated his power. And pure engineers, most useful during China’s intense phase of building, had seen their star wane in Beijing.
Enter what Li Cheng of the University of Hong Kong calls “technocrat 2.0”. Over the past five years officials with specialised training have staged a comeback. Engineers are in the mix, but their degrees are wide-ranging, from life sciences to quantum computing. A large number have also studied economics and finance. And state-owned firms are the ultimate finishing school.
Some officials have always migrated from state businesses to politics. But in the past decade the door has opened more widely. In 2019 the party reworked its appointment system, creating a mechanism to shepherd more people, more quickly, from state companies into government. In 2022 Mr Li counted 86 officials born in the 1970s who had made it by then to vice-level provincial posts; 54% had worked in industrial companies or financial firms.
Why is the party turning to state executives? State firms—coddled, bloated and slow—are hardly models for the dynamic economy that the country’s leaders want to build. Politically, however, there is much to recommend them. Truly national firms are not beholden to any one place. Their bosses have managed complex issues, and many know the world beyond China. Lu Dongliang, now governor of Shanxi, secured access to resources in Africa and South-East Asia as head of Chalco, the listed arm of the world’s biggest aluminium producer. Zhuge Yujie, the new governor of Qinghai province, ran Shanghai’s port, the world’s busiest. Feng Chucheng of Hutong Research, a consultancy in Beijing, thinks the rise of state executives reflects the party’s preference for leaders who, it hopes, can bring both technological self-reliance and economic resilience.
Dipping into state firms also broadens the talent pool for the party. It has gaping holes to fill. At an important plenary meeting last week, just 74% of the party’s Central Committee (which began with 376 members) showed up in Beijing. That was the lowest attendance rate in the post-Mao half-century, confirming the extent of Mr Xi’s purges. Some observers think these removals could come back to haunt Mr Xi by thinning out his bench for future appointments. In reality they are unlikely to be a constraint: China has no shortage of strivers eyeing powerful posts. It has even more now that state employees are also in the running.
Mr Xi’s dominance can be stifling for the bureaucracy: loyalty to him is a prerequisite for advancement, which saps officials’ initiative and derring-do. Yet the conveyor belt from state firms to high office shows that loyalty is a necessary, not sufficient, condition. To truly get ahead officials need to have demonstrated expertise and competence, not just ideological bona fides. In that sense the renewed emphasis on technical abilities is commendable.
But in another way it is a worrying portent for the economy. During China’s decades of turbocharged growth, much of its energy derived from the retreat of the state sector and the rise of private companies. Under Mr Xi the tide has shifted. Private entrepreneurs are struggling while state firms, once again favoured by state banks and central planners, are emboldened. The systematic recruitment of state executives into government only adds to the momentum. Private companies must form party cells, but no private entrepreneur has ever become a full member of the Central Committee. For ambitious graduates entering the workforce, the signal is clear: throw your lot in with China Inc.

epub_37.text:
How the Democrats will wield their power
United States
| Subpoena season
How the Democrats will wield their power
The party has control of Congress, at last. Now it must govern
Nov 5th 2026
In Democrats’ quest to restrain Donald Trump over the past two years, no tool was more frequently deployed than the sternly worded letter. Democrats sent these missives regularly; the president and his associates ignored most of them. Such is the plight of the minority party in Congress, which lacks power to call hearings or issue subpoenas, much less pass laws.
That will change when Democrats grab the gavel on January 3rd, having won a
thumping majority
in both the House and Senate. They will probably have around 260 seats in the lower chamber. The task now is to live up to the twin promises of the campaign: boosting the fortunes of ordinary Americans and checking the president. Their hope is that substantive victories will pave a path back to the White House in 2028. The risk is that they fall short, or overreach, and create an opening for a Republican recovery.
The main problem is that the Democrats’ win, though triumphant, still leaves them far short of the 290 seats in the House and 67 in the Senate that would have given them a veto-proof majority. They are unlikely to advance major legislation. They may, however, manage to make modest deals with the president that appeal to his populist instincts, such as capping drug prices.
Indeed, the first order of business for Hakeem Jeffries, the presumptive speaker of the House, will be to try to reinstate the funding that Republicans cut for Medicaid, the health programme for the poor, and the subsidies for individual insurance on the Obamacare exchanges. Democrats will also move to end the Iran war and scrap Mr Trump’s tariffs, which they argue (correctly) have driven up costs. One bill, the “End Trump’s Tariff Tax Act”, would repeal levies on Canada and various laws that Mr Trump has used to support his trade war. Most of these initiatives stand little chance of becoming law; the point is to force confrontation with Mr Trump and telegraph their priorities to voters.
Yet Congress does have an important tool at its disposal: the budget. Government funding expires on December 11th. Letting it lapse at that point seems unlikely; Democrats will not want to welcome their new majority with a shutdown. Instead, Congress will probably agree to stopgap funding through February or March, then hash out a proper budget for the rest of the fiscal year—which is when Democrats might extract concessions on health care, tariffs and other priorities, if they are savvy and Mr Trump is pliable.
Achieving other big policy changes will be difficult. Democrats have long grumbled about spending money on a costly, ferocious deportation campaign rather than basic support programmes. However, Republicans have already moved to protect funding for immigration enforcement through the remainder of Mr Trump’s term. The president continues to try elaborate legal methods to sustain his tariffs, none of which require congressional approval.
As for the Iran war, Democrats could try to bar funding to prosecute it, though that would require bringing some Republicans on-side to overcome the Senate filibuster—and even among Democrats, cutting off all funding is controversial. It is more likely that Democrats could make money contingent on more thorough disclosure about the war, from casualties to weapons stockpiles, says Damian Murphy, a former Democratic congressional staffer now at the Centre for American Progress, a think-tank. The Pentagon has largely kept lawmakers in the dark over the past year. Democrats imposed similar reporting requirements during the Iraq war after flipping Congress in 2006.
If progress on economic issues may prove incremental, Democrats could be more aggressive in their efforts to check the president. In the Senate, Democrats can block Mr Trump’s judicial appointments and cabinet nominees. That would matter most if one of the conservatives on the Supreme Court were to leave the bench before the 2028 election—two are in their late 70s. Then Senate Democrats, led by Chuck Schumer, would probably copy the tactic of Republicans who refused to consider Merrick Garland, Barack Obama’s nominee, in 2016. Meanwhile, lower-court confirmations will definitely stop. Republicans will ram through as many as possible in November and December, before the Democrats take over.
Oversight will dominate the agenda. Democrats will move to issue subpoenas to officials and force testimony. Exposing the administration’s perceived self-dealing will be the biggest focus. Mr Trump has supplied them with ample material and voters have taken note. Two-thirds of Americans say Mr Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself; in exit polls, nine in ten said government corruption was a major factor in their vote. Democrats may, for instance, explore how a manufacturing firm whose investors include Donald Trump junior, the president’s eldest son, secured a loan from the Pentagon, and whether Gulf states have sought leverage over Jared Kushner, Mr Trump’s son-in-law and foreign envoy, by investing billions in his private-equity fund. Democratic leaders also talk up plans for hearings on tariffs, Iran, the draconian immigration agenda and much else.
Democrats know full well that the administration will stonewall by asserting the right to keep certain communications confidential. So instead they will seek information from firms and people who have dealt with the White House. Mr Trump will try to shield those communications, too. In August the Office of Legal Counsel issued an advisory opinion outlining an expansive scope for “executive privilege”. Yet firms are not waiting to get right with the incoming majority. “We couldn’t even get an email returned from these guys for two years,” says a Democratic aide in the Senate. “Now they all want to let us know how they’re not MAGA.”
Democrats will seek to show that they are the party of clean government. Cue a raft of reform proposals. A ban on stock-trading by lawmakers may well pass. The rest are meant as messaging. Jamie Raskin, the incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee, wants to require pardon brokers to register under federal law, much like lobbyists representing foreign governments. He also wants to force Mr Trump to disgorge the luxury jet he received from Qatar. Robert Garcia, who will chair the House Oversight Committee, wants to stop bosses of federal contractors from donating to political campaigns or parties. He calls this closing the “Musk loophole”.
The risk for Democrats is that they get bogged down in futile attempts to boot Mr Trump from the White House. They have already impeached him twice. The party’s base and lawmakers in safe seats will demand a third attempt. Democrats in the House have introduced seven such resolutions in his second term. A recent one failed in a procedural vote, but not before gathering support from 70% of the Democratic caucus. People need to “understand the constitutional math”, says Mr Raskin, that is, the two-thirds majority required in the Senate to convict and remove a president. Mr Raskin was the lead House impeachment manager after Mr Trump tried to steal the 2020 election; he says the tool is no “panacea”. If any conduct were to get a president barred from office, that would have been it—and still the Senate let Mr Trump off the hook.
Mr Jeffries’s goal will be to maintain the majority in 2028, which means he will have to protect competitive seats held by moderates; targeting the president will not be a winning message in their districts. Democratic leadership will probably try to satisfy the base by impeaching cabinet officials instead. Pete Hegseth, the secretary of war, will probably be the first target, for waging war without congressional authorisation and ordering extrajudicial killings of alleged drug traffickers, among other things. Robert F. Kennedy junior, the health secretary, may be next, having presided over the worst measles outbreak in 35 years.
Election landslides often engender hubris, and Democrats are not immune. After a historic victory, the same voters who elected Democrats so resoundingly may soon accuse them either of timidity or overreach. Messrs Schumer and Jeffries have their work cut out.

epub_38.text:
The Democrats have won the biggest congressional landslide in 50 years
United States
| By the numbers
The Democrats have won the biggest congressional landslide in 50 years
Black, Hispanic and young voters helped power the party’s victory
Nov 5th 2026
GEORGE W. BUSH described his party’s midterm loss in 2006 as a “thumping”; Barack Obama called his setback four years later a “shellacking”. There may not be a sufficient superlative in the English language for the magnitude of the midterm defeat that Republicans suffered on November 3rd, but Donald Trump might call it “yuge”.
When The Economist went to press on November 5th, Democrats were expected to win the national popular vote for the House of Representatives by 13 percentage points, the largest congressional margin of victory for either party since 1976, in the wake of the Watergate scandal. They are on track to win around 260 of the 435 seats in the lower chamber, more than they obtained amid the financial crisis of 2008. The party has secured at least a 54-46 majority in the Senate, including victories in five states that Mr Trump won by double digits in 2024. Betting markets are nearly certain that it will win the two remaining uncalled races in Alaska and, shockingly, Mississippi, which backed Mr Trump by 23 points two years ago.
In state contests, Democrats comfortably unseated Republican governors in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, and are expected to claim another in Alaska. By winning state legislatures, too, they gained unified control of government in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, and are likely to do so in Arizona as well.
A wave this big washes up everywhere. In 343 of the 346 contested House districts with at least 80% of votes counted, Democrats won a higher share of the vote than they had in the 2024 presidential election. But the trend was most pronounced in the South, a repudiation of the notion that the region is particularly unresponsive to national trends, due to its high concentration of loyal Democratic black voters and loyal Republican white Evangelicals. Compared with 2024, Democrats gained two more points of margin in the region, on average, than the party did outside it. It was only the jaw-dropping Senate upsets in South Carolina and probably Mississippi that rendered the otherwise stunning wins elsewhere in the South look more ordinary: Democrats won North Carolina’s Senate race by 20 points and Georgia’s by 18, and came within two points of winning Louisiana’s. The party is likely to flip five or six House seats in North Carolina that had not been considered competitive.
The region’s Republican state legislators may well bear some responsibility for their party’s woes. After the Supreme Court earlier this year weakened an important provision of the Voting Rights Act, in Louisiana v Callais, lawmakers in Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee redrew their House maps to eliminate majority-black districts. That seems to have sparked a backlash. Turnout in a midterms election is always lower than in a presidential one. In Deep South states, however, the decline in turnout was smallest in counties where most voters are black, and largest in those with the fewest black residents. Outside this region, where the Supreme Court’s ruling did not prompt further redistricting, there was no such disparity.
Across the country, pre-election polls detected a “last in, first out” pattern to Republican support: the Hispanic, Asian and younger voters who had moved right from 2020 to 2024 said that they planned to abandon Republicans in 2026 in even greater numbers. District-level results and exit polls both show they kept their word. Democratic gains were largest in areas with big shares of residents who were foreign-born or of Mexican descent, and comparatively small in those with lots of older voters. Although Hispanic and Asian voters were much more likely to list prices or the economy as their most important issue, rather than immigration, it is little surprise that the party waging a sweeping deportation campaign suffered an unusually harsh electoral rebuke in the places where most immigrants live.
The scale of Democrats’ victory in the popular vote, along with the concentration of their gains in Republican-voting areas, also disproves the conventional wisdom that entrenched partisan polarisation gives modern parties a relatively high floor of support. Neither Barack Obama nor Bill Clinton, two popular Democratic presidents, ever won the White House or had their party win the House by such a big margin. According to the NORC Civic Health & Elections Project (CHEP), a large pre-election survey, Democrats managed to peel off a healthy slice of erstwhile Republican backers: 6.5% of respondents who said they voted for Mr Trump in 2024 supported a Democrat for the House this year, compared with just 2.8% of those who said they plumped for Kamala Harris in 2024 and opted for a Republican House candidate this time.
Democrats also enjoyed a strong advantage in turnout. In chep’s data just 7.6% of former Harris voters stayed home or supported third parties, compared with 12.2% of Mr Trump’s. And despite the overall decline in voter numbers from a presidential election to a midterm, fully 14% of this year’s electorate did not vote in 2024. CHEP estimates that Democrats won these new entrants by 22 points.
With victory of an almost unimaginable scale in hand, Democrats are already licking their chops in anticipation of the 2028 election cycle. If they secure the expected 56 seats in the Senate, where terms last for six years, they will be clear favourites to hold the upper chamber regardless of which party wins the presidency. If Democrats can manage a second consecutive wave election two years from now, as they did in 2006 and 2008, they could plausibly hope for a 60-vote supermajority that would enable them to pass legislation without Republican support.

A political revolution in Texas
United States
| Lone Star politics
A political revolution in Texas
What will Democrats do with control of America’s most iconic red state?
Nov 5th 2026
“EVERYTHING IS BIGGER in Texas, including the shock of this win,” Gina Hinojosa said in her victory speech on November 3rd. Though she had spent months telling voters that a Democrat could win the governorship, she clearly hadn’t believed it. At an election-night watch party for James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate, staffers refreshed early-voting results pages, wondering if
stellar numbers
were a glitch—pundits had reckoned he could win only narrowly. By midnight, bleary-eyed Texans in “Talafreako” shirts flooded downtown Austin cheering in disbelief: Democrats had swept Texas, claiming the Senate seat by a 12-point margin, replacing every Republican statewide official on the ballot, picking up one congressional seat and flipping the Texas House. Republicans had outspent them more than two to one. It was a stunning upset in what has been America’s biggest red state.
Democrats won back some Texans who had voted Republican in 2024. This year average margins of victory in four South Texas districts topped 20 points, as dismay over economic issues and immigration-enforcement tactics sent voters rushing back to Democrats. The party also, at last, convinced more longtime Republicans to try something new. Collin, Denton and Tarrant counties, Republican-leaning suburbs north of Dallas, all flipped. Democrats won four of the five congressional seats that
Texas Republicans
gerrymandered last year, ostensibly in their favour.
What will Texas Democrats do with their new power? Kendall Scudder, the state Democratic Party chairman, insists Texas Democrats are different from their national counterparts. “A lot of us really believe that the government should provide you with positive services, be fair to everybody and get the hell out of your lives,” he told The Economist the morning after the election. The task now, he added, is to “start dispelling these myths that they perpetuate through Fox News that we’re a bunch of tax-and-spend liberals, but instead be responsible stewards.” Asked whether the party would prioritise rolling back social policies, such as Texas’s strict abortion ban, he didn’t respond directly. Instead, he said he hopes Democrats in Washington can reverse the cuts of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, particularly to health care. Texas has the country’s highest rate of uninsured citizens; less money for rural health care is due to force hospital closures across the state.
Ms Hinojosa’s defeat of Greg Abbott, a three-term governor, was even more of a surprise than Democrats’ victories in Congress. Constraints on her power within the state remain. Her Trumpian campaign promise to send every Texas household a $1,500 cheque, dubbed the “corruption tax refund”, could cost the state $17bn and is unlikely to gain the support of the Republican-controlled state Senate. State agencies, university boards and policy commissions are staffed by some 2,500 bureaucrats, many of whom serve six-year terms and none of whom the governor can sack. Nor can Ms Hinojosa reshape the courts. Seven of the state’s nine Supreme Court justices were appointed by Mr Abbott.
Nevertheless, she plans to start dismantling many of Mr Abbott’s policies. She campaigned against data centres, which Mr Abbott initially welcomed, and wants to end “corporate welfare”, which businesses fear will mean ending tax breaks. Ms Hinojosa and Mr Talarico also fought bitterly against the state’s $1bn school-voucher scheme, which launched this autumn. Expect Ms Hinojosa to fire the Republican education commissioner and for Sarah Eckhardt, the new Democratic comptroller, to start scrutinising public funding for private schools.
The party’s other priorities include anti-corruption legislation and cutting property taxes; those levies rose by 86% during Mr Abbott’s tenure. Nathan Johnson, the incoming attorney-general, may join other blue states—still a surreal phrase—in suing the Trump administration. “After getting punched in the face for 30 years, it’s now time to get to work,” says Jason Sabo, a Democratic lobbyist in Austin. The immediate task for Democrats is staffing up. “We don’t have the muscle,” says Mr Scudder, who joked that he has suddenly realised he must plan an inauguration.
Democrats’ thrill at winning in Texas is tempered by the knowledge that this year was unusual. Dissatisfaction in Texas, as elsewhere, was extreme. Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee, was an abysmal candidate and Mr Abbott’s long tenure provided Democrats with an easy target at which to direct voters’ angst. Republican candidates and deep-pocketed donors are likely to attempt a broad, well-funded comeback. In the Lone Star State political realignment doesn’t happen overnight, says Cal Jillson of Southern Methodist University. “Even if Democrats don’t disappoint,” Mr Jillson explains, “Texas is not a blue state now.” The party will work hard to make it so.

The prairie fire behind the Democrats’ big win
United States
| Plains-speaking
The prairie fire behind the Democrats’ big win
Wins in Iowa and Kansas revived the left’s rural populism
Nov 5th 2026
WHILE RUNNING for governor of Iowa, Rob Sand, a Democrat and the state’s auditor, reprised a campaign slogan used by Iowa Democrats of an earlier era: “It’s time to rotate the crops.” Voters agreed. Iowans elected Mr Sand to be their first Democratic governor in 15 years. Democrats won a Senate seat and flipped three congressional districts in the Hawkeye State, too. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, the pastor of America’s largest United Methodist church, was the first Democratic senator elected by the state since 1932.
Mr Hamilton’s victory is the most stunning and idiosyncratic of these results. He had the challenge of competing in a state that Donald Trump had won by 16 points in 2024. He had the benefit, however, of possessing ample charisma in a race against an opponent lacking it. The Republican incumbent, Roger Marshall, a doctor, is a dismal campaigner. It didn’t help that he was plagued by reports that he sued his patients to collect medical debts.
Across Democrats’ victories on the Plains, a few common themes emerge. Mr Hamilton was buoyed by the unpopularity of Donald Trump’s war with Iran, as were Democrats everywhere and those in farm states in particular. The war has increased the price of petrol, diesel and fertiliser—all crucial inputs for farms. Sarah Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister who flipped a red district that contains liberal Des Moines and rural southern Iowa, yoked her Republican opponent to the president. One of her ads featured Mr Trump describing himself as “the best president for Iowa” and asking Iowans to re-elect the incumbent, Zach Nunn. That Mr Trump’s endorsement was used as an indictment of Mr Nunn reveals the extent of Iowans’ dissatisfaction with the man they have thrice backed in presidential campaigns.
Democrats in the Plains were also able to harness surging national populism and give it a distinctly local character. Agrarian populism spread through the Plains during the Gilded Age, and reared again during tough times for farmers in the 1930s and 1980s. Josh Turek, Iowa’s Democratic senator-elect, calls himself a “prairie populist”. Mr Sand, incensed that Iowa’s Republican legislature curtailed his powers as auditor, campaigned for more transparency and less corruption. Sam Forstag, a millennial firefighting paratrooper, looks likely to win a House seat in western Montana. He preached economic populism and the need to get money out of politics—ideas that could hold appeal in a red state once home to New Deal Democrats and a strong labour movement.
When pressed on policy, these candidates resemble Democrats in other states. Mr Turek denounces billionaires, wants to raise the minimum wage and reverse federal cuts to welfare. Yet they avoided alienating Republican voters by using distinctly post-partisan rhetoric and expressing discontent with the record of both major political parties. Mr Sand started his town halls by singing “America the Beautiful” and encouraging voters to clap for Republicans in attendance. Democrats in Middle America sometimes complain that their coastal strategists fall in love with rural candidates who seem straight out of “central casting”, without considering how authentic those candidates appear to actual rural Americans. In this cycle, Kansans and Iowans seemed to see themselves in the Democratic challengers.
That was not true for Dan Osborn, a populist independent who lost a Senate race in Nebraska. Unlike Messrs Turek and Hamilton, he seemed to have contempt for Trump voters. Leaked audio revealed him saying: “Billy Bob in fucking Red Cloud, Nebraska, who lives next door to the fucking Trump store as you pull into town, and is waving the Trump flag, all he knows is he’s on the winning team.”
This year’s victories on the Plains will bolster Democrats’ hopes that the region offers more opportunities.  Democrats have long bemoaned their loss of support in Iowa since the state helped launch Barack Obama to the presidency in 2008, then padded his win four years later. As the party prepares for a presidential contest two decades after Mr Obama’s first election, they hope that Iowa will offer promising terrain, as will its neighbours.

Hero or liability? The debate over Abdul El-Sayed
United States
| Moderates v Progressives
Hero or liability? The debate over Abdul El-Sayed
Michigan’s pugnacious populist wants to shake up the Democratic Party
Nov 5th 2026
“I tell my friends he’s like our generation’s JFK,” says Imran Aijazuddin, referring to his friend, Abdul El-Sayed. The mood at Dr El-Sayed’s election-night party is similarly exuberant. The pugnacious populist won the hard-fought Senate race in Michigan by seven points, exactly as he had predicted in May. He will be the first Muslim to serve in the upper chamber. And his victory gives the left wing of the Democratic Party a powerful new voice in Washington. Moderates, though, have a different take on the result.
Nearly everyone agrees that it was an exceptionally ugly and chaotic race. Donald Trump referred to Dr El-Sayed as a “jihadist”. Mike Rogers, his Republican opponent, falsely accused Dr El-Sayed of believing that America deserved the September 11th attacks. Then, in the final days of the race, Haley Stevens, his defeated rival in the Democratic primary, endorsed Mr Rogers. She had become increasingly angry about Dr El-Sayed’s confrontational style and fierce criticism of Israel.
Had Dr El-Sayed lost, moderate Democrats might have taken comfort in a setback for the insurgent left. The unwaveringly self-assured Dr El-Sayed has made little secret of his disdain for the party’s establishment. He has talked of backing primary challenges to Democrats with whom he disagrees, such as John Fetterman, a senator from Pennsylvania. “Ideally, you put one ogre on a pike and then everyone else gets the message,” he told donors.
Such combativeness appeals to progressives. Bernie Sanders, the democratic-socialist senator from Vermont, called Dr El-Sayed’s primary win “the most extraordinary victory…in modern American politics”, praising his defeat of the “Democratic establishment”. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive congresswoman, lauded his “agenda that speaks directly to working people”. Dr El-Sayed backs Medicare for all and universal free child care. In his victory speech, he declared that winning a Senate seat was never the goal. His ambition, rather, is to “transform our politics”.
Yet Dr El-Sayed’s victory was less impressive than his supporters suggest. His seven-point margin was modest compared with the scale of the Democrats’ national gains. His race was close enough that the hated Democratic establishment had to put plenty of money to work in Michigan to support him. Other Democrats won in deep-red territory, such as Kansas and South Carolina, while Dr El-Sayed merely retained a seat already held by his party.
Candidates in the mould of Dr El-Sayed underperformed elsewhere, too. Based on endorsements by leftist groups and opposition to Democratic Party leadership, we identified 32 such Congressional nominees before the election. Most ran in deep-blue districts. But among the eight who stood in places that Kamala Harris won by fewer than ten points in 2024, their average vote shares were 1.5 percentage points lower than you would expect based on past voting and demography.
That is unlikely to dim Dr El-Sayed’s zeal. The party’s comfortable Senate majority gives him plenty of room to snipe at its establishment—and to cement his status as a hero of the progressive left.

epub_42.title: Republicans are in for a brutal presidential contest
epub_42.text:
Republicans are in for a brutal presidential contest
United States
| Lexington
Republicans are in for a brutal presidential contest
And Democrats suddenly have a unifying agenda
Nov 5th 2026
If future HISTORIANS want to pinpoint the start of the campaign for the presidency in 2028, they might consider the moment late on election night of 2026 when Chris Christie, the once and probably future Republican presidential candidate, brought the hammer down on the vice-president, J.D. Vance.
As stunning results came in from Ohio, Mr Christie, serving as an analyst on ABC, zeroed in on the most vile act of the midterms: the choice by that state’s Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, to broadcast an advertisement in which the mother of his opponent, Amy Acton, called her a liar. Dr Acton had not seen her mother, Donna Arthur, in nearly 50 years, not since Ms Arthur fled with her husband after he was charged with raping his stepdaughter, Dr Acton, then 12.  When the ad drew criticism from some Republicans, Mr Vance said he was disgusted by their “whining” and praised Mr Ramaswamy’s “audacity”.
Mr Vance will be remembered for that embrace “more than anything else” from this campaign, Mr Christie predicted, as he helped make that so by recalling it on ABC. “He stood behind that ad!” Mr Christie expostulated. “A man who wrote a book on Catholicism stood behind that ad. It’s a disgrace.” Mr Christie later added that the Trump era was over and that, for voters, “character matters”. That was perhaps a rosy inference, one of many being made—including that gerrymandering can backfire and the richest man in the world cannot buy an election outcome—yet, like the others, one borne out by facts. Dr Acton thumped her opponent. She is the first woman elected to serve as governor of Ohio, and the first Democrat in 16 years.
This was, in all, a bad election outcome for Mr Vance. Despite repeated trips to his home state of Ohio, he also saw his old Senate seat there go to a Democrat, Sherrod Brown. Moreover, as the vice-president’s dabbling with profanity and innuendo on the campaign trail had already shown, the cruel, vulgar style of MAGA politics never really worked for anyone but Donald Trump, and even for him the act has worn thin. Worse, still, Americans have also repudiated the substance of Trumpism.
Mr Vance has laboured to position himself as Mr Trump’s heir. But he can expect brutal competition if he does, in the end, choose to run. He wants to ascribe Republicans’ defeat solely to the war on Iran, from which he has gingerly distanced himself. But, protean though he is, Republican challengers will not let him duck responsibility for the full Trump agenda. Some of those historians may instead date the start of the presidential campaign to November 2nd, when Ron DeSantis, Florida’s Republican governor, accused unnamed members of his party of “gaslighting” Americans by pretending the war had not raised costs, as well as “corporatism” and failures on artificial intelligence and big tech.
Republicans are paying the bill for their strong leader and his idiosyncratic agenda. In the campaign to come, they must battle over what their party stands for, if not trade wars on friend and foe, shooting wars in the Middle East, state capitalism, public debt, self-enrichment in office and unchecked executive power. By contrast, Democrats, who for two years have lacked a national leader or a coherent politics besides opposing Mr Trump, emerge from the midterms with a blueprint for unifying the party and winning nationally. In his eccentric, Republican-defeating way, Mr Trump even did the Democrats a favour on election day by appearing to take an issue that bitterly divides them off the table. He said he would stop $4bn in aid to Israel by the end of the year.
Success in the South and Midwest brings the Democrats a ballasting geographical diversity. To hold their gains, let alone build on them, they will have to appeal to the socially moderate voters—Latino, black and white—who made the victories possible. Candidates such as James Talarico and Josh Turek, senators-elect from Texas and Iowa, tapped into anger against both parties, talking up decency, bipartisanship and even, at times, Mr Trump.
They also embraced an economic populism that is the through-line for successful Democratic candidates from North Carolina to Michigan to Texas. One of the canniest and most ambitious Democrats, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, released a five-page memo on election day describing her campaigning for candidates from the centre to its left. The memo did not mention climate change or any social issues but touted her focus on “economic populism, confronting concentrated wealth and power, and revitalising American democracy”. Words such as “justice” and “equity” made no appearance.
That Democratic leaders are aware of the  danger of tying up Congress in futile impeachment proceedings may not prevent them from being dragged down that path. But this was also a bad midterm outcome for the party’s radical legislators, since its big House majority will deprive them of leverage. The priorities of the party’s precious new office-holders are to begin lowering prices by ending the war in Iran and to restore congressional authority over tariffs. Beyond that are such equally popular measures as banning stock-trading by members of Congress and reversing tax cuts for millionaires, a move Mr Trump has, in the past, suggested he could support. A veto would mean, for Democrats, a compelling campaign issue.
In fact, opportunities beckon for Mr Trump, too. He may yet have the chance to memorialise himself not just by “regrassing” the White House lawn, an achievement he celebrated the day before the election, but by, say, accomplishing landmark legislation to reform immigration. That would deprive Mr Vance and the Republican Party of a cherished campaign issue, illegal immigration. But Mr Trump would not care about that.

epub_44.title: El Salvador’s president thinks he can eliminate Haiti’s gangs
epub_44.text:
El Salvador’s president thinks he can eliminate Haiti’s gangs
The Americas
| Gangbusters
El Salvador’s president thinks he can eliminate Haiti’s gangs
Nayib Bukele has dispatched 2,000 troops to the island
Nov 5th 2026
President Nayib Bukele has gained fame around the world for making El Salvador safer—albeit in a deeply vexing way. Leaders from Latin America trek to see the mega-prison in which he has locked up thousands of men accused of being in gangs, often without due process. Even domestic critics acknowledge that his round-ups have improved everyday life for most people. But now Mr Bukele wants to go further. Since October 22nd he has deployed over 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers to gang-ridden Haiti. He has warned its gangs (in Haitian Creole) that he can “finish with you too”.
Haiti has slumped into appalling chaos since its last elected president, Jovenel Moïse, was assassinated in his bedroom in 2021. Gangs control most of the capital, Port-au-Prince, as well as some areas outside it. At least 16,000 Haitians have been killed during the anarchy; 1.5m have been displaced (see chart). Two years ago Mr Bukele boasted that he could sort the mess out.
A pretext emerged on October 18th when four Salvadoran aviation technicians serving in Haiti as part of a UN-backed “Gang Suppression Force” (GSF) were ambushed and disappeared. Although they are probably dead—bodies purported to be those of the Salvadorans were handed over for testing on October 24th—Mr Bukele says he is mounting a rescue mission. Few believe that finding lost comrades is his sole aim, given what he has said about Haiti before, and the number of men he has sent. The Salvadoran force in Haiti now outnumbers all the soldiers serving with the GSF, who are drawn from six countries including Chad and Guatemala.
Mr Bukele’s operation marks the largest deployment of foreign troops to a country in the Americas, outside the remit of a UN mission, in many years. Much about it is murky, not just the scale of his ambitions. In 2024, speculating on the possibility of intervening, Mr Bukele said he would need a resolution from the UN, along with Haiti’s consent, and for costs to be covered.
Only one of these preconditions is clearly in place. On October 28th, six days after Salvadoran troops started to arrive, Haiti’s government said it had authorised the deployment (the terms of the agreement are not public). The United States also appears to have given a nod. Donald Trump is reported to have told Mr Bukele, during a phone call, “You have to do what you have to do.” Some Salvadoran troops flew in on an American military plane. Countries including Colombia and Haiti’s neighbour, the Dominican Republic, have also pledged logistical support—citing their joint membership of the “Shield of the Americas”, a group of countries that have promised to work with Mr Trump to combat gangs in the region.
Mr Bukele says El Salvador is paying at least 90% of the operation’s expenses. But some doubt this can be true; they wonder if money from the United States is involved. Deploying 2,000 soldiers to a country with no infrastructure, where even the water will make you sick, is extremely expensive, says Adam Isacson of the Washington Office on Latin America, a think-tank in the United States.
The UN confirms the Salvadorans are not working within the remit of the GSF. (Mr Bukele reportedly promoted the general in charge of his contingent to three stars before dispatching him, perhaps so he outranked the two-star Mongolian general leading the UN team.) The deployment risks creating “confusion and challenges for co-ordinating operations and for determining accountability for any possible violations of international law”, says William O’Neill, the UN’s expert on human rights in Haiti. It could be the beginning of the end for the GSF, says Jake Johnston of the Centre for Economic and Policy Research, another Washington think-tank.
What might Mr Bukele achieve? “He may get some tweets out of this; videos of stuff that goes boom,” says Mr Isacson. A brief deployment may impress Salvadorans. But at least some people believe Mr Bukele could make Haiti safer in the long term. Luis Contreras, a Salvadoran security analyst, thinks the gangs are no match for soldiers. “Any army could do it,” though it might take a while, he says.
Haiti’s situation is so desperate (half the population of 12m suffer acute hunger) that many in the region welcome Mr Bukele having a go. Haitians have to be “pragmatic”, says Jean Walnard Dorneval, a former Haitian defence minister. “We cannot simply sit idly by for fear of collateral damage while gangs have been traumatising the population.” There is a chance that Mr Bukele’s iron-fist reputation may scare gang leaders into negotiating.
Yet the risks of getting bogged down are huge. Mr Bukele may underestimate Haiti’s problems: on October 29th he insisted that El Salvador “lived through a nightmare that was even more horrific than what the Haitian people are enduring right now”. Pacifying El Salvador required both tough law enforcement and negotiations with gangs. A large army, police force and a functioning administration were able to round up tens of thousands of men. In Haiti the gangs govern territory, levy taxes and hold military-grade weapons. Mr Bukele “does not know the terrain and tactical environment”, says Frank Mora, a former Pentagon official.
The worry, if Mr Bukele’s ambitions in Haiti turn out to be large, is of a scorched-earth strategy that kills a lot of civilians. Human-rights groups are already reporting increased casualties in the area where the Salvadorans went missing. The UN force in Haiti operates cautiously; its troops rarely leave their base. Many observers, including in the Trump administration, mock its weakness: they think Haiti’s agonies are being drawn out by a “bunch of ninnies and losers not willing to use enough force to show who is boss”, says Mr Johnston. Their certainty may soon be put to the test.

epub_45.title: André “Mad Dog” Janones is a hero of the Brazilian left
