André “Mad Dog” Janones is a hero of the Brazilian left
The Americas
| Brazil’s election
André “Mad Dog” Janones is a hero of the Brazilian left
Can politicians elsewhere in the world replicate his online campaigns?
Nov 5th 2026
The night he was re-elected as Brazil’s president, snatching victory from what seemed like sure defeat, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spoke to supporters in the streets of São Paulo. Lula, as the left-wing leader is known, gestured to a guest by his side. “I want to thank this comrade here, our general, who played a pivotal role in this campaign,” he told the crowds.
The man feted on October 25th was André Janones, a 42-year-old congressman for a small environmentalist party who some think was the architect of Lula’s surprise victory. He is the brains behind “Lula’s Army”—a channel on WhatsApp that acquired more than 10m followers in the three weeks before the run-off vote. Its success has made Mr Janones a cult hero on the Brazilian left. It has also caught the eye of leftist leaders around the world—including Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s prime minister, and Claudia Sheinbaum, Mexico’s president—who wonder if they can emulate his strategy in their own countries. “It’s replicable and I think it’s necessary,” Mr Janones tells The Economist. “In all honesty, I think this could be what sweeps the far right off the map.”
After Lula performed poorly in the first round of voting on October 4th, Mr Janones—a former lawyer whom colleagues dubbed “Mad Dog” for his scalding of right-wing candidates in advance of the elections in 2022—promised despairing left-wingers that if they followed his orders they could turn things around. At his request, Brazilians banged pots and pans when Lula’s rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, was interviewed on television. They flooded Instagram with images of themselves wearing Brazil’s national colours and making an “L” shape (a pro-Lula symbol) with their fingers. Mr Janones held late night livestreams on which he refused to speak until at least a million viewers had tuned in. “EVERYONE, URGENT! GET TAPPING, AND MAKE THIS VIDEO EXPLODE!” was a typical command.
Behind all this, says Mr Janones, lay a studied plan to game the algorithms that drive social networks. He ordered his followers to comment on and “like” pro-Lula posts before sharing them, to boost their engagement. He told his “army” not to respond to misinformation about their candidate, on the basis that any engagement could widen a post’s reach. Actions of the army were carefully co-ordinated. “When four million people posted the exact same photo at the exact same time, the algorithm interpreted it like a plane crash or a terrorist attack like 9/11 and blocked the reach of any other posts. That’s how we glitched the algorithm,” he says.
Lula’s Army was far from the only thing that helped swing the election. Having for weeks run an old-fashioned campaign, Lula himself began posting selfie-style videos online. In the weeks before the run-off, his government pushed through an amendment guaranteeing workers two days off a week, and forgave sole traders their federal tax debts. But Mr Janones’s channel “was a turnout machine”, says David Nemer at the University of Virginia, bringing out pro-Lula voters who had abstained in the first round. “It gave a campaign that had just proved it couldn’t talk to the internet a voice that could.”
WhatsApp groups inspired by Mr Janones’s effort are popping up around the world. Guides detailing his techniques are circulating online in French and Japanese. He has been invited to advise politicians in Colombia, Venezuela and the EU, among other places. The week after Brazil’s election he turned up in Argentina, where he met members of the Peronist opposition. And Mr Janones says he plans to continue mobilising Lula’s Army at home in order to press a conservative-dominated Congress to pass Lula’s bills.
The lawmaker has some reservations about his digital playbook. He says he felt uncomfortable encouraging people to ignore pro-Bolsonaro posts, rather than push back against them. But like many in the Brazilian left, he believes social media have long handed their opponents an advantage—and that the ends justify the means. “My strategy is a strategy of war.”

epub_46.title: Can the pope’s tour of Latin America win back disenchanted youth?
epub_46.text:
Can the pope’s tour of Latin America win back disenchanted youth?
The Americas
| Long time no see
Can the pope’s tour of Latin America win back disenchanted youth?
Feminism and mysticism are providing reasons to question the faith
Nov 5th 2026
Pope Leo’s tour of South America, beginning on November 6th, is a marathon. Over 12 days he is traveling some 31,000km, visiting Uruguay, Argentina and Peru and giving around 40 speeches. In some ways it is a homecoming: the pontiff spent two decades as a missionary in Peru. The roadshow, coming three weeks after the pope underwent surgery for lung cancer, will draw big crowds. A bigger question is whether it can help win back Latin America’s waning faithful. The region’s educated young, in particular, are gradually going off organised religion.
In the decade to 2020 the share of people around the world who say they do not identify with any organised religion—call them the “nones”—grew by a percentage point, to 24%. This shift may appear small, but behind it lies much change. Every religion other than Islam stagnated or shrank over that period, when taking population growth into account. The share of people who say they have no religious affiliation declined slightly in Asia and barely budged in Africa or the Middle East. But it soared in Europe and the Americas. And of the three countries where the share of “nones” grew the most, two (Chile and Uruguay) are in Latin America.
To see what this looks like on the ground, trek to Uruguay—the country in which Pope Leo is beginning his grand tour. Its constitution has long enforced an exceptionally strict division between church and state. Easter week, known as “Holy Week” in the rest of Latin America, is called “Tourism Week”. Christmas is dubbed “Family Day.” Not by chance, Uruguay legalised marijuana, gay marriage and abortion much earlier than its peers.
The share of Uruguayans who identify as Catholic has fallen by almost half since 1995, to 33%. Only 9% of Uruguayans say they practise the faith regularly. Many young people are unenthused by the pope’s visit, the first since 1988. “I just think: what a waste of money,” says Lucía Castillos, a 31-year-old caterer in Montevideo, the capital. “How much are we spending on this visit that we could be giving to people who have nothing to eat?”
Ms Castillos says her scepticism towards the church grew during a recent upswell of feminism all across Latin America. What began as mass rallies in Argentina in 2015 protesting against killings of women later swept into Chile and Mexico, where demonstrators also demanded access to abortion. “Catholicism springs from the premise that women are inherently flawed,” she believes. “That vision just doesn’t square with feminism.”
Some of Latin America’s new “nones” are unapologetic atheists. “To me, it all seems crazy,” says Virginia, a 29-year-old primary school teacher in Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina: “A dove impregnating a virgin, evangelical Christians speaking in tongues, Orthodox Jews dressed in wigs.” But the evidence suggests that many of these people are in fact swapping organised religion for a much looser kind of spiritualism.
Many of them tell pollsters they believe in esoteric things, such as “energies”. Syncretism and folksy superstition is common. Some Brazilian “nones” dabble in Candomblé and Umbanda, two traditions that combine Roman Catholicism with west African religious practices. Mexicans of all stripes celebrate the Day of the Dead, a Mesoamerican spin on All Souls’ Day. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, embodies this growing spiritual mish-mash. The libertarian has a strong interest in Judaism but has not denied rumours that he has also sought a medium’s help to speak to his dead dog.
Organised religion remains a powerful influence on the region’s politics, even if its grip on hearts is loosening. Recent years have seen increasingly vocal interventions in many countries by evangelical Protestant groups, and politicians are putting in much more effort to court them. Evangelicals were firm supporters of Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil’s president from 2019-23, and of his son Flávio who recently failed in his bid to win the same job.
The godless in Latin America remain more likely than those elsewhere to say that organised religion helps society, rather than harms it. The Catholic church is still the most trusted institution in Latin America, according to Latinobarómetro, a polling organisation, well ahead of outfits such as armies and the media. That reflects a history of (mostly) do-gooding, as well as the dim view many Latin Americans take of their secular institutions, such as legislatures and the courts. The result is that the pope’s words and actions on the road will be scoured for political subtext.
Some in Argentina hope that Leo’s four-day stop there could squeeze a touch more humility from Mr Milei—who is broadly succeeding in stabilising an economy in crisis but can be aggressively unsympathetic towards people affected by his policies. Before becoming president in 2023 Mr Milei had lambasted Leo’s predecessor, Francis. He called the late pontiff, who was Argentine, an “imbecile” and “the representative of the devil on earth,” though he later apologised. Pope Leo plans to visit a centre for disabled children. Argentine bishops have repeatedly expressed concern about the impact of Mr Milei’s cuts on the poor and sick.
The pope’s last stop, in Peru, ought to be much more straightforward. It remains one of the most devout countries in the region. And many Peruvians have warm memories of his years working in the country. Even in a rapidly secularising region, good deeds are infallibly popular.

Paraguay’s swaggering digital bank has fallen
The Americas
| Ueno no more
Paraguay’s swaggering digital bank has fallen
The president could be next
Nov 5th 2026
Editor’s note (November 5th): Shortly after this story was published Paraguay’s president, Santiago Peña, resigned.
Ueno Bank is ubiquitous in Paraguay. The bank sponsors stadiums, music festivals, the national football squad, a bar, and the country’s top racing driver. Its credit cards garner big cashbacks at supermarkets. Though it only received a full banking licence in 2023, the fintech startup now caters to 2.9m Paraguayans: almost two-thirds of the adult population. At craft fairs co-organised by the country’s first lady, glamorous Ueno promoters in tight jeans issue indigenous artisans with card readers.
For many Paraguayans, accustomed to keeping their cash under the mattress, Ueno helped them open their first bank account. Its branches offered touchscreens, frothy coffees and comfy sofas: a far cry from the awkward hours, staid decor, hefty deposit requirements and scowling security guards of competitors. Often likened to Monzo or Revolut, Ueno hoped to achieve a $1bn valuation and thus become Paraguay’s first unicorn.
That was until 3:23am on November 3rd, when the Banco Central del Paraguay (BCP, the central bank and banking regulator) seized control of Ueno and began to formally dissolve it. Police collared Ueno’s CEO, Miguel Vázquez, and took him to a high-security jail. Other executives from the bank were hooded and cuffed. They face charges including breach of trust, irregular book-keeping, and attempted fraud. Tearful depositors, frozen out of their savings, had to be held back from branches by the police. The BCP’s president Carlos Carvallo, himself Ueno’s boss until three years ago, resigned at the request of Paraguay’s president, Santiago Peña.
Protesters marched towards the presidential palace. The opposition said it was preparing to impeach Mr Peña, who until last year held shares in Ueno Holding, a related company. His vice-president, Pedro Alliana, also faces impeachment. In a video message, Mr Peña said that 98% of Ueno’s clients would get their money back through deposit insurance and that those responsible for the crisis would be punished: “The financial system is strong.”
Behind Ueno’s collapse lie a series of events that tarnished its youthful image. The bank’s share of government business has ballooned on Mr Peña’s watch. Around $850m of public money is now deposited with Ueno, including a tenth of the country’s public pensions funds. Itti, a sister company of the bank, handles reams of sensitive citizen data after winning more than a dozen state contracts. The president has “a direct responsibility” for the crisis, says Rafael Filizzola, a centre-left opposition senator. “This is a criminal conspiracy to use public funds in private businesses linked to Peña.” (Mr Peña has denied any wrongdoing.)
Also under scrutiny is fast-and-loose lending by Ueno itself. Last month it emerged that the bank had disbursed roughly $150m to small companies linked to its shareholders and employees, seemingly breaching regulatory rules and putting its own balance sheet at risk. Senators loyal to former president Horacio Cartes—whose family owns a different bank, and who has recently fallen out with Mr Peña—began to pile on pressure.
As the negative headlines multiplied and investors took fright, Ueno’s $350m bonds due in 2031, issued in March, lost around 12% of their value. Last week, the company announced a $100m recapitalisation. It was too little, too late. BCP officials said on Tuesday that Ueno’s solvency ratio has fallen below half the required minimum, and that its investigators had uncovered more irregularities.
“Uncertainty reigns,” says Esteban Caballero, a political analyst. The ruling Colorado Party controls both houses of Congress, but is split between supporters of the president and Mr Cartes, his former patron. A banking reserve fund has been authorised to reimburse Ueno’s clients up to the value of $38,000 within 15 days; lawmakers have voted to speed this up. Beyond that amount, the BCP will only offer “the greatest protection possible”. As for Ueno, another financial institution was recently rumoured to be negotiating over its acquisition. Some worry that biometric information Ueno gathered from its clients could be sold to the highest bidder. “This is sensitive data,” says Maricarmen Sequera of TEDIC, a digital-rights NGO.
Others fear the scandal could take the shine off South America’s star non-oil economy, which expanded by 6.6% in 2025. Unlike a crisis in 1995 that wiped out half of Paraguay’s banks, the broader financial system is safe, says Fernando Arriola, a former Wall Street banker and the director of Paraguay’s fintech chamber. But medium-sized companies that stored their cash with Ueno will suffer. “This will affect the market,” Mr Arriola adds, blaming regulators for being asleep at the wheel, Ueno for lending too generously to associates, and the president for failing to avoid perceptions of favouritism.
Mr Peña often calls Paraguay an “awakening giant”. If the sorry tale of Ueno is anything to go by, that colossus has feet of clay.

The latest Ebola outbreak could be the worst ever
Middle East & Africa
| Viral loads
The latest Ebola outbreak could be the worst ever
New cases in Kenya and Nigeria show that the outbreak is unchecked
Nov 5th 2026
“SANITISE,” says the security guard outside a school in Nairobi, gesturing towards a dispenser. Since Kenya reported its first-ever case of the Ebola virus last month many venues in its capital have made visitors disinfect their hands and get their temperatures checked. Officials tell people to avoid large gatherings. “I want to appeal to Kenyans going forward that we can also avoid handshakes or hugging,” said Patrick Amoth, the director-general at the health ministry. “We can just wave.”
The precautions reflect growing concern about the spread of an Ebola outbreak that emerged in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo this year. The Kenyan case involved a businessman who had been living in eastern Congo but returned home to Kenya via Uganda on October 3rd. He died two days later. Kenya has since reported eight more cases (and another death), all of them contacts of the first. On October 20th another of Africa’s largest economies, Nigeria, reported its first case of Ebola in a decade. A woman who had travelled to Uganda tested positive in Abuja, Nigeria’s capital.
Since the outbreak was officially declared in May there have been more than 10,500 confirmed cases of the gruesome and terrifying virus. Almost half (5,130) have so far resulted in death, with all but four of the fatalities in eastern Congo. Fewer than a quarter of new cases there occur in patients who are known contacts of previous cases, says Jean Kaseya, the director of Africa Cdc, a public-health body. So long as authorities are in the dark about the virus, the epidemic will keep growing.
Ebola spreads via direct contact with an infected person’s bodily fluids. Suspected patients must be tested and positive cases isolated. Direct contacts of patients should be identified and tested, too. Health workers need protective equipment to avoid falling sick themselves.
Attempting this in eastern Congo can be like trying to give someone a haircut with toy scissors in a house on fire. Health workers are few in number and poorly paid. Testing kits and isolation facilities are scarce. Bad roads make it difficult to reach patients and bring in supplies; so do the scores of militias that terrorise the region.
The long-suffering population has a deep lack of trust in the Congolese state. Many eastern Congolese believe Ebola is a fiction, concocted by venal bigwigs to embezzle donor funds. On October 24th a machete-wielding mob in eastern Congo killed a nurse whom they accused of spreading Ebola by contaminating water supplies. In September a politician from the ruling party was beaten to death after he went on the radio to urge people to take precautions against Ebola.
The worst Ebola outbreak on record happened between 2014 and 2016 in west Africa, where the UN’s World Health Organisation recorded at least 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths. Haphazard surveillance means it is hard to compare the current epidemic with the one that ended a decade ago. But this outbreak, which involves a rarer strain of Ebola known as Bundibugyo, seems to be spreading and killing more quickly. Mr Kaseya fears that on current trends it “will be the worst Ebola outbreak ever” within another year.
Given the scale of the outbreak in Congo, which has more shared borders than anywhere else in Africa, it is unsurprising that Ebola has been found in nearby countries. Though Uganda officially closed its border with Congo in May, it is a porous frontier. Kenya’s first Ebola patient crossed into Uganda from Congo last month before flying to Nairobi. He subsequently slipped through screening at the airport in Kenya undetected, despite showing symptoms of Ebola on his journey.
The Nigerian case is more troubling. Officials in Uganda claimed at first that the woman had visited eastern Congo. This seems false. She is thought to have been at Uganda’s main airport on the same day as Kenya’s first patient. But there is no evidence yet that they came into contact with one another. All of which raises questions about whether, despite Uganda’s denials, there are active cases in the country. “My biggest concern is that the source of the Nigerian patient’s infection remains unexplained,” says Ahmed Kalebi, a Kenyan pathologist.
Countries such as Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda have relatively strong health systems. They should be able to stop the virus from exploding as it has in Congo.
But there are still three concerns. The first is that Congo is a large country—with an ongoing war in the east involving M23, a Rwandan-backed force. There is a lot of room for further spread. The second is that Ebola could take off in the most fragile of Congo’s bordering states: Burundi, South Sudan and the Central African Republic. The third worry is that the longer the outbreak persists, the greater the secondary effects. In the west African outbreak thousands more babies and mothers died than would have otherwise been the case because of disruptions to health services. Doctors working in Congo say fewer children are being immunised and malaria is on the rise.
The good news is that there are efforts to find an effective vaccine against Bundibugyo. On October 23rd the first participants in clinical trials in eastern Congo received shots of Ervebo, a vaccine that protects against a more common strain. Scientists are also working on a bespoke jab. But it will be months, at best, before a proven vaccine is produced. For many people that will be far too late.

Hackers are exploiting Africa’s digital identities
Middle East & Africa
| Digital ghosts
Hackers are exploiting Africa’s digital identities
Governments are embracing new databases. So are criminals
Nov 5th 2026
EARLIER THIS year hackers targeted Senegal’s agency for issuing passports and identity cards. The attackers claim to have stolen sensitive data from the west African country, including biometric information and immigration records. The authorities told citizens that their data were safe. But some of the loot seemingly ended up on the dark web. It was not the only successful recent cyber-attack on the state. In May, criminals targeted the national treasury. Last year hackers demanded a ransom of $10m after breaching the tax authority.
Senegal is not alone. As African governments digitise government services and grow their national-identity databases, they are struggling to protect citizens’ data. Incidents such as the recent discovery of a vulnerability in PHP, a programming language commonly used by governments, show that the problem is not limited to Africa. But the continent has less money and talent to bolster its cyber-security. And as artificial intelligence (AI) expands attackers’ toolkits, African governments will urgently need to find ways to secure their systems.
Their problems often stem from efforts to improve public services. Of the 800m people worldwide who have no legal proof of who they are, more than half live in sub-Saharan Africa. Without a formal identity many find it impossible to join welfare programmes or health-insurance schemes, send children to school, own land, open bank accounts or activate sim cards. Countries like Uganda, where almost 80% of people have a digital ID, can now more easily track their people and close gaps in provision. (Around a decade ago fewer than 10% of Ugandans had some legal proof of their identities.) A digitally savvy state is better equipped to spot fraud, collect taxes and safeguard elections.
Yet governments are failing to secure the growing number of access points for hackers. That is mainly because there are not enough qualified people who can help them do it. Mastercard, the payments firm, reckons that Africa has 200,000 unfilled cyber-security jobs, equivalent to about a quarter of the current workforce. Banking and telecommunications firms snap up the few qualified engineers and security analysts. As ai accelerates, Africa’s skills gap is widening.
Money is another problem. According to a survey by Interpol, nearly all African members cited “resource constraints” as an obstacle to improving cyber-security. Protecting databases is expensive. Software is often installed and managed by foreign firms because there are too few qualified local engineers. Importing these services uses scarce foreign currency. Computers need reliable power, which many African grids do not provide.
Some countries are trying to bolster their defences. In Ghana, firms must report major breaches to the Cyber Security Authority within a day of spotting them or risk fines or the imprisonment of bosses. Kenya has an incident-response centre that regularly publishes reports on cyber threats. But other countries are lagging behind. Only 16 on the continent have ratified the African Union’s Malabo Convention, which is supposed to encourage pan-African digital standards.
In the short term, governments are trying to encourage citizens to be more careful. Ghana’s “Be cyber smart” campaign urges people to protect their passwords, avoid dodgy links and keep private information private. Rosemary Kisembo, who runs Uganda’s identity register, says that “people share more about themselves on Facebook” than with the government, a sign she takes as Ugandans’ lax approach to data security.
The gaps in funding and skills are difficult to close. Wide variation in connectivity, compute capacity and digital literacy among African countries hinders collaboration. But governments could do more to work together. Sharing intelligence about attacks could help them anticipate vulnerabilities. But weak supranational institutions—and national pride—have hampered efforts.
Some countries deny there is an issue. Nigeria’s identity-management body, for example, still claims that its database was not compromised, even though journalists have found national-identification numbers for sale on the black market since 2024. It is hard to solve the problem unless it is identified first.

America’s allies oppose more war in Iran. They may not get a say
Middle East & Africa
| Nervous neighbours
America’s allies oppose more war in Iran. They may not get a say
Economies are shrinking and a deal remains elusive
Nov 5th 2026
THE DIPLOMATS and military officers gathered last week for the Manama Dialogue, an annual talkfest in Bahrain’s capital, all had the same questions—and no answers. As they nibbled puff pastry at the Ritz-Carlton, their conversations invariably came back to Donald Trump’s threats to resume his war with Iran after the midterm elections. Would he do it, and when? Might the Iranians strike first?
There were almost no Americans on hand to ask: the Trump administration sent only a pair of mid-ranking officials, and both were tight-lipped. To some Gulf officials, the unusually small delegation seemed like a snub. “They could at least try to reassure us,” grumbled one.
Gulf states are reluctant to offer such blunt criticism in public, lest they antagonise the president. But they are unanimous that they do not want another round of fighting—unlike in February, when some were equivocal. This time even the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which has taken the most hawkish stance towards Iran, is urging Mr Trump not to strike. “We in the UAE don’t believe that a military solution is viable,” says Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president.
Behind the scenes, diplomats are scrambling to find a deal. Envoys from Qatar shuttling back and forth to Tehran have encountered two big obstacles, however. One is Mr Trump’s seeming insistence that a new agreement include at least some concessions related to Iran’s nuclear programme. The Iranians refuse to discuss it. Instead they are gloating at Mr Trump’s drubbing in the midterms.
The other is how to sequence an agreement. America and Iran both want to avoid a repeat of the memorandum of understanding, the vague agreement they signed in June and which collapsed within weeks. Each side wants the other to move first. Iran insists that America start by lifting its naval blockade and removing a range of sanctions. Only then will it reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The Americans fear Iran would simply rush to export a glut of stored oil, easing some pressure on its economy, then fail to take reciprocal steps.
Participants in Manama were split on how soon America might act if talks fail to yield a deal. Some suggested Mr Trump may wait several weeks. America is still building up its forces. It has also announced talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on November 10th, a curious thing to do if it were planning to imminently restart a war that would make Abu Dhabi a target.
Citizens and expats alike are nervous: the Gulf has not felt this tense since April, when Mr Trump was threatening to wipe out Iranian civilisation. Some residents are stocking up on food, water and cash. If the war resumes, “you might start to question, why do I stay here?” says Laith Alajlouni of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, a British think-tank.
Gulf states would be
less able to defend themselves
, having depleted their air-defence interceptors. They would also have smaller fiscal buffers to cushion the economic blow. Saudi Arabia had expected to run a deficit of 3.3% of GDP in 2026; it hit that mark by July and may now exceed 6%. Five of the six Gulf economies are expected to shrink this year. Three will see a double-digit contraction.
The IMF thinks the Gulf could bounce back quickly next year: its latest forecast pencils in 9.1% growth. But that depends on a lasting peace. Some big events are already being scaled back or postponed. The Asian Cup, a football tournament, was meant to start in Saudi Arabia in January. It has been booted to December 2027.
The region will also have fewer escape routes than it did last time. Saudi Arabia was relatively safe earlier this year: Iran attacked it less fiercely than most neighbouring countries. That let Bahrain’s national carrier shift operations to the kingdom. Planes landed in nearby Dammam, and buses carried passengers the rest of the way. Now, though, Dammam’s airport is being targeted by the Houthis, an Iran-backed militia in Yemen. Two people were killed there in a drone attack last month.
Since the midterm elections Mr Trump has sent mixed messages. He told one journalist that he might order a “heavy hit” and another that he was in no rush to do so. Rulers throughout the Gulf would like to believe the second one—but February taught them to beware.

Gulf states brace for war with Iran—again
Middle East & Africa
| Out of rounds
Gulf states brace for war with Iran—again
Their air defences are dangerously depleted
Nov 5th 2026
DRIVE ALONG Bahrain’s King Khalifa causeway into Manama, the capital, and the war damage to America’s main naval hub in the Gulf is apparent: destroyed communication antennae on one side; blackened buildings on the other. Gashes in high-rise  buildings  are boarded up.
Iran fired more than 700 missiles and attack drones at Bahrain at the height of the American-Israeli war on Iran between February 28th and April 8th. Most were intercepted but some inflicted real damage. Iran hit not only military targets but also a desalination plant, refineries and an aluminium factory. A similar trauma was felt elsewhere in the Gulf (see map).
Now a second round of the war looms. To the east, the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group is sailing to join two others in the Arabian Sea. To the west, an American airlift is ferrying military equipment to bases in Israel and Jordan, including more Patriot air-defence batteries. American strikes against Iranian anti-aircraft missiles on Qeshm island this week were seemingly provoked by threats to American drones and jets, but may also serve to prepare the battlefield.
Gulf states fear that President Donald Trump may lash out abroad after
being wounded in the midterm elections
at home (see Briefing). They also expect to be the target of Iran’s wrath, as it threatens to respond “without geographical limitations”.
Stocks of Western missile interceptors are
severely depleted worldwide.
Ukrainian and other systems may help Gulf states reduce the threat from drones,  though these are improving fast. Israeli intelligence officials, meanwhile, express surprise at the speed of Iran’s build-up of missile stocks since the ceasefire.
After weeks of air strikes during Israel’s and America’s  Operation Epic Fury, many question what can be achieved by more bombing—“a little Epic Fury”, as Mr Trump called it. The pair probably struck all the easy targets and the main nuclear sites at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan were previously bombed in 2025, burying some 400kg of highly enriched uranium.
What remains are mostly hard-to-reach places, such as underground “missile cities” that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has been showing off on television. Entrances to such facilities were bombed in the first round but many seem to have been excavated since. American stocks of the biggest bunker-buster bombs appear to be running low.
Much attention focuses on mysterious work at “Pickaxe Mountain”, possibly another nuclear facility. It is buried so deep in granite that it may be beyond the reach of conventional bombs (raising unsubstantiated claims that Mr Trump might use a nuclear weapon against it).  Officials in the United Arab Emirates (uae) say they are “braced for the worst”, and vow to defend their country.
The uae endured the heaviest Iranian fire in the war, facing a total of more than 2,800 Iranian missiles and drones, perhaps because of its close ties with Israel. But it also boasts the region’s most powerful air defences with overlapping layers of  interceptors, supplemented by guns on attack helicopters, home-made electronic-warfare gear and perhaps Israeli laser weapons. Saudi Arabia will find it harder to defend its territory, given its larger size and sprawling infrastructure. It also faces threats from both Iran and its Yemeni ally, the Houthi militia
.
As America pulls forces and equipment farther from Iran—mainly to Israel and Jordan—the future of its bases in the Gulf is open to question. Increasingly, Gulf leaders are looking for protection elsewhere. Saudi Arabia, for instance, has signed the Mecca pact with Pakistan and Turkey, which have deployed or are thinking of sending  forces. What they would do in an actual war remains to be seen.
Deeper integration among Gulf countries would help—not least in setting up joint air defences. But ever-bickering Gulf states have mainly sought national or bilateral security deals rather than collective ones. Gulf states' ability to stand together against the Iran challenge, admit Emirati officials, “has proven hollow”.

epub_53.title: How the Houthis built their war machine
epub_53.text:
How the Houthis built their war machine
Middle East & Africa
| Extreme DIY
How the Houthis built their war machine
The rebels in Yemen are outgrowing their dependence on their patron
Nov 5th 2026
ALI AL-WAZIR is no ordinary businessman. The 47-year-old Yemeni, who is known as “Prince”, plies his trade in Guangzhou in southern China. The bustling port is about 7,000km (4,500 miles) from Yemen. But distance has not prevented Mr Wazir from playing a part in his country’s long civil war. In 2024 he was accused of supplying the Houthis, the Iran-backed rebels that rule much of Yemen, with materials to help them build weapons. America’s Treasury placed him under sanctions. Last year it blacklisted several more Houthi-linked traders for doing the same.
Once dismissed as ragtag insurgents—rebels in flipflops—the Houthis are now
one of the most dangerous militias
in the Middle East. Since they took control of northern Yemen more than a decade ago, they have built up a formidable arsenal of drones and missiles—aided, in part, by the likes of Mr Wazir. The Houthis’ smuggling networks stretch from the Horn of Africa to China. In recent weeks they have hit Saudi Arabia, which supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government, with one strike after another. At a summit in Tehran last week
Saudi Arabia put pressure on Iran
to rein in the Houthis but the region is preparing for more war.
The Houthis first got their hands on serious kit in 2014 after they seized Sana’a, Yemen’s capital. A short-lived alliance with Ali Abdullah Saleh, a former president, and his loyalists in the army gave them access to Soviet-style Scud and Tochka missiles. At the same time Iran, which was cultivating the Houthis (also Shia) as part of its “axis of resistance”, increased its support. When Saudi forces intervened in Yemen in 2015, Iran supplied the rebels with ballistic missiles, drones and other heavy weapons. Iranian advisers and operatives from Hizbullah, a militia in Lebanon, taught them how to use them.
Today the Houthis are developing a war machine of their own. On September 21st Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, their leader, boasted that they now build their weapons “from scratch”. That may be bluster but analysts are increasingly convinced that much of the rebels’ arsenal is built inside Yemen. “The speed and ambition of the Houthis’ military production has surprised a lot of observers,” says Fabian Hinz of Conflict Armaments Research (CAR), which tracks the illicit arms trade. While most of the group’s weapons are still based on Iranian designs, some—such as medium-range drones—can be built largely without Iranian parts.
Production mostly happens out of sight, in caves in the Yemeni highlands, making it hard to monitor. Data from The Century Foundation, a think-tank in New York, nevertheless point to a shift in their activities (see chart). During the 2010s most of the shipments that were seized going into Houthi territory contained ready-to-use weapons, such as guns and rockets. Iran was by far the biggest supplier in the mid-2010s. Now most of these consignments contain parts to build weapons, such as motors, wiring and propellers. China has overtaken Iran as the biggest source of such goods.
Lots of these items are “dual-use”, meaning they plausibly have civilian as well as military applications. Houthi smugglers sometimes try to outfox Yemeni authorities by slapping innocuous labels such as “industrial equipment” on drone kits. Other goods seem purpose-made for the arms industry. In October CAR suggested that parts for an Iranian-designed ballistic missile, seized in the government-held port of Aden, were made to order by a Chinese company. Saudi officials have complained to China, to little avail. “China is happy to turn a blind eye to its citizens participating in trade that supports the Houthis’ weapons industry,” says a Western diplomat.
Breaking this supply chain will be hard. American sanctions have achieved little: Houthi businessmen continue to operate in China. The rebels have been under a United Nations’ arms embargo for more than a decade. But the mission that inspects cargo ships sailing to Houthi-held ports is feeble. It reports dodgy vessels to the Saudis and their allies, but has no powers to stop them itself.
Even if it could, much would slip through. Some goods travel overland through the United Arab Emirates and Oman. Others are smuggled via Djibouti and Somalia. Tim Lenderking, America’s envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2025, says the Houthis move contraband “from big boats, onto small boats, onto tiny boats, onto pack animals and onto people’s backs”. Smugglers hide ammunition in lorries carrying fruit and vegetables. Yemen’s government—a patchwork of squabbling groups—struggles to co-ordinate enforcement. “Different operation rooms are controlled by different factions,” says Baraa Shiban of the Royal United Services Institute, a think-tank in London. “It’s a nightmare.”
Making their own arms helps the Houthis keep fighting when supplies from Iran are disrupted. But the Islamic Republic also benefits from their self-reliance. Under its doctrine of “mosaic defence”, Iran’s regime has tried to make different parts of its armed forces capable of fighting independently. A similar idea underpins its axis of resistance. “Iran has made efforts to enable its allies to produce locally,” says Mr Hinz. Hizbullah has built drones and tried to convert rockets into precision-guided missiles by itself. But the militia has been weakened by Israeli attacks and disruption to its smuggling routes through Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad.
The Houthis are in a better position. While the rebels still get plenty of weapons and intelligence from Iran, they are outgrowing their dependence on the regime. That may explain why the
Houthis are unbowed
even as the war launched by America and Israel has weakened their patron. The rebels see themselves as more than a mere Iranian proxy but as the real rulers of Yemen. They have sought support from Russia and are fostering connections with armed groups in Africa. The Houthis want to be a “little Iran in their own little neighbourhood,” says Barbara Leaf, a former American diplomat. Their ambition, as well as their firepower, is growing.

epub_55.title: War-battered Ukraine risks a demographic collapse
epub_55.text:
War-battered Ukraine risks a demographic collapse
Europe
| No babies, boom
War-battered Ukraine risks a demographic collapse
Birth rates are plunging and Russia is celebrating
Nov 5th 2026
Alyona’s waters broke in her hometown of Kramatorsk, 10km from the front line. The city has no functioning maternity ward, so an ambulance took her to Sloviansk, a short drive under a canopy of anti-drone netting. Complications then forced her to make an hours-long trip to Kharkiv, where on October 8th she gave birth to a son. That hospital had its dangers too: during air raids mothers and newborns are rushed to a bunker. But it was safer than Kramatorsk, where on the same day a Russian bomb killed 30 people.
Alyona is one of the few. Births in Ukraine are falling, in part because there are fewer adults. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 the population inside government-controlled territory has fallen from about 37m to 27m-28m (see chart 1). Around 3m-5m Ukrainians now live under Russian occupation, and millions more have emigrated. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, puts combat deaths at over 50,000; an independent estimate is closer to 150,000. Thousands of civilians have been killed, and Russia has deported over 20,000 children to Russify them.
Wartime, moreover, is not good for starting families. The fertility rate has dropped from 1.2 children per woman in 2020 to 0.8-0.9, lower than any big country but South Korea. The replacement rate, needed to keep the population stable, is 2.1. In the first half of 2026 deaths outnumbered births by more than three to one.
Ukraine’s birth rate has lagged behind the mortality rate every year since independence in 1991, when the country (including Crimea and Donbas) had about 52m inhabitants. The war has turned that gap into a chasm. Russia’s population is getting smaller too, but Ukraine’s predicament is far worse. For a country under attack by its imperial neighbour, a demographic collapse is an existential worry (see chart 2).
The refugee exodus accounts for the largest decline. Over 5m Ukrainians live abroad, mostly in Europe. Russia’s redoubled drone and missile attacks this winter could drive thousands more to leave. Worse, fewer refugees now say they plan to come home. The share has fallen from 74% in late 2022 to 43%, according to the Centre for Economic Strategy (ces) in Kyiv. Most refugees are children and women under 44, compounding the damage. “We are also losing our future,” says Ella Libanova, director of the Mykhaylo Ptoukha Institute for Demography in Kyiv.
At home, mobilisation, combat casualties and wartime uncertainty are shrinking the pool of prospective fathers and mothers. Most Ukrainian couples are putting off childbearing, says Svetlana Aksyonova, another demographer, adding: “The longer you postpone having children, the greater the risk the child will never be born.”
Ukraine’s exemption of men under 25 from conscription was intended to cushion the demographic decline. But hundreds of thousands of young men have gone abroad; since August 2025 Ukraine has allowed men under 23 to do so. Many who remain have no intention of starting a family.
Recent projections see at best a slower decline—assuming the war ends within a few years. The generation born in the 1990s and 2000s is Ukraine’s smallest in modern history, so it cannot expect a post-war “baby boom”, says Olga Dukhnich of the Frontier Institute, a Ukrainian think-tank. The government’s demographic strategy, adopted two years ago, envisaged a slight population rebound by 2030. But it also envisaged peace in 2026 and returning to 1991 borders, which no longer looks possible.
A more realistic scenario from the United Nations projects an annual decline of 0.7-0.9% for the next couple of decades. That would leave Ukraine with about 25m people in 2040, assuming no recovery of occupied territory. If war stretches into the 2030s it would exacerbate the crisis, leading millions born in the 1990s to forgo having kids altogether. The fertility rate could go as low as 0.6 children per woman, says Ms Aksyonova, with most births in the country’s safer west. Frontline areas would be on a path towards depopulation.
To slow the decline, Ukraine is offering incentives. A new law pays parents 50,000 hryvnia ($1,100) per newborn, plus 7,000 hryvnia per month for the first year. Other programmes help pay for child care. Since 2024 Ukraine has covered infertility treatment for women. Soldiers can freeze their eggs or sperm free of charge. Yet subsidies have a limited effect on birth rates even in peacetime, experts say, let alone in war. “How can you encourage having children in such conditions?” asks Ms Libanova.
Russia is celebrating Ukraine’s decline. “This is not just a crisis,” Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said in May, “but evidence of the biological death of a nation.” Anton Kobyakov, an adviser to Vladimir Putin, advocates settling Russians in Ukraine as Catherine the Great did in the 18th century. “All that remains [for Ukraine] is extinction, and only Russia can save the country,” he said in September. That is nonsense; Ukraine can survive as a smaller country. But such remarks suggest Russia is starting to view depopulation as a war objective.
When the war finally ends, immigration could help. Ukraine’s economy is already starved of workers. The country faces a labour shortage of 2.5m people, says the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. Only about 9,500 migrant workers are registered in Ukraine, and companies keen to hire foreigners complain of bureaucratic obstacles. But the government prefers to seek new workers at home, among women, war veterans and displaced persons.
That is difficult. Veterans struggle to find work, and though wartime data are unavailable, experts think female labour participation has not risen much. Limited child care appears to be the main barrier. Still, immigration is seen as a last resort. Ukraine would open up to foreign workers “only after we fully explore the potential” of Ukrainians at home and abroad, says Dariia Marchak, the deputy economy minister. But there will be too few of them to rebuild the country after the war, says Hlib Vyshlinsky of CES. “I’m a hundred percent sure Ukraine will need foreign workers.”
Some Ukrainians are defying the obstacles to having children. Daria, strolling with her boyfriend in a park in central Kharkiv, says she has just moved to the city from Odessa to start a family. (Her boyfriend looks both touched and surprised to hear it.) Others are going to greater lengths. Liudmyla, a soldier in her late 30s near Dnipro, in eastern Ukraine, says she started freezing her eggs last year. Before the war she dreamed of two children, but now she wants three. “One for the dead,” she says, paraphrasing Taras Shevchenko, Ukraine’s national poet, “one for the living, and one for the yet to be born.”

epub_56.title: The leftists who want to seize Berlin’s apartments
epub_56.text:
The leftists who want to seize Berlin’s apartments
Europe
| The means of habitation
The leftists who want to seize Berlin’s apartments
Die Linke’s radicalism makes it hard for it to form a coalition
Nov 5th 2026
FORMING COALITIONS in Germany is usually a pedestrian affair. Not in Berlin. On September 20th Die Linke, a populist-left outfit, won an election in the capital, one of Germany’s three city-states. But its attempt to build a leftist coalition with the Greens and Social Democrats has been hindered by scandal and strife. Conservatives say Die Linke is riddled with antisemites and pals around with terrorist-coddlers. Hardliners in the party rage against their leaders for conceding to Zionist principles. Senior Social Democrats are urging their comrades in Berlin to pull the plug.
Undeterred, the three parties began negotiating a coalition deal on November 2nd. Its centrepiece will be one of the most radical expropriation plans ever proposed in western Europe: Die Linke’s signature policy to “socialise”, in the preferred lingo, the rental properties of big corporate landlords. “Housing is a human right. And we want to take that right out of the hands of speculators,” said Elif Eralp, Die Linke’s mayoral candidate, before the election.
The idea dates to a referendum held in 2021, after years of surging rents in the once-cheap capital (see chart). Only around 15% of Berliners own their homes, and a clear majority backed a plan to seize properties of corporations that own over 3,000 units, with compensation. The city government kicked it into the long grass. But the idea persisted, and last year the campaigners behind the 2021 initiative wrote a draft bill that could inspire the law to come. Die Linke placed the idea at the heart of its election campaign.
The three notional governing partners have agreed to lift the threshold at which socialisation kicks in to 10,000 units. That means roughly 160,000, or 15%, of Berlin’s private rental homes would be taken into public hands (nearly 130,000 of these belong to Vonovia, Europe’s biggest corporate landlord). Compensation would be capped at €16bn ($18bn). Rental payments in the expropriated flats could service the loans the city or its housing companies incur to finance the compensation. Details will be worked out in coalition talks.
The proposal is all the more ambitious for resting on a never-used article in the German constitution which says “Land, natural resources and means of production…may be transferred to public ownership or other forms of public enterprise.” For decades this clause was ignored as a relic from a time when the young federal republic had not yet committed to market principles. But then the expropriation campaigners latched on to it.
Most economists are deeply sceptical about the proposal. It would do nothing to inspire new construction, though the parties have separately pledged to build 100,000 homes. It would also protect existing tenants, many of whom are not in need, while doing little for newcomers or outsiders. Indeed it is likely to have a chilling effect on construction in the city, says Michael Voigtländer at the  German Economic Institute in Cologne.
And investors are horrified. German ministers have been peppered with questions from foreign firms and politicians worried that investment is no longer safe in Germany. Friedrich Merz, the conservative chancellor, has promised to pass a national law to forestall Berlin’s scheme: a striking intervention in state affairs by the federal government.
Opinions differ fiercely on whether that is possible. Mr Merz’s proposal “is so obviously unlawful that it might not even need to be challenged in court”, says Niklas Schenker, a Die Linke member of the Berlin parliament and one of the brains behind the initiative. But opponents say a well-crafted law to protect private investments is perfectly plausible—and that the expropriation proposal itself violates the well-tested legal principle of proportionality. Germany’s constitutional court, in Karlsruhe, is likely to have the final say.
A second hurdle for the plan is working out how to compensate landlords. Mr Voigtländer puts the full market value at around €25bn. But German law does not mandate compensation at full market value, says Isabel Feichtner, a legal scholar at the University of Würzburg. The draft bill suggested that Vonovia and the others could expect to get 40-60% of market value; its proponents say landlords should not profit from land-value appreciation. But Karlsruhe may take a different view.
The court could also frown on the period of repayment: the draft bill proposed 100-year bonds. Berlin cannot afford to further burden its state budget, and borrowing costs are rising. Put it all together, and it is hard to imagine Berlin’s plan bearing fruit. That will not stop it from consuming political energy, deterring investment and harming Germany’s reputation.

epub_57.title: Will Poland’s war over the rule of law ever end?
epub_57.text:
Will Poland’s war over the rule of law ever end?
Europe
| Quagmire
Will Poland’s war over the rule of law ever end?
Liberals and populists are locked in an eternal struggle over the courts
Nov 5th 2026
The scene outside Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal on November 3rd, as the court met to approve its draft budget, was unusually rambunctious. Hundreds of right-wing protesters gathered around a stage flanked by Polish flags and a large picture of the Virgin Mary. Speakers hurled abuse at the European Union; at Donald Tusk, Poland’s prime minister; and at the “usurpers” of the court—that is, the judges, appointed by parliament, whom Mr Tusk had helped to take their seats, despite obstruction by his populist-right opponents.
The latest episode in the sorry saga of Poland’s top court began on October 30th, when the judges marched into the court to assume their duties while police sealed the area. Approved by parliament between March and September, they had until then been blocked by the court’s president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, both aligned with the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. Mr Nawrocki is by law required to attend justices’ swearing-in ceremonies, but he had refused, giving Mr Swieczkowski an excuse to claim they were not legitimate.
One of the new justices, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, promptly announced she was suspending Mr Swieczkowski for a month and taking his place. Protesters and opposition leaders gathered outside, calling it a coup. Mr Nawrocki cut short a trip to Senegal in mid-air, flew back to Warsaw and forced his way into the building. By November 3rd the situation had calmed and the budget meeting went ahead, but judges named by the previous PiS-led government boycotted it.
The struggle over the court goes back to 2015, when Mr Nawrocki’s predecessor, also a PiS ally, refused to swear in three judges chosen by the outgoing parliament. The new PiS government then packed the court with its own partisans. That led to years of wrangling in European courts, and the EU blocked billions of euros in funds. Since Mr Tusk and his Civic Coalition (KO) returned to power in 2023, parliament has picked eight judges to fill vacancies. Mr Nawrocki refuses to swear in five of them.
Four former presidents of the tribunal have defended Mr Tusk’s move. The European Commission, agreeing with opinions issued by European legal bodies, said the right to appoint the judges lay with parliament. But Ms Korwin-Piotrowska’s case for suspending the court’s president is shakier. Marcin Wiacek, a former national ombudsman, says he has “serious doubts” about its legality: it creates “a weapon any future government could wield”.
Officials say there was no other way to break the deadlock. “Swieczkowski’s strategy was to hold the court hostage,” says Dariusz Mazur, the deputy justice minister. On October 31st Mr Tusk said that there can be “no compromise” in
restoring the rule of law
. But the suspensions are sure to be challenged in Polish courts, and could then reach European ones.
After a decade of lawfare, the court’s credibility is shot. In late 2025 the EU’s top court ruled that it no longer met the requirements of an independent tribunal. Fought over by two camps, one headed by the president, the other by the prime minister, the court has become a political trophy. The tug-of-war will probably continue until parliamentary elections, scheduled next year. In trying to undo the knot entangling the court, Mr Tusk has tightened it further. Mr Nawrocki, meanwhile, can simply play for time. PiS may return to power in 2027 in a coalition with even more extreme populist parties, and try to oust the new justices.
Many Poles care little for either side’s legal arguments, and ask only for a functional court. They are helpless, frustrated bystanders. Some analysts and legal scholars believe that only a complete “reset” can salvage the tribunal. That would require a political compromise between PiS and KO, as well as constitutional changes.
Yet the two sides are less interested in fixing the court than in controlling it and scoring points ahead of elections. “Each one is out to consolidate and mobilise its core supporters,” says Anna Materska-Sosnowska, a political scientist. “Neither is prepared to back down.”

epub_58.title: France’s unhappy countryside turns to the populist right
epub_58.text:
France’s unhappy countryside turns to the populist right
Europe
| Fermenting discontent
France’s unhappy countryside turns to the populist right
In long-suffering villages, Marine Le Pen has come to stand for hope
Nov 5th 2026
Across the Gironde estuary from the chateaux of Haut-Médoc lie the less fashionable farmlands of the region around Bordeaux. They have been triply battered of late: by extreme heat, higher energy costs and a global decline in the drinking of everyday wine. Many farmers have given up. Blackened piles of vines lie in fields ready to be burned. This year 1,095 winegrowers in the Gironde have ripped out 7,825 hectares (19,336 acres) of vines. Over a quarter of the region’s vineyards have been destroyed since 2023.
In the city of Bordeaux, rioters have set barricades ablaze in recent weeks. But here in the countryside France’s discontent is quieter and less visible. In the town of Blaye, pupils blockaded their secondary school, but it passed off calmly; on a weekday after school teenagers can be found playing cards at pavement tables in the Bar des Sports. The feeling is distress rather than rage. Locals are sceptical about the future and worried about the cost of filling the tank in a place where a car is essential, and think the government is doing nothing to help. “I’m sad, not angry,” says a vineyard owner, who is packing it in after 30 years due to the collapse of exports to China and of wine-drinking in France, adding: “We have a president who doesn’t listen.”
For decades rural Gironde tilted to the left, while the centre-right ruled in the prosperous city of Bordeaux. For 20 years the parliamentary constituency around Blaye was held by a Socialist, before swinging to the centrist party of President Emmanuel Macron in 2017. At parliamentary elections in 2022, however, the seat was captured by Edwige Diaz of Marine Le Pen’s populist-right National Rally (RN). Two years later she was re-elected in the first round, with 53% of the vote. In September the 39-year-old Ms Diaz, whose grandfather was a Spanish Communist, was elected to the Senate.
“We are permanently campaigning here,” says Ms Diaz. “All year round we are at the markets, people see us, they know us.” She has driven herself to a small village for the retirement party of a local gendarme. At the wine bar opposite the church she meticulously greets customers one by one. The RN’s support now comes not only from farm labourers and the working class but from shopkeepers, pharmacists and other traders. At legislative elections in 2024 the party was the most popular countrywide among working-class voters (57% of whom backed it) as well as white-collar employees (44%). “The left has become more radical and defends Gaza more than farmers,” declares Ms Diaz. “People also know they have nothing left to hope for from Emmanuel Macron or his dauphins. Next to that, Marine Le Pen’s discourse is serious and reassuring.”
Once a champion of the politics of indignation, Ms Le Pen has begun to leave the fury to the populist-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his Unsubmissive France (LFI) party. These days the RN leader is making a pitch, however improbably, as the candidate of comfort and promise. At her big campaign speech in the city of Orléans on October 25th, she dressed in a powder-pink jacket and spoke about “beauty” and “hope”.
A local focus on improving daily life has enabled the RN to put down roots in unlikely places. The village of Saint-Savin has seen better days; two of its tattoo parlours are boarded up. For 12 years the village was run by the left, but in March for the first time voters elected an RN mayor, Frédérique Joint. She has turned the street lighting back on at night. In October the village held a three-day fête, complete with a torchlit procession from the church, soapbox-racing through the streets, a DJ and la country dancing. “With the loss of the vineyards, we’re losing our terroir, our savoir-faire, our traditions,” says Ms Joint. Local budgets are squeezed by higher prices in the supermarket and at the pump. “People have a need to get together at festive feel-good events.”
There is plenty of red-meat identity politics at play, too, in places like this, with local candidates appealing to Christianity and the preservation of tradition. But the populists’ turn towards mundane governance issues offers some hope in hard times, and is part of a broader normalisation. “We are witnessing a major shift,” wrote Luc Rouban, a political scientist at Sciences Po university, in a recent research note, “with LFI taking the RN’s place on the fringes…LFI frightens moderate left-wing voters far more than the RN frightens moderate right-wing voters.”
In some ways France’s anxious, bitter mood is perplexing. The country provides its citizens with an unusually protective cradle-to-grave welfare state. Public social spending, at 32% of GDP, is higher than in any other European Union country but Finland. The French on average retire earlier and live longer as pensioners than most of their neighbours.
Yet something has broken in voters’ trust in government and in their faith in the social contract. Confidence in mainstream politics is collapsing. Just 16% of all respondents told a poll in October that Mr Macron is a good president, a record low since he was elected in 2017. In another, 81% held the government responsible for the recent violence. Consumer confidence has fallen to its lowest for 13 years. After a decade in office Mr Macron and the centrist politics he ushered in no longer represent promise, but disappointment. One winegrower in the Gironde says simply that he feels “defeated”. Such distress is shifting the balance of hope to the RN.

epub_60.title: Andy Burnham promises three foreign-policy overhauls
epub_60.text:
Andy Burnham promises three foreign-policy overhauls
Britain
| Politics
Andy Burnham promises three foreign-policy overhauls
He speaks to The Economist. In Antigua, of all places
Nov 5th 2026
Andy Burnham was a foreign-policy novice when he became Britain’s prime minister in July. His 30-year political career has been occupied almost entirely with domestic affairs, and he has seemed content with that. On being elected the MP for Makerfield in Greater Manchester, he promised to apply a “Makerfield test” to every decision he makes.
Flying to Antigua for the Commonwealth heads of government meeting, known as CHOGM, may not seem an obvious way of delighting his constituents. But the prime minister shows an increased awareness that foreign and domestic policy often come to the same thing. He is taking his Makerfield test global. “That should be our starting point for policy always,” he says.
Mr Burnham treated the summit on November 3rd and 4th as a dry run for what he calls an “autumn of diplomacy”, consisting of five closely packed international shindigs. Speaking to The Economist during his Antigua trip, the prime minister seeks to dispel the impression he has little interest in foreign affairs and insists that Britain can cut a distinctive figure on the world stage. It is the first chance for Mr Burnham to prove he is Britain’s prime minister rather than its mayor.
“Britain is back” after “a difficult decade”, Mr Burnham says. The country commands “unique trust among nations”. At the CHOGM, he claims, other leaders have approached him, saying: “Where have you been? We need you.” He promises “a new relationship” with the Commonwealth, with the Middle East and with the EU, which could mean reversing Brexit.
On coming to office, the prime minister’s recent predecessors all said something similar. Boris Johnson boasted of “global Britain”. Rishi Sunak wanted to undo the reputational catastrophe caused by the premiership of Liz Truss. Sir Keir Starmer even declared: “Britain is back on the world stage.”
Mr Burnham does at least have a clear staging post at which he can test his global ambitions. All his summiteering, he says, is aimed at a successful G20 meeting, to take place in Manchester in November 2027. Working towards “a global set of standards” on artificial intelligence will be “the top issue”, Mr Burnham suggests. He wants to build on the success of Britain’s AI Security Institute to position the country as an honest broker between the tech superpowers of America and China, although he admits it “feels challenging” to forge a framework that both countries could sign up to. “We’ve got to hold out the need to find global agreements on AI,” he says. “If we don’t, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify.”
Not every member of the G20 will be welcome in Manchester. Asked whether Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, will be invited, Mr Burnham answers flatly: “No”. Sanctions on the Kremlin will keep him away, with Russia represented by more junior officials. The prime minister promises to maintain military and financial backing to Ukraine for as long as the country’s war with Russia continues, and is open to committing British troops to a future peacekeeping force if a deal to end the conflict is agreed.
By contrast, Mr Burnham is keen to host Xi Jinping, China’s president, at the get-together. He points out that Mr Xi visited Manchester in 2015, and promises that “he will see a big difference”. The city has developed quickly, thanks in part to Chinese cash. This economic collaboration could be a pattern for future UK-China dealings, the prime minister suggests: “We proceed carefully, but I’m sure there is a real opportunity there.”
Of the three foreign-policy overhauls Mr Burnham promises, the one on Europe remains the most important and the most ambiguous. He says he is open-minded about Britain’s relationship with the EU, but is keen to promote new analysis from the Treasury which concludes that a deal with Brussels on food standards and energy could boost the economy by as much as 0.4% of GDP. This is, he says, “a number that you cannot ignore”. More details should emerge at a summit in Brussels on November 20th; calls within Labour for Britain to rejoin the EU are growing.
His “new approach” to the Middle East, led by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, combines a spikier attitude towards Israel with security co-operation with Gulf states such as Saudi Arabia. Mr Burnham says putting sanctions on Israeli settlers was “the right thing to do”, but is open to working more closely with the country’s government if Binyamin Netanyahu is forced out following the inconclusive election in October. On the Commonwealth, the prime minister braved a domestic political backlash by promising to open a “structured dialogue” on the legacy of the British empire which could result in a formal apology for slavery (he has ruled out cash reparations).
Mr Burnham’s trip to Antigua coincided with America’s midterm elections in which Donald Trump’s Republicans were battered. He expresses optimism—not shared by all British politicians—that the scale of the president’s defeat may make him more constructive, for example by pushing him to end the war in Iran so as to ease pressure on oil prices. “What I take from the result and the president’s reaction is that we’ve got an opportunity to refocus around the issue that everyone everywhere is struggling with, and that’s [the] cost of living,” the prime minister says. The result of the midterms could be a harbinger for Britain and other countries, he hints: “The pendulum has swung away from populism in other parts of the world.”
There is no sign of Mr Trump backing down on one of the thorniest issues in the transatlantic relationship. The Chagos Islands host an American naval base. To the president’s chagrin, Sir Keir wanted to hand them to Mauritius. Mr Burnham suggests he is rethinking whether to give up British sovereignty over the archipelago. His government will “recast the arrangement”, he says, citing as a possible precedent the deal between Denmark and America which allows America greater access to Greenland for military purposes.
Alongside Mr Burnham’s diplomatic efforts, he is pulling together a “ten-year plan” which will lay out proposals to move more parts of the economy into “public control” and boost manufacturing employment. This was expected in December, but he now admits it may be delayed until the new year. Rumours in Westminster that the document will be thin are “underestimating the significance” of the plan, the prime minister insists: “I will lay out my very clear vision for Britain.”
But like leaders before him, he has found that he cannot sideline foreign policy completely. “There are so many issues now that you can’t deal with in national borders,” says Jill Rutter of the Institute for Government, a think-tank. The problems of Makerfield will not be solved without keeping an eye on Michigan, Mauritius and Mykolaiv too.

epub_61.title: How is King Charles III doing?
epub_61.text:
How is King Charles III doing?
Britain
| To bleat or not to bleat?
How is King Charles III doing?
Quite well. Not least because he has stopped complaining
Nov 5th 2026
“My great problem in life”, King Charles III once said as Prince of Wales, “is that I do not really know what my role in life is.” Becoming king in 2022 has amply answered that particular complaint. Charles is now Charles the Third, by the Grace of God of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and of His other Realms and Territories, King. He is Head of the Commonwealth. He is also Keeper of the Cows, Seigneur of the Swans and the Duke of Normandy. (Which might come as news to the French. Not to mention the cows.)
Today the question is not whether Charles has a role but whether he is doing his many jobs well. It has been four years since the longest-reigning monarch in British history died and the longest-serving heir-apparent took over. Four years is, in one way, no time at all: Charles’s mother reigned for 17 times as long. Yet in this time the king has been diagnosed with cancer, seen one brother arrested and survived four British prime ministers.
He has welcomed Donald Trump for a state visit and endured the president’s threats to annex his realm of Canada. On November 3rd he gave a speech in Antigua as head of the Commonwealth. He broached the subject of slavery (a tricky matter because some countries are demanding reparations), calling it a “shameful chapter of history” that filled his soul “with the most profound personal sorrow”.
Britain’s most prominent job—CEO of the Firm—is also its oddest. Unlike most CEOs Charles did not apply for his post, interview for it or, apparently, want it. (Though like all CEOs, heads of the Firm can be removed, as the king’s predecessor Charles I proved.) At first, many had doubts about Charles III. Are “the monarchy’s days numbered?” wondered a British headline in 2022. “Traditional monarchy died with the queen”, ran another in 2023. One commentator suggested that the monarchy was like an appendix: “We’ve long evolved past needing them.” Everyone kept forgetting to call Charles “King”.
Yet Charles is doing quite well. According to YouGov, a pollster, his favourability rating stands at 58%. That is not as high as Prince William’s (74%) but higher than Prince Harry’s (29%). Robert Hardman, the king’s biographer, says that Charles has “confounded his critics” in his reign so far.
Several things have helped Charles, including a honeymoon period, a strong work ethic (he was back to work within three months of his cancer diagnosis in 2024) and a willingness to sack poor performers: he stripped the Andrew formerly known as “Prince” of his title in 2025. The king’s changed attitude has also helped. Broadly speaking the moanier the royal, the less they are liked. The late queen (reputed motto: “Never complain, never explain”) was loved, as Princess Anne continues to be. The emotionally incontinent Harry and Meghan are increasingly loathed. Charles has, finally, learnt his lesson: the former “Prince of Wails” has largely stopped complaining.
Good timing has helped too. For decades Charles seemed like a crank. He talked to plants and fretted about the Patagonian toothfish. He built Poundbury, a likeable British town that intellectuals like to dislike. Everyone laughed at him. But things have changed. Sustainable farming is spreading, Poundbury is expanding, architecture is softening. There is a mood, insiders say, of “I told you so.”
The final cause of success is, perhaps, his pulling power. To stand in a room filled with world leaders and watch Charles enter is startling. All—Volodymyr Zelensky, Emmanuel Macron, Giorgia Meloni—have eyes only for him. As he enters heads turn, conversations silence, ears strain to catch his every word. World leaders have achieved their greatness; Charles had his thrust upon him. Yet he is the one they want to meet. And, from state visits to AI summits, he leverages this. Meeting the king is, says Mr Hardman, “a bucket-list item for world leaders”.
This, as few know better than the king, is ludicrous. In 1995 Charles produced a Shakespeare anthology. In it he singled out a speech on kingship in “Henry V“ that left him “wondering in amazement” at Shakespeare’s “insight”. It is not a cheery speech. Kingship, Henry says, is a “hard condition”. For what “have kings” that commoners do not, “save ceremony”? A king is gossiped about and judged. He must empathise with his people’s sorrows but has little rest himself. Some years ago Charles sneaked incognito into a production of “Henry V”. Sir Jonathan Bate, an academic, recalls that as that speech began, the future king gave “a kind of shiver”.
What is the point of a king? To judge from Shakespeare: not much. Merely to articulate others’ feelings and not bang on about his own. To provide ceremony. A hard condition; possibly a pointless one.
But then earlier this year, Charles was invited to America. The old king stood to address its new “king” in Congress. And, as Charles gently teased and reprimanded Mr Trump, he was given one standing ovation after another. It was nothing: ceremony, mere ceremony. But ceremony can be useful. And these days people sometimes even remember to call Charles “King”.

Britain
| Sexual behaviour
Britain’s ban on some pornography is based on flimsy evidence
Once again, correlation and causation are not the same
Nov 5th 2026
Parents are aghast. Many young Britons appear to be choking one another during sex. According to a survey by the Institute for Addressing Strangulation, part of a charity, 66% of sexually experienced 16- to 34-year-olds have been on the receiving end. Not all consented to it in advance. The government blames porn. So, from November 6th, pornography depicting strangulation or suffocation will be outlawed. So will porn depicting incest, and fantasies in which performers pretend to be underage.
The notion that porn changes behaviour has been around at least since 1986, when the Meese report in America argued that it was likely to cause an increase in sexual violence. But the evidence is far from conclusive. A review in 2016, looking at 20 years of porn research, concluded that methodological shortcomings and “biases in the literature” prevent researchers from drawing conclusions about porn’s effect on adolescents. A further review in 2023 similarly concluded that most studies had “substantial limitations” that preclude any firm conclusions.
Nicole Prause, a neuroscientist, says that studies often find a correlation between what people watch and what they do. They have done so with choking. But researchers disagree on which way causality flows. “It’s a chicken-and-egg situation,” she says. Anti-porn campaigners point to a body of research showing that people who use more pornography engage in more sexual harassment and aggression. But who uses the most porn? Generally it is teenage boys with a tendency towards sensation-seeking and a troubled family history. Those are all risk factors for aggressive sexual behaviour in their own right.
Even the independent review of pornography by Lady Bertin, which the British government has used to justify its restrictions, noted that “research has commonly confused correlation and causation”. Those two things are always hard to unpick, but especially so when it comes to adolescents’ porn use. An ideal study would involve exposing some to pornography (or, teenagers being what they are, to more porn) but that would be unethical.
Some evidence comes from studies that follow the same people over a period of time to assess whether changes in porn use predict later changes in behaviour. Researchers in Croatia followed over 1,500 students for three years. They confirmed a well-established link between “hostile masculinity”, a personality type, and sexual aggression. But they found no evidence that pornography use increased an individual’s odds of sexual aggression—a conclusion, they wrote, that is “difficult to reconcile with the view that pornography use plays a causal role in male sexual violence”.
Countries that have repealed strict porn laws provide a natural experiment. They are not perfect, since a ban on pornography does not make it disappear. Still, research comparing rates of sexual crime before and after the liberalisation of porn laws in the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Japan and Sweden found no evidence of a relationship between pornography and sexual violence.
Young people do learn about niche sexual practices from pornography. It has introduced some to the concept of choking. But other media carry the message, too. Earlier this year Romania came third in the Eurovision song contest with a song titled “Choke Me”. In one American study, a young woman claimed to have first come across choking by reading smutty fan fiction about the band One Direction.
Where someone first sees something does not necessarily tell you why they want to do it. A study in Australia tested several variables to see what might predict whether an individual has a positive perception of choking during sex. Having seen choking in porn had little predictive value. Having previously tried choking or having discussed it with friends was much more likely to predict positive attitudes towards it. Other surveys find that the majority of sexual choking is consensual and pleasurable for those involved. Perhaps young people are choking each other during sex mostly because they like it.
