Britain makes the path to permanent residence more arduous
Britain
| Immigration policy
Britain makes the path to permanent residence more arduous
It is unlikely to save the “billions” that the government claims
Nov 5th 2026
Shabana mahmood’s parents arrived in Britain from Kashmir in the 1970s. The father of the home secretary was a civil engineer and her mother ran the family shop. That generation of arrivals from the Commonwealth faced few barriers to permanent residence and citizenship.
Immigrants to Britain today must pass tougher tests. On November 2nd Ms Mahmood announced changes to permanent residence, known as Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR), that will impact thousands of migrants on similar paths to her parents. Ms Mahmood backtracked on her initial hardline proposals. Yet in trying to use ilR to do three things at once—deter migrants, improve integration and control costs—she risks achieving none at all.
The Labour government has played tough on immigration since winning power in 2024. The tightening of visa rules helped cut net migration from non-EU countries over the past three years from 1m to 350,000. However, under existing rules, nearly 2m migrants who arrived in 2020-24 were soon to be eligible to apply for ILR and the welfare benefits it confers. Ms Mahmood claimed that allowing them to do so would cost the country billions.
So the government has shifted the goal posts. Last November it proposed doubling the time to ILR from five to 10 years, but extending it up to 15 for those in lower-skilled jobs including 400,000 care workers. Four-fifths of the 200,000 people who responded to its consultation, many of them immigrants, disagreed. Andy Burnham convinced Ms Mahmood to water down the policy after becoming prime minister in July. The result is a fudge.
The new rules have raised the bar on English-language fluency. Migrants must have a spotless criminal record (some MPs would fail on this basis). They or their partners must have contributed to the Treasury’s coffers. But the biggest change is the minimum-residency period. The standard five-year ILR pathway will now vary from three years for attractive migrants such as high-earners and entrepreneurs to 30 years for asylum-seekers who crossed the English Channel illegally. About 1.4m people are now expected to be granted settlement between 2026 and 2030 (see chart).
The changes retrospectively penalise about 230,000 skilled workers earning less than £50,000 ($67,000) a year, as well as 100,000 people holding care-worker visas who the government suspects have never worked in the sector. For these groups eligibility for ILR will double to ten years. But exceptions have been made for most holders of health and care-worker visas, for whom the government is paymaster. Some 600,000 workers and their dependants will still be eligible for ILR after five years.
The group most affected by the changes are refugees. Under old rules, those granted asylum protection would be eligible for ILR after five years. Henceforth, asylum status will be reviewed every 30 months, to determine whether a country has become safe. The period to ILR eligibility will be 30 years for people who arrive illegally, as around half of asylum-seekers do, and 20 years for those who arrive on a visa. Bangladeshis, Nigerians and Pakistanis, who often obtain visas, will be treated differently from Afghans, Eritreans and Iranians, who cannot acquire them.
As well as deterring small-boat crossings, Ms Mahmood is trying to improve the integration of refugees. ILR eligibility will be cut by ten years for those who earn at least £12,600 for three years. At present, just one in four working-age refugees earn at least £10,000 five years after gaining asylum. Ben Brindle of the Migration Observatory, a think-tank, points out that evidence from Denmark—a country Ms Mahmood has tried to copy—suggests residency carrots act as incentives for those close to qualifying, but others give up.
The changes are likely to save nothing like the sums the government trailed. Ms Mahmood implied that sticking with the five-year ILR would cost £10bn. Those numbers were misleading as they were predicated on the lifetime fiscal costs of care workers, not a five-year deferment of ILR. A rough calculation suggests that extending ILR to ten years for 350,000 people will save £450m. Refugees, meanwhile, can still claim benefits prior to settlement. Ms Mahmood maintains that her changes will “save billions” but that will depend on whether ILR changes migrants’ behaviour. And that remains to be seen.

epub_64.title: Spare a thought for the European shag
epub_64.text:
Spare a thought for the European shag
Britain
| Seabirds
Spare a thought for the European shag
But other seabirds off Britain’s coast are showing signs of resilience
Nov 5th 2026
Pity the European shag. An agile diver, it is clumsy on land and barely waterproof. Winter storms off Britain’s coast can be deadly. Between 1986 and 2024 shag numbers dropped by 71%, according to the Seabird Monitoring Programme (SMP).
Almost two-thirds of British seabird species are in decline, according to the latest census. Oil spills are thankfully less frequent than they were in the 20th century, but other threats loom, including climate change, overfishing, avian flu and invasive rats.
Yet some birds, especially in the auk family, are holding up. Razorbill numbers have grown by 110% since 1986, according to the smp. Erin Taylor, an SMP ornithologist, speculates that auks might adapt better to warming seas than other seabirds. Deeper dives and flexible diets expand their prey options; short migrations keep them close to their North Sea breeding grounds. By contrast, Arctic terns, which were added to the conservation “red list” in 2024 after population declines, migrate to polar regions where the climate is changing rapidly.
Tim Birkhead, an ornithologist who has studied guillemots on Skomer Island off Wales for over 50 years, thinks there might be something special about Britain’s south-west waters. He credits the bird boom to a stroke of oceanographic luck. Nutrient-rich upwellings, marine protected areas and the absence of industrial sand-eel fishing may all play a part, but the mechanisms are not fully understood.
Even such havens are fragile. An outbreak of avian flu on Skomer in 2023 killed roughly a third of breeding guillemots, and many dead auks have washed up on Britain’s coast this year.
Rigorous scientific monitoring can make a difference. Tracking colonies takes skill, effort and money (drones are increasingly used to survey hard-to-reach locations). When data showed that little terns were breeding earlier in spring, leaving their eggs vulnerable to high tides, conservationists built up beach heights to lift nests away from danger. Even the shag was moved off a conservation red list in 2024. There is hope for it yet.

epub_65.title: Investor seeks AI Adonis
epub_65.text:
Investor seeks AI Adonis
Britain
| Venture capital
Investor seeks AI Adonis
British venture capital resembles a cruel dating game
Nov 5th 2026
FINDING A VENTURE capitalist to back your startup has never been easy. That is why Metal, a platform that helps match founders to investors, exists—and can charge $1,200 a quarter. Even so, it is a surprise to Sameer Nusrat, a manager at Metal, when on a Monday morning 100 people pack into a bougie co-working space in east London for an event he is hosting: “Is your dream vc into you?” For a growing number of founders in the capital, the answer to that question is “no”.
This year is shaping up to be a record one for venture capital in Britain. Investors, many of them American, have already poured over $26bn into startups, almost matching their splurge during the covid-19 pandemic. At the same time, artificial intelligence has made analysing startups simpler than ever, notes James Wise of Balderton Capital. Research that used to take a day can now be done in minutes. In theory, it has never been easier to find a Prince Charming in a Patagonia fleece (still the vc outfit of choice) or for him to find you.
Yet more information and money only seems to have made investors pickier. Since 2023 the total value of vc deals in Britain has risen, but their number has fallen, according to PitchBook, a data firm (see chart). In the first half of 2026 nearly three-quarters of investment went into startups working on ai, much of it to a small cohort of companies. vcs seem to have a favourite type, and they obsess about a narrow set of founders. The dating pool is becoming more exclusive.
Venture capital has always obeyed the power law: a handful of companies supply the bulk of a fund’s returns. AI is further concentrating those returns by consuming an outsize share of funding (fintech, once a darling, is struggling by contrast). A British firm may never match the returns early investors in Anthropic are likely to receive when America’s leading ai lab goes public. Indeed, on November 4th Sequoia Capital, a large vc firm, announced it would close its London office to focus on Silicon Valley. Still, thanks to its strong research base and DeepMind, Google’s ai unit, London is a good place to place smaller bets.
Founders have always mattered, but investors are now concentrating on an ever smaller group of potentially elite performers. One is David Silver, a hoodie-wearing AI pioneer and philosopher-poet who left DeepMind to co-found Ineffable Intelligence, a new frontier ai lab. On Ineffable’s website, a “note from Dave” describes Mr Silver’s vision for the company, as a place “where my precious hours can create the greatest impact”. Investors swooned. Within months he had raised $1.1bn, a British record for a seed round.
Increasingly the biggest cheques are going to impressive founders, almost regardless of the startup attached to them. Isomorphic Labs, which uses ai to try to discover new drugs, is the latest brainchild of DeepMind’s co-founder, Sir Demis Hassabis. Nscale, a data-centre provider, is led by Josh Payne, a former coal miner backed by Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and the former Meta executive Sheryl Sandberg (“The only person I’d ever seen write like that is Mark Zuckerberg,” she gushed). These ai Adonises hoover up most of the capital, just as a few hotties on Tinder get most of the right swipes.
Smaller funds, which are unable to outbid American capital for today’s stars, must find tomorrow’s as early as possible. To do so, British VCs are hosting roundtables and hanging around coffee shops. Universities are not the hotspots they used to be. A recent report by Beauhurst found that investment into spinouts raising money for the first time fell by more than two-thirds in the first half of 2026. The most exciting startups can still be founded by academics, says Jonno Evans of iq Capital, a “deeptech” outfit that focuses on the most innovative technologies. “But very often they’re not.”
The most desirable matches are those who have done all this before. Take Steven Richardson, a former detective from Merseyside. His ai startup was recently valued at $400m based on—publicly at least—a single word on a website (“INVESTIGATE”) and his track record of founding and selling Riven, an AI redaction tool. Or Chad Edwards, a 35-year-old self-avowed “craft-beer nerd” already on his second billion-dollar company. Cusp AI, which plans to use AI to discover new materials, is backed by Jeff Bezos of Amazon. Rob Lacher, who runs Visionaries, a small European fund, is particularly drawn to founders who can “turn their childhood obsession into their job” and have a gift for storytelling.
To woo their favourite founders, British vc is becoming less stingy. Liquidation preferences, the jargon for who gets paid first when a startup exits or is wound down, are now as founder-friendly in Britain as they are in America, notes Jamie Moore of Orrick, which measures these things. Venture-capital funds are paying greater attention to matters like regulatory compliance and board composition, challenging their long-held reputation for favouring growth over governance.
The most prized founders do not always welcome such advice. In a recent podcast interview, Nik Storonsky, the founder of Revolut, one of Europe’s most valuable private companies, described how a vc on its board tried to fire one of his top performers. vcs, he said scathingly, are “cheerleaders” who think they can play the match better than professional players. So deep is his disdain that Mr Storonsky started his own fund, QuantumLight, to compete with them, in much the same way Revolut seeks to disrupt banks. vcs will have to become more useful to founders, says Saul Klein of Phoenix Court, a high-performing fund. Otherwise it will be their turn to be jilted.

epub_66.title: Britain’s landlords deserve some love
epub_66.text:
Britain’s landlords deserve some love
Britain
| Bagehot
Britain’s landlords deserve some love
Who will speak for the HMO Hero?
Nov 5th 2026
Of all the tax increases Labour have introduced since 2024, one passed with barely a murmur. When John Healey, the chancellor, popped another two percentage points on tax on “income from property” last month, few complained. It was to be expected. Successive governments have hammered landlords, including those who own a “house in multiple occupation” or two, for a decade. Will anyone speak for the hmo Hero?
Not Labour, that is for sure. Mr Healey’s tax rise came after a similar increase the year before. The Renters’ Rights Act, which was passed last year, introduces rent controls in all but name. For just £47 ($63) a tenant can challenge any rent rise, with a tribunal determining whether it is the local market rent. The tribunal can even reduce rents already agreed on. Market prices are, apparently, too important to be left to the market.
Yet when it comes to landlords, Labour are only following in the Tory party’s footsteps. George Osborne, the former Conservative chancellor, removed tax breaks on mortgage interest and replaced them with a less generous tax credit. Landlords were also hit with a 3% stamp-duty surcharge when buying property (which became 5% under Labour). It was under the Tories that the British dream of owning someone else’s home became a nightmare.
Buy-to-let landlords are easy to hate. Partly, it is jealousy. The buy-to-let mortgage was invented in 1996, at the start of a colossal house-price boom, during which real house prices across Britain almost trebled in a decade. It proved a sensational investment: someone who bought in 1996 enjoyed higher returns than most big stock markets.
Partly it is because renting in Britain is often miserable. Britain’s private-rental sector is dominated by amateurs. George Orwell’s caricature of a slum landlord in the 1930s is not far off reality today: “A poor old woman who has invested her life’s savings in three slum houses, inhabits one of them, and tries to live on the rent of the other two—never, in consequence, having any money for repairs.” About half of landlords own just one property. Rather than a well-organised property company, a typical English landlord remains a baby-boomer wondering why their savings product is ringing at 2am to complain about a leak.
At times it seems as if the government sees every private renter as a public-policy failure. What should private renters do if government policy leads to rents going up? Buy a home with the support of the government, comes the reply. The idea that renting is a necessary part of a dynamic economy is alien in a country that treats it like an embarrassing affliction. A world in which everyone owns is one in which people are unable to drop everything and change cities for another job.
Building more homes is the best fix for expensive housing. But a higher proportion of rentals can still help. A terrace in a city can house either a small family or half a dozen young renters, if broken into flats or turned into an hmo. Landlords are often painted as parasites. This is unfair. They are worms, playing a vital part in the housing food chain, digesting what others would waste.
Hammering them may backfire, eventually. The Office for Budget Responsibility has warned that potential landlords may steer clear, reducing rental supply and pushing up rents. Housing supply is a fractious political debate in Britain; landlord supply is its forgotten cousin. What reason do landlords have to stay? Spectacular returns are long gone. At 5.8%, the typical gross yield on a buy-to-let property is barely higher than the yield on a ten-year gilt, the closest thing to risk-free return. Buy-to-let offers return-free risk. Who is likelier to default: the government or a tenant?
And yet economic logic goes out the window when it comes to Britons and property. The government is harder on landlords than it should be; likewise landlords appear to be suckers for punishment. It would be economically rational for more to leave, yet surprisingly few do. Well-reasoned predictions of a mass landlord exodus and rental supply crunch have been made repeatedly in the past decade. Neither has come to pass. Indeed, the stock of rental homes has grown by about 1% a year since 2021, says the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, a leftie think-tank. Chris Norris of the National Residential Landlords Association puts it delicately: landlords are “not entirely rational actors”.
Would more rational actors be welcome? British governments of various stripes have long called for  institutional investors to replace Orwell’s grannies. Renters should be careful what they wish for. Lazy landlords are a blessing and a curse. A Boomer landlord who would rather not worry on their cruise might not raise a good tenant’s monthly rent; a corporation will do what the spreadsheet says. Whether smart money wants to invest in a sector with low returns and huge regulatory risk is another matter.
Perhaps only Britain’s crack squad of hmo Heroes are foolhardy enough for the task. Come 2030, landlords will have to climate-proof their properties at a cost of up to £10,000. And any landlord who banks on strong house-price growth may end up disappointed. The government has not yet equalised the rates of capital-gains tax and income tax, but rumours that it will do so persist.
These risks are known, yet still the hmo Heroes march towards gunfire. Banks have seen no drop-off in the number of people taking out new buy-to-let mortgages. It is brave to the point of foolishness. At some point it becomes a form of intergenerational altruism, with wealthy boomers investing in a buy-to-let when doing almost anything else with their money would leave them better off. Still it is a lousy financial decision that someone else can live in. Why try to stop them? Britain may not like its landlords, but it would miss them if they were gone.

epub_68.title: The digital world is making Islam more diverse
epub_68.text:
The digital world is making Islam more diverse
International
| Virtual virtue
The digital world is making Islam more diverse
Muslims are young, online and playing by their own rules
Nov 5th 2026
IT began BY accident. In 2018 Omar Suleiman, a soft-spoken Texan imam, realised that a scammer was impersonating him on Instagram to solicit donations. He decided to create a genuine account. A community of followers began to grow, especially during the pandemic, when he started live-streaming on YouTube every night, talking about how Islam can help with things like uncertainty and grief.
Mr Suleiman now has more than 3m followers on Instagram and a TikTok account with 22.2m likes. His followers hail from all over the world. Many watch him because their local imams do not really grapple with the issues they care about, he thinks. Some followers tell him his teachings have changed their lives.
The world’s 2bn-odd Muslims are younger, on average, than people of other religions: in 2020 the Pew Research Centre, an American public-policy institute, found that the median age for the faith was 24, versus 33 for non-Muslims. They are also very much online. An upcoming survey from Arab Barometer, a research firm, found that 60% of 18- to 29-year-old Muslims in the Middle East are both “heavy internet users” and “highly engaged” on social media. Around 30% of British Muslims use social media a “great deal” for religious information, according to a recent study by the Digital British Islam project.
What these young, Muslim digital natives find online is shaping the future of their religion. And what they are discovering is a cornucopia of doctrines and outlooks that is far more varied than what they might encounter at their local mosque. Although religious authority in Islam typically derives from scholarly expertise, many of the biggest online influencers are simply opinionated laypeople eager to vent. They espouse a dizzying array of theologies, from the conventional to the extreme. They are creating a more heterodox faith.
Muslims used to learn about religion primarily at their mosque. Cassette sermons became popular in the 1970s and TV imams followed in the 1990s. These democratised access to religious teaching to some extent, but the internet has hastened the shift. Online, “People can explore who they are,” says Renasha Khan of King’s College London, because they can seek information in private, without the mediation of local religious leaders. In particular, they can pick and choose among textual interpretations, rather than subscribing wholesale to a single school of thought.
Nadya Lim, a 35-year-old from Singapore, uses Muslim Pro, an app that has been downloaded 190m times, to check the timing of the five prayers devout Muslims perform each day and the direction of Mecca, towards which they are supposed to pray. She also regularly consults Google for answers to such questions as where the nearest mosque is or how to apply Islam’s injunction against praying while menstruating if her period is late.
The internet has not only allowed Muslims like Ms Lim to take greater control of their own faith, but has also exposed them to a wider range of views. Being a Muslim feminist, at least in public, was once very rare. But Muslim feminist influencers are building followings online, even if they are not yet mainstream. In Nigeria, Wardah Abbas, a Muslim writer, has gained popularity by challenging more conservative views on gender, which she argues are rooted more in culture than in Islam itself. “We don’t care what you have to say about this religion. We want to do our own personal research,” she says. Amina Wadud, an American theologian nicknamed “The Lady Imam”, describes herself as an “ally” to gay and transgender Muslims.
Some lifestyle influencers encourage Muslims to break the mould in more subtle ways. “Ayahsvoice”, a Briton with more than 14m likes on TikTok, describes herself as a “scholar of pink cherry Islam” and says that her account is for Muslim women who “struggle to fit in the religion”. Her make-up tutorials are generally light on theology. But she openly rejects Hadith, the collected sayings and doings of the Prophet Muhammad—a fundamental departure from orthodox Islam. She argues that the misogyny espoused by some male Muslim influencers stems more from the Hadith than from the Koran.
Muslim lifestyle influencers are also popular in Indonesia. Many promote or sell their own modest clothing on Instagram. Ummu Alila, one such influencer, who has around 500,000 followers on the app, offers head coverings and denim dresses designed to comply with Islamic principles. Ummu Alila founded the firm with her husband, Felix Siauw, a preacher who built a big following online in the mid-2010s. He was a member of Hizbut Tahrir Indonesia, which agitated for a transnational Islamic caliphate (it was banned in 2017). Now he and she opine online together about everything from touring Istanbul to infidelity.
Social media also offer believers perspectives from parts of the Islamic world far from their own. Mr Suleiman, the Texan imam, has plenty of followers in the Middle East. Ms Lim says in the past “people received only one side”, but she now gets ideas from influencers such as Mufti Menk, a popular scholar from Zimbabwe.
There is, inevitably, plenty of incendiary content, too. Muhammad Hijab, who is associated with a group of young British Muslim influencers nicknamed the “Dawah Bros”, has 1.3m subscribers on YouTube. He likes to debate atheists and non-Muslim religious leaders, producing pugnacious videos with titles like “Anti-Islam preacher humiliated”.
Some commentators talk of a Muslim “manosphere”, which blends Islamic theology with macho chauvinism. When Andrew Tate, an influencer wanted in Britain on charges of rape and human trafficking, converted to Islam in 2022, Mr Hijab interviewed him to welcome him to the faith. In 2022 Mr Hijab travelled to the city of Leicester, where there had been clashes between Hindus and Muslims. He told crowds of Muslim men, many of them masked, that Hindu nationalists were “pathetic, weak and cowardly”.
It is not clear whether online influencers have steered Muslims in a more liberal or conservative direction overall. But they have fostered a sense of digital community. Ishtiaque Ahmed of the University of Toronto argues that Muslims’ access to a wide range of information has spurred the emergence of “a spirit of global Islam” online. Those who are opposed to Israel’s war in Gaza, for example, have a place to unite and discuss their cause. The diaspora from Muslim-majority countries can also access teachings from back home more easily, says Ali Riaz of Illinois State University.
Some mainstream imams denounce the more novel teachings spreading online. “I have been excommunicated a number of times and I’ve been accused of being a sell-out, a heretic,” says Ms Abbas, the Nigerian feminist. But most forms of Islam have always been decentralised, without an institutional hierarchy or a supreme leader like the pope. Years of study at well-known institutions, such as Al Azhar in Cairo, do not guarantee digital prominence. In the age of the internet, notes Ibrahim Abusharif of Northwestern University, “Authentic scholars and pathetic pretenders can compete for audiences.”
The profusion of interpretations of Islam circulating online makes some governments wary, too. In 2024 Manahel al-Otaibi, a popular Muslim online fitness instructor, was sentenced to 11 years in prison in Saudi Arabia for sharing pictures of herself in immodest clothing and for supporting an end to Islamically inspired laws that allow men to control the movements of their wives and some female relatives. In 2017 Salman al-Ouda, a prominent Saudi cleric with more than 9m followers on X, was arrested just days after he tweeted a prayer of reconciliation between Saudi Arabia and Qatar, in apparent opposition to the Saudi government’s blockade of Qatar.
In democracies the popularity of Islamic influencers has prompted a different sort of response from politicians. Bernie Sanders, an American senator, got Mr Suleiman to speak at a rally when he ran for president in 2020. In the run-up to Indonesia’s presidential election in 2024, politicians sought the support of popular Muslim influencers such as Haikal Hassan, who has about 2m Instagram followers. Such figures are also prominent in Bangladeshi politics. After Tarique Rahman became prime minister earlier this year he sought the advice of Sheikh Ahmadullah, a preacher with 3.5m YouTube subscribers, about amending laws on donations to charity—a pillar of Islam.
The internet is not everything. In many Muslim-majority countries beliefs are still primarily shaped by local scholars. Nurudeen Lemu, one such scholar, says that much of what is debated online is not very useful in Nigeria. “Religion is not copy paste. An online response backed by a Pakistani, a Saudi, an American, an Australian, to a Nigerian Muslim is contextless,” he says, pointing to differences in everything from eating habits to clothing.
Mr Lemu even plays down the risk of extremists exploiting the digital world to foster Islamist terrorism. In surveys he has conducted of detained jihadists in northern Nigeria, he found that “less than 1% of recruitment was online” over the past decade. “They were using cassette tapes! There is a gentle rise as internet access has gone further and batteries last longer, but it usually requires a friend.”
Moreover, online preachers can only supplement local ones, rather than supplant them, since taking part in communal services in person is important in Islam. Most Muslims consider attendance at Friday prayers compulsory for able-bodied men, for instance. About 40% of American Muslims attend services once a week. Bouziane Zaid of the University of Sharjah has found that Middle Eastern youths still tend to turn to a local imam first for serious advice on personal matters. Local imams and congregations will always be influential—but they are now just one of many forces shaping young Muslims’ beliefs.

Fear united Europe. Nationalism may tear it apart
International
| The Telegram
Fear united Europe. Nationalism may tear it apart
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin made Europe serious about its own defences. That may not last
Nov 5th 2026
FOR MOST of the past 800 years, the sight of German soldiers inspired dread in Lithuanian hearts. Today, as a small Baltic state with Russia as a direct neighbour, Lithuania is happy to host a permanently deployed German armoured brigade.
The aggression of Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and the might-makes-right callousness of his American counterpart, Donald Trump, have not only scrambled Europe’s calculations about power, but also the continent’s balance of fear. In 2029 Germany, Europe’s largest country, plans to spend 3.5% of GDP, or €162bn ($182bn), on defence. That is more than the combined defence spending of Britain and France last year. Far from being alarmed by German rearmament, many neighbours are counting on it.
Put bluntly, after decades of underinvestment in defence, mainstream European leaders have a horror of being abandoned by America before the region is strong enough to deter Russia on its own. Their fears mounted after Mr Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. They turned to near-panic after Mr Trump was re-elected in 2024, and he made clear his scorn for Ukraine and its allies in NATO and the European Union, and his preference for ending the Ukrainian war on terms favourable to Russia.
European leaders broadly agree on the need to support Ukraine and prepare for America to become, at best, NATO’s offshore protector of last resort. That shared task helped Britain repair ties with allies that take defence seriously, including nuclear-armed France, big-spending Germany, and Ukraine’s most loyal supporters in northern and eastern Europe. A common foe puts Brexit squabbles in perspective.
The balance of fear has changed, too, in Germany, where the public had to overcome its unease about military might. Though cold-war West Germany maintained one of NATO’s largest armies, politicians allowed citizens to indulge in a comfortable fantasy, portraying post-1989 Germany as a commerce-minded, pacifist friend to all. Some on the left treated Germany as something like a recovering addict to militarism, which if allowed even a sniff of gunpowder might go on a terrible bender before waking with a headache to discover it had occupied Luxembourg, once again.
Such angst was cured by Mr Putin and above all by Mr Trump. German defence spending grew in earnest after Ukraine’s invasion in 2022, inspiring what Germany’s then-chancellor, Olaf Scholz, called a Zeitenwende, or “turning-point”. Spending surged after 2024 and the return of an America-First president.
European unity is, however, more fragile than it appears. Over the next 12 months, elections will be held in Spain, France, Poland and Italy. In several cases, parties on the nationalist right are poised for power. Some right-wing populists have histories of sympathising with Russia, including Marine Le Pen, front-runner in the French presidential contest, and Roberto Vannacci, a former general and Russia-admirer challenging Italy’s conservative prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, from her right. If Poland’s feuding politicians agree on one thing it is on loathing Russia. Still, some Polish conservatives cast Ukraine as needy, ungrateful and too slow to acknowledge crimes committed by Ukrainians against Poles during the second world war. Aid for Ukraine should come with conditions, they growl. Above all, the nationalist right is united in opposing deeper European integration, even in pro-EU Spain, where the Vox party may enter government. An exultant Ms Le Pen has predicted that a year of elections will transform the EU from a would-be superstate into a “Europe of nations”.
Alas, a nationalist wave could also derail Europe’s rearmament. To avoid frightening its neighbours, Germany can grow its armed forces and defence industries only if it puts its fiscal and military might at the service of NATO and Europe, argues Liana Fix, the author of a new book, “Germany Rearmed: The Return of War and the End of Illusions”. To be a “European” power means, in effect, to act within the Franco-German alliance in which Germany has bound its strength since 1945. But that creates a dilemma. Ms Fix fears a division of Europe into a north-eastern bloc, including the Baltic states, Britain, Nordic countries and Poland, which still seeks to deter Russia, and a Mediterranean bloc of southern governments ready to appease Mr Putin, to buy his oil and gas and to focus security spending on hardening borders against poor-world migrants. Germany would have a national interest in securing Poland and the Baltics as a buffer against Russia, Ms Fix writes. But if France does not want to join a northern bloc, Germany’s national and European interests would be at odds.
True, as Ms Le Pen scents victory, she has moderated her formerly Putin-friendly rhetoric. Casting herself as an heir to Charles de Gaulle, she pledges to maintain strong armed forces. But at a minimum her sharp-elbowed, France-first approach to industrial spending could derail multinational defence projects. At worst, Europe would conclude it cannot rely on France in a crisis.
The Trump administration’s role is both unhelpful and incoherent. Mr Trump continues to push Europeans to spend more on defence. At the same time, he seeks detente with Mr Putin and offers noisy support to pro-Russian parties on Europe’s nationalist right, including Germany’s largest opposition party, the Putin-friendly, Ukraine-spurning Alternative for Germany. But if Europe has no need to deter Russia, it is unclear why Mr Trump thinks it needs to rearm: the continent is hardly about to take on China.
Europe needs to learn the right lessons from the Trump era. The MAGA shock made Europeans, led by Germany, serious about their own security, at long last. To complete the task, Europe must now shun Trump-style populist nationalism, which risks wrecking that project. Anything else would be a fearful blunder.

epub_71.title: Firms are racing to protect themselves from AI cyber threats
epub_71.text:
Firms are racing to protect themselves from AI cyber threats
Business
| Hack to the future
Firms are racing to protect themselves from AI cyber threats
Hackers have unleashed a devastating wave of attacks. More may follow
Nov 5th 2026
The corporate world is under siege. In a matter of weeks a flurry of serious cyber-security incidents have shaken the confidence of bosses in their defences. Thousands of new software vulnerabilities have been discovered, aided by artificial intelligence. That, along with a slew of hacks, has led many to argue that cyber-risk is entering a perilous new phase.
So testing was the past month that some analysts have called it “Black October” (others, “the Hackening”). First AI was used to discover a critical flaw in PHP, a widely used programming language that underpins most websites. The vulnerability was leaked before patches could be deployed, so many websites were temporarily taken offline to be fixed. Then hackers stole some $6.3bn from Binance, a crypto exchange. November has been no easier. Across Europe, supermarket freezers have had their temperatures cranked up, destroying millions of euros worth of food. At Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, a French bank, funds have been stolen in a burst of fraudulent transactions.
Governments have been hit, too. Air-raid alert apps have been hacked in both Ukraine and Russia. Cyber-criminals have swiped data from Denmark’s population registry, America’s Department of Homeland Security and the FBI. Japan has declared a cyber-security state of emergency. On November 3rd Richard Horne, head of Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre, warned that in the coming months there may be an “unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents”.
Even before this onslaught, the threat was growing. Remote work and an increase in internet-connected devices created more vulnerabilities. The prevalence of digital currencies made it easier for hackers to make money from their exploits.
AI has exacerbated the danger. In April Anthropic, a frontier lab, said it would not release Mythos, its latest model, to the public. Instead a limited number of software providers and financial institutions were granted access to help them plug gaps in their cyber-defences. OpenAI, a rival lab, soon launched a similar effort. In recent months frontier models have unearthed huge numbers of security flaws: the count of “common vulnerabilities and exposures” reported to software-makers and specialist cyber-security organisations is soaring (see chart 1).
Worryingly, however, the cyber capabilities of open-weight models have been rapidly improving in parallel, making it easier for even novice hackers to identify vulnerabilities (see chart 2). Moreover, AI has sped up the process of exploiting a vulnerability once it is discovered. Working out how to do this used to take days or weeks; now it can take hours. That means there is far less time for defenders to patch flaws in their software. The technology is also fuelling “social engineering” attacks, with models being used to automate phishing emails and clone the voices of employees.
Employees’ adoption of AI in their everyday work is adding to the problem. This makes companies a “ripe target” for hackers, says Nicole Carignan of Darktrace, a cyber-security firm. Surveys suggest that most workers use some type of AI service that has not been vetted by IT teams. On October 21st the maker of LiteLLM, a popular open-source AI tool, announced that it had again been compromised by hackers, following a similar incident in March that put thousands of organisations at risk.
Businesses are scrambling to respond. At big institutions up to a fifth of IT resources are being rerouted to finding and fixing security flaws, says Vanessa Lyon of BCG, a consultancy. Firms are prioritising software that is exposed to the internet, such as websites and apps. Mark Hughes of IBM, an IT giant, says that in cases where no patch is available yet for vulnerabilities that have been unearthed, he is telling clients to contain the at-risk software, perhaps taking it offline or limiting which staff have access.
Companies are also fighting AI with AI. Models can be deployed not just to scan for vulnerabilities, but also to spot and neutralise suspicious activity and catch phishing schemes. Goldman Sachs, for example, has greatly increased the share of the bank’s AI budget that it allocates to cyber-security, according to people familiar with the effort. Managing such spending requires careful planning. “How do you make sure you don’t run out of tokens mid-breach?” asks Charlie Lewis of McKinsey, another consultancy. He notes that some firms are setting aside tokens for emergencies, while others are establishing procedures to fast-track spending approvals in the event of a cyber-attack.
Yet a variety of challenges may undermine the defenders. One is human gullibility, which even the cleverest cyber-defences will struggle to compensate for entirely. The heist of Binance, allegedly orchestrated by North Korean hackers, was reportedly caused by an employee downloading malware onto their work computer during a fake job interview.
A second challenge is “operational technology”, the industrial hardware used on factories and shop floors. This type of machine typically runs on decades-old software, and has often been ignored by cyber-security teams because ancient code made it hard for hackers to get at. Yet, as seems to have been the case in the recent freezer attacks, AI is now being used to understand and manipulate such software.
Then there is the reality that many smaller firms lack the necessary resources to invest in cyber-security capabilities. Such businesses can then be used as gateways to other targets, including larger enterprises. The source of a recent hack of Polymarket, a betting platform, was a security flaw in a website-monitoring tool it used called DebugBear.
Some large companies are providing their smaller suppliers with cyber-security advice. Government programmes offer support, too. The PHP incident may furnish a template for how these businesses will be defended in future. Major providers of cloud infrastructure, such as Amazon and Cloudflare, quickly put in place a number of protections for their customers, such as firewalls, that shielded small businesses without them having to lift a finger.
Cyber-security has always been an arms race, and the advent of AI has handed attackers a devastating new weapon. In time the balance may shift back in favour of defenders, as software providers race to offer AI-powered solutions. Until then, businesses will have to confront a dangerous new world.

epub_72.title: As hackers run riot with AI, its makers want to cash in
epub_72.text:
As hackers run riot with AI, its makers want to cash in
Business
| Protection money
As hackers run riot with AI, its makers want to cash in
OpenAI and Anthropic spy a big opportunity in cyber-security
Nov 5th 2026
There has never been a better time to be a North Korean hacker. Last year the country’s cyber-thieves stole $2bn-worth of cryptocurrency, triple the level two years before, according to Chainalysis, a research firm. This year’s haul is on course to be much bigger. On October 29th $6.3bn was swiped from Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange. America’s Federal Bureau of Investigation has pointed the finger at the hermit kingdom.
The theft is but one example of a
worrying pattern
. Recent weeks have brought what looks to be a sharp acceleration in the frequency of damaging hacks. The details behind many remain murky. But what is clear is that advances in artificial intelligence have handed new powers to cyber-criminals, who are using it to churn out malware, execute sophisticated “phishing” schemes and, increasingly, to comb through software code looking for vulnerabilities.
The danger is, paradoxically, a golden opportunity for frontier labs. Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s finance chief, says she thinks cyber-security will become a “huge business” for her company over the next two years. It recently hired an executive from Wiz, an Israeli cyber-security firm owned by Google, to pitch its software to enterprises. Likewise, in paperwork recently filed for its forthcoming stock-market debut, Anthropic, OpenAI’s arch-rival, described cyber-security as “one of our most important near-term opportunities”. Yet cashing in on the cyber-risks posed by AI will be tricky for the model-makers.
Some expect that spending on cyber-security software—which reached $150bn last year, according to IDC, a data provider—will increase dramatically as firms recognise the growing threat. Greg Brockman, a co-founder of OpenAI, recently predicted that in time the figure will “vastly outstrip” spending on all other software. Last month Andreessen Horowitz, a venture-capital firm, urged firms it has invested in to consider doubling their outlays.
For AI labs, detecting cyber-vulnerabilities looks like a strong fit for their technology. Like coding, it is a “verifiable domain” where models can learn from answering questions correctly, explains Nazneen Rajani, chief executive of Collinear AI, which provides model-evaluation services.
Yet success will require persuading companies to rethink how they spend their cyber-security budgets. The business of identifying and patching vulnerabilities is highly fragmented, with customers historically tending to purchase tools from a variety of vendors and hiring IT consultancies to help with implementation. Anthropic and OpenAI are instead pitching the idea of letting their bots roam across an enterprise’s entire code base and fix weaknesses as they are found.
Lately the cyber-security market has been consolidating around a few so-called platforms, including independent vendors such as Palo Alto Networks and cloud giants such as Microsoft. But they also offer tools for other tasks where AI models are currently of less help, such as ensuring only approved users can access systems.
What is more, these incumbents have spent years building trust with their clients. Over the past few months, by contrast, the leading AI labs have had trouble controlling their own creations, with embarrassing episodes such as one in July where an OpenAI system
hacked into Hugging Face
, a model library, without being told to do so. Some in the cyber-security industry are sceptical that the model-makers will ever be able to forge the relationships needed to become leading cyber-security providers. Instead, the opportunity may lie in distributing their technology through others, while encouraging businesses to rewrite code securely from scratch using their models. The North Koreans will be hoping they fail.

epub_73.title: Besieged by war, Saudi Aramco continues to gush profits

Besieged by war, Saudi Aramco continues to gush profits
Business
| Barrelling along
Besieged by war, Saudi Aramco continues to gush profits
Higher oil prices comfortably make up for bombed facilities
Nov 5th 2026
SAUDI ARAMCO has proved remarkably resilient this year. Since war broke out with Iran, the world’s biggest oil company has faced attacks on its facilities and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, through which most of its barrels were shipped. Yet its cash gushers continue to flow. On November 3rd it reported an adjusted net profit for the quarter from July to September of $31bn, up by 9% from the previous year (see chart).
Aramco has been under fire before. In March 2022 Houthi rebels backed by Iran struck storage facilities in Jeddah, a year after an attack on a refinery in Riyadh. In 2019 they attacked the East-West pipeline, which carries Aramco’s oil to the Red Sea, along with two of the company’s processing facilities. This conflict has brought far more upheaval. But although production is down from pre-war levels, prices are up, and the business has been finding new ways to get its oil to market.
Aramco has been forced to continuously adapt over the past nine months. Soon after the conflict erupted in February the company began to transport more of its oil via the Red Sea, rather than the Persian Gulf. In July, when the Houthis blockaded the southern passage through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, it redirected its vessels north, to make greater use of the Suez-Mediterranean pipeline. Attacks on the East-West pipeline in September cut the volume of oil reaching the Red Sea, so Saudi Arabia has been sending tankers through the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman, where they transfer oil to the vessels of customers unwilling to make the journey themselves. (The pipeline has recently been repaired, with flows to the Red Sea recovering.)
Last month Aramco pushed around 7m barrels of oil a day to the market, up from 4.5m in July and not far off the figure in February, before the war. Overseas storage facilities in places such as the Netherlands and South Korea have also proved useful.
Aramco’s ability to weather the conflict is helped by fat margins. Its upstream costs, at $11.50 a barrel last year, including operating and capital expenditures, are a small fraction of the $95 a barrel fetched in its most recent quarter. The cost of restoring damaged facilities has so far been modest, with capital expenditure in the first nine months of 2026 down by 4% from the year before.
But transport has
become much more expensive
. According to the International Energy Agency, an intergovernmental body, the cost of shipping oil from the Persian Gulf to Asia is more than five times what it was before the war, as inefficiencies have reduced the availability of tankers. Some are stuck for days performing ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Those collecting barrels from the other end of the Suez-Mediterranean pipeline must then travel all the way around the Cape of Good Hope to supply customers in Asia. Aramco has had to bear some of the pain. It currently discounts the light crude it sells in Asia by about $5 a barrel, compared with the Dubai benchmark, up from $2 a barrel last month.
Besides expanding the East-West pipeline, Aramco intends to develop new export routes—which could become a costly endeavour and run up against the region’s volatile politics. One option under consideration is a pipeline from the oilfields in Saudi Arabia’s east to Duqm on the coast of Oman. Rystad Energy, a consultancy, estimates that it would stretch for around 1,000km and cost up to $7bn to build, equivalent to 14% of the company’s annual capex budget. An alternative is to restore the 1,500km Iraq-Saudi pipeline, which runs from Basra in Iraq to Yanbu, the Saudi port on the Red Sea. (The current pipeline was shut off during the first Gulf war in 1990, and has fallen into disrepair in the decades since.)
Amin Nasser, Aramco’s chief executive, has argued that investments in pipelines would quickly pay for themselves. That may well prove true if oil prices stay elevated and the Gulf’s other export routes remain unreliable. A resolution to the conflict with Iran may be hastened by Donald Trump’s defeat in the midterms. But during his earnings call Mr Nasser noted that global oil inventories are running low, and suggested that the need to replenish storage could result in elevated demand for two years after the war. For Aramco, then, the profits will keep flowing.

epub_74.title: Can a DoorDash-Instacart fusion stand up to Amazon and Walmart?
epub_74.text:
Can a DoorDash-Instacart fusion stand up to Amazon and Walmart?
Business
| Shopping spree
Can a DoorDash-Instacart fusion stand up to Amazon and Walmart?
The proposed merger shows the danger that delivery startups face
Nov 5th 2026
In the mid-2010s apps delivering victuals on demand cropped up everywhere. At a time when investors found cash-torching gig-economy startups alluring, some delivery businesses attracted valuations of many billions. But the days of their explosive growth are over. So far in 2026 downloads of standalone delivery apps in America and Canada are down by a fifth from the same period a year before, estimates Sensor Tower, a market-intelligence firm.
Today consolidation is in order. On October 29th DoorDash, a meal-delivery firm, said it would buy Instacart, a competitor focused on groceries, for $17bn. DoorDash expects the merger will eventually yield $500m of extra profit a year as the two firms fuse their software systems and advertising arms. If the merged entity is to take on Amazon and Walmart, which within a few years have come to dominate America’s online-grocery market, it will need every penny.
Online sales now account for a fifth of Americans’ spending on groceries, according to Brick Meets Click, a data provider. They have grown by more than 20% year on year for eight quarters. Yet the boom has benefited retail behemoths more than gig-economy disrupters. Walmart
learned to be a tech firm
and Amazon a grocer faster than newcomers could gain a foothold.
The two giants now account for 55% of America’s online-grocery sales, reckons Wedbush, a financial-services firm. Their expansion has squeezed Instacart and DoorDash, as well as others such as Uber Eats and Grubhub. Lately the upstarts have had to rely more on paid referrals and ads to win customers. “Everybody is fighting for the scraps left after the top players,” says Aaron Cheris of Bain, a consultancy.
In search of scale and new markets, delivery apps worldwide have been on a shopping spree. Last year DoorDash snapped up Britain’s Deliveroo just as Prosus, a technology-investment firm that owns delivery apps around the world, bought Just Eat Takeaway, a Dutch rival. Uber is poised to snaffle Delivery Hero, based in Berlin; it also considered gobbling up Instacart at least twice.
DoorDash’s purchase of Instacart, however, is about expanding within America. It will help DoorDash move further into groceries, which need more complex software than takeaway meals because workers have to shop in-store and find substitutes for missing items rather than just waiting for a brown-bagged restaurant order. It also allows DoorDash to combine Instacart’s ad business, which enjoys enviably high margins, with its own. For Instacart the deal offers the protection of scale: DoorDash’s market value of $73bn is more than five times its own.
Even under the deal-loving Trump administration, the merger is not sure to go through. As the midterm elections have shown, “
affordability”
is the hottest of political topics. Regulators may frown on deals that they suspect will push grocery bills up. Last month DoorDash and Instacart (as well as Uber and Walmart) were among the firms from which the Federal Trade Commission, a competition regulator, requested information on their use of personalised pricing.
DoorDash and Instacart argue that greater scale will mean lower costs and hence cheaper groceries. What is more, they add that their combined platform will help corner shops fend off the grocery giants. DoorDash has gone so far as to roll out a website called Shop Local Together, replete with mentions of affordability.
Even if regulators can be convinced of the merits of a deal, the combined business will be far from a guaranteed success. A combined DoorDash and Instacart should outmatch its gig-economy peers. But to thrive it will have to stand up to the world’s biggest retailers. That is a much harder sell.

epub_75.title: Is curiosity all it’s cooked up to be?
epub_75.text:
Is curiosity all it’s cooked up to be?
Business
| Bartleby
Is curiosity all it’s cooked up to be?
A quality that everyone lauds has its complexities
Nov 5th 2026
In any DISCUSSION about the human qualities that will matter to employers in an AI-inflected future, a few traits recur: taste, judgment, empathy, expertise. One of these bingo-card words is curiosity. Curious people are more likely to explore the contours of new technologies, runs the argument, and to master new skills. If you want a workforce that is capable of adapting to rapid change, inquisitiveness is a superpower.
It’s almost impossible to be against curiosity—which explains why job candidates tend not to brag about being totally uninterested in the world around them. But when everyone agrees on something, it’s usually worth wondering if there’s another side to the story.
True, curiosity has lots of benefits. Intellectual curiosity is predictive of academic success, according to a meta-analysis by Sophie von Stumm of the University of York and her co-authors. Inquisitiveness helps learning. A study by Matthias Gruber of Cardiff University and his colleagues found that people have better recall of information that they were eager to find out about (and even of things they had learned incidentally when they were in a state of heightened curiosity).
Curiosity also aids creativity. In a paper by Lydia Paine Hagtvedt of Akamai Technologies and her co-authors, participants were asked to guess how Harry Houdini had performed an illusion in which he made an elephant disappear. Those who were told their answer was close but not correct did better on a subsequent challenge to think up new tricks than a control group who had been told they had guessed correctly. The itch to solve a puzzle is an effective way to get people exploring lots of different ideas.
That same itch can benefit organisations in other ways. Curiosity hooks the interest of consumers. There must be better reasons to upgrade to LinkedIn’s premium tier, but none more powerful than wanting to see who on Earth keeps looking at your profile. If charity collectors solicit unusual amounts of money rather than the usual round numbers ($8.23, say, rather than $10), people appear to be more likely to donate. The specificity of the request piques interest, disrupting that rehearsed speech about needing to get to a meeting.
A sense of mystery can also be used to screen for curious job candidates. Google once stuck a maths problem on a billboard without revealing that it was the one paying. Anyone interested enough to solve the problem was led to a recruitment site.
Nonetheless, the intuition that curious employees must be wholly good for organisations is worth querying. For one thing, curiosity is inherently distracting. The first two paragraphs of this column, for example, contain one of the longest words in the English language whose letters appear in alphabetical order; a wildly curious person will start hunting for it now rather than reading on.
Inquisitive colleagues pull on loose threads, asking ever more questions and requesting ever more data. They may find something valuable, or they may just delay a decision. Curiosity entails moving from your immediate focus to something else that has drawn your attention, explains Spencer Harrison of INSEAD, a co-author of a paper on “productive inefficiency” that explores how short-term detours can lead to potential long-term pay-offs.
Curiosity is also closely associated with autonomy. Participants in a study by Nicola Schutte and John Malouff of the University of New England were asked to watch a video. Those who had some choice of what to watch were more curious about its subject-matter than those who were assigned one.
That raises questions for organisations about how much leeway employees should have to explore questions which interest them. In “The Scientific Mindset”, a new book, Stefan Thomke of Harvard Business School describes Booking.com’s  culture of experimentation. The travel site is famous for allowing product teams to launch their own A/B tests of new features, roughly 1,000 of which are running in parallel at any one time. Such decentralisation would be a leap for many firms.
An organisation that hires curious people is always going to be better off than one that selects people who are dead behind the eyes. But making the most of curiosity means accepting trade-offs—the time spent wandering down blind alleys, the experiments that go on largely out of sight. There’s almost nothing bad about curiosity. Almost.

epub_76.title: America’s copper giant has big dreams—but cautious plans
epub_76.text:
America’s copper giant has big dreams—but cautious plans
Business
| Scratching the surface
America’s copper giant has big dreams—but cautious plans
Freeport-McMoRan’s strategy hints at doubts that prices will continue to rise
Nov 5th 2026
Among the few areas of bipartisan consensus in Washington these days is the belief that securing access to critical minerals is vital to the national interest. In many cases Chinese miners have already established a daunting lead. But not in copper. That is thanks in no small part to Freeport-McMoRan, an American miner that is the world’s second biggest producer of the red metal, after BHP, a diversified Australian giant (see chart 1).
“Today really is Freeport’s time,” says Kathleen Quirk, chief executive of the Phoenix-based miner. Electrification and the artificial-intelligence boom will keep lifting copper demand, she argues, yet new supply is scarce and slow to develop. In the past 15 months copper prices have surged by 40%, bringing Freeport’s share price with them (see chart 2). That, combined with new technology and greater political support, leads Ms Quirk to suggest that America may be on the cusp of a copper version of the shale revolution. People once assumed that the country would remain dependent on imported oil and gas; instead it became a major exporter. Ms Quirk reckons her industry could see something similar.
One day, perhaps. But the strategy now being pursued by America’s copper giant will contribute only modestly. Last month Freeport said it was aiming to lift its total output of the metal to 4.5bn-5bn pounds by 2030, up from a projected 3bn in 2026. Its approach is strikingly incremental.
Freeport’s first priority is to restore output at its biggest mine—Grasberg, in Indonesia, which usually accounts for over 35% of its output (and is 51% owned by the Indonesian government). Since a giant mudslide in 2025 that killed seven workers, production there has been below par. Ms Quirk expects the site to have fully recovered by the end of 2027.
Next is to selectively expand existing sites. Most advanced is a plan to double the capacity of Bagdad, an 81-year-old mine in Arizona. On November 4th Freeport said its board had approved the $4.5bn investment, which Will Tankard of CRU, a consultancy, describes as “low risk”. Freeport says the project, which has all its permits, will break even at $4 a pound; copper trades near $6.40 today.
Bagdad’s doubling could add up to 250m pounds a year of copper supply by 2030. Freeport is also studying another mine expansion in Arizona, and seeking permits for one at El Abra in Chile, though neither will start before the next decade.
The final focus for Freeport is on new technology. At most of its mines it deposits ores that contain too little copper into giant stockpiles. These now hold about 40bn pounds of copper, says Ms Quirk.
To extract more from that ore, Freeport is experimenting with new forms of “leaching”, which uses acid to dissolve copper from rock. Last month the miner said it had tested a solution in the lab that may let it recover 800m pounds of copper a year from the stockpiles by 2030, up from a current annualised rate of 220m. Trials are planned in the field next year.
In 2025 Freeport has also converted Bagdad’s fleet to autonomous trucks. Ms Quirk says it plans to do the same elsewhere in America within the next few years to ease labour constraints, allowing it to produce more from existing mines. The company recently opened a centre in Phoenix to remotely perform dispatch work that used to be done on site.
For investors, however, Freeport has recently lost some of its lustre. From a peak in August, its share price has fallen by more than 20%. Partly that reflects disappointment over a downward revision to its projected sales and an upward revision to its capital expenditure over the near term. But it also points to discontent over the miner’s cautious approach.
Freeport has signalled little appetite for big acquisitions. Its strategy also lacks the “greenfield” projects that would be needed to vastly expand output—and turn America into a global copper power. That may reflect uncertainty over whether copper prices will continue to surge. A slowing global economy and the stagnation in China’s property market are weighing on demand. Tom Price of Panmure Liberum, a broker, reckons that this year’s price rally was caused mostly by hedge funds treating copper futures as a proxy for AI investment. If the data-centre binge comes to a halt, Freeport’s restraint will prove wise.

epub_77.text:
The break-up of CVS marks a turning point in American health care
Business
| Careworn
The break-up of CVS marks a turning point in American health care
The trend towards vertical integration may soon reverse
Nov 5th 2026
In the 1960s two brothers in Massachusetts co-founded a drugstore chain called the Consumer Value Stores. Today CVS is America’s largest such business. Yet over time it became much more than a pharmacy, first by expanding into the booming business of negotiating bulk discounts with drugmakers, and then by offering its own health-insurance plans. In all three markets it is one of America’s largest companies (see chart).
On November 4th CVS announced that it would unwind this vertically integrated model, by splitting in two. One half will be made up primarily of its insurance arm and the pharmacy-benefit manager (PBM) that negotiates drug prices, with annual revenue of around $300bn. The other will take its retail pharmacies and walk-in clinics, which together make a little over $90bn in sales a year. Measured by revenue affected, it is the largest break-up in over a decade, and the largest ever in health care. It also signals a turning point for the industry.
When CVS purchased Aetna, a health insurer, in 2018, it hailed the deal as the start of a new model for American health care. Companies would become more efficient by integrating and controlling large swathes of the country’s convoluted health system. At times the insurance arm has been a source of pain; two years ago profits were plummeting after the company misjudged the cost of services for patients on its health plans. But since then David Joyner, the boss of CVS, has restored Aetna to health—and proved the profitability of the vertically integrated model.
So why abandon it? The explanation may lie in an increasingly hostile political environment. Lawmakers in America—both Republicans and Democrats—have become critical of vertically integrated health-care firms, blaming them for passing high costs onto consumers.
Critics have been particularly focused on tie-ups between pharmacies and PBMs. Combining with PBMs allowed drugstore chains to share in the often opaque cut of rebates that these middlemen took from pharma companies, and to direct more business to their stores. Politicians now decry this as anti-competitive. In 2025 Arkansas became the first state to pass a law barring the integration of pharmacies with PBMs, though it is held up in the courts following a challenge from CVS and others. Neeraj Sood of the University of Southern California thinks other states will soon follow. Tennessee already has.
Investors appear nervous about the break-up plan. CVS’s share price fell by 13% following the announcement. That may reflect the poor prospects for the retail arm following a split. CVS’s pharmacy business is the market leader, and has fared better than competitors like Walgreens, which was taken private in 2025. But adjusted operating margins have fallen from 7.1% in 2021 to 4.7% this year, reckon analysts at JPMorgan Chase, a bank. Threats abound. Drugmakers such as Eli Lilly and Novo are bypassing pharmacies by selling weight-loss jabs and other medicines directly to consumers. E-commerce firms including Amazon are also muscling into the drugstore business.
Moreover, even CVS’s insurance-and-benefits arm may come into politicians’ cross-hairs before long. “If every insurer has their own PBM, there’s no incentive for new PBMs to come onto market,” says Dr Sood, as many of the potential customers are already spoken for. The end of vertical integration in American health care may just be getting started.

epub_78.title: The quest for immortality has become serious business
epub_78.text:
The quest for immortality has become serious business
Business
| Forever bound
The quest for immortality has become serious business
As entrepreneurs peddle scans and supplements, biotechs are probing the mysteries of ageing
Nov 5th 2026
On a quiet street in the posh London neighbourhood of Chelsea resides HUM2N, a longevity clinic. Inside, a man in socks, gloves and a headband steps into a fridge-sized cabinet chilled to -110°C. A few minutes of “cryotherapy” leave him, by his own account, invigorated. Next door a woman lies in a hyperbaric chamber—a pressurised capsule resembling a small submarine—breathing pure oxygen. Other clients take intravenous drips of NAD+, a molecule that cells need to turn food into energy; or have their blood drawn, mixed with ozone and put back. A package of five sessions at the clinic costs £3,000 ($4,025).
The quest to live for ever has lately garnered new interest. Dario Amodei, boss of Anthropic, an artificial-intelligence lab, has suggested that his technology could raise the human lifespan to 150 years. Sam Altman, his counterpart at OpenAI, has put more than $180m into Retro Biosciences, a startup aiming to add ten healthy years to human life. The powerful beyond Silicon Valley are eager, too. Last year Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were overheard musing that organ transplants might one day make immortality possible.
HUM2N’s clients range from bosses to athletes to patients in their 80s with chronic disease, says Mohammed Enayat, its founder. As the world ages, interest in living longer is seeping into the mainstream. Across the OECD, a club of mostly rich countries, nearly a fifth of people are aged 65 or over; by 2050 more than a quarter will be. One of the loudest evangelists is Bryan Johnson, a tech entrepreneur who hopes never to die. He has turned his regime into a Netflix documentary and a YouTube channel with more than 2m subscribers.
Two very different industries are looking to seize on the opportunity. The first is a colourful and lightly regulated group of clinics and online businesses selling supplements, scans and treatments of sometimes dubious efficacy. The second is slower moving but more consequential. Working in concert with the world’s biggest drugmakers, a crop of biotechs is developing medicines that might slow ageing itself—or even reverse it.
The prize is enormous. Pharma bosses long dismissed obesity as a niche market. GLP-1s proved them wrong, and made Eli Lilly the first drugmaker worth $1trn. A medicine that slowed ageing could be bigger still. “You can sell one year of life,” muses Alex Zhavoronkov, the founder of Insilico Medicine, an AI drug-discovery firm. “How much can you charge?”
Such a drug may be years away, if it comes at all. Into the gap has rushed a business catering to the impatient, one that sits largely outside conventional health care. Insurers cover almost none of it, so customers pay in cash.
First comes measurement, on the belief that tracking everything will catch problems early enough to fix them. Providers offer blood tests, genome sequencing and full-body scans that promise to spot cancers or autoimmune disorders before symptoms appear. Prenuvo, one such firm, charges around $4,000 for an MRI scan of a patient’s entire body. Many sell annual subscriptions, retesting customers regularly to look for changes. Neko Health, a Swedish provider backed by Daniel Ek, a co-founder of Spotify, raised $700m in July ahead of its launch in America.
Next comes treatment. Much of that takes place in longevity clinics like HUM2N. Some estimates put the number of these at about 800 in America alone. The label is unregulated and vague, says Andrea Maier of the National University of Singapore, who co-founded a longevity clinic herself. At too many, she says, customers pick their own treatment, as though ordering pizza. “It’s not care.”
The most adventurous patients head to Roatán, an island off Honduras, where clinics offer gene therapy, stem-cell infusions and other experimental treatments. Others turn to social media, where a growing number of influencers peddle elixirs. Mr Johnson’s company, Blueprint, sells supplements, a powdered “longevity mix”—and olive oil. Then there are the many online businesses selling injectable “peptides”, including the “Wolverine stack”, a combination that is claimed to speed the repair of muscles and tendons.
Little of this rests on solid science. The American College of Radiology, a professional body, says there is “no documented evidence” that full-body screening is cost-effective or prolongs life. Such scans can lead to over-diagnosis, turning up harmless anomalies that prompt needless further tests. The treatments fare no better. Studies of NAD+ supplements have been inconclusive or shown limited effect. Peptides are a wild west, with vendors often labelling them as “for research use only” to dodge regulators.
In parallel, drugmakers are looking for scientifically proven ways to add healthy years—a far more arduous process. America’s Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not treat ageing as a disease, so there is no route to approving a medicine that slows it. Would-be longevity drugs must instead win approval to treat a specific condition, often one linked to ageing, and then try to expand to others.
GLP-1s show how that might work. First approved for diabetes and then obesity, these drugs have since been shown to help with heart disease, sleep apnoea and kidney problems, all of which become more common with age. By lowering the risk of such conditions, the drugs may thus help people live longer. At a conference last month Lilly and Novo, its Danish rival, presented data suggesting that patients taking their GLP-1s were ageing more slowly. The yardstick was “ageing clocks”, which estimate how old a body really is (as opposed to how many birthdays it has had) from chemical marks on DNA or the mix of proteins in the blood. Novo found the biological age of the hearts of patients on its GLP-1s to be up to four years younger compared with those on a placebo, though all were overweight or diabetic. Lilly calls its own results preliminary.
Whatever GLP-1s turn out to do for ageing, they have already changed how big pharma thinks about the opportunity. Five or ten years ago drugmakers were chasing rare diseases, says Stephen Roper of L.E.K., a consultancy. But GLP-1s have re-established the appeal of mass-market drugs.
Rather than develop longevity treatments themselves, pharma giants mostly buy options on biotechs’ work. Lilly has struck a deal with Insilico worth up to $2.75bn. Novartis, a Swiss drugmaker, has one worth up to $550m with BioAge Labs, another biotech. The ranks of such startups are growing. Last year longevity biotechs raised $18.4bn, more than in the previous ten years combined (see chart).
Insilico calls its products “dual-purpose therapeutics”, each targeting ageing and a specific disease at the same time. A drug aimed only at ageing, argues Dr Zhavoronkov, its boss, would struggle to attract serious investors. Insilico’s most advanced candidate, rentosertib, treats idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a disease that scars the lungs. It entered a late-stage trial in July, making it one of the furthest along of any drug designed with ageing in mind. In an earlier trial of 42 patients, ageing clocks suggested that those on the drug were biologically younger than those on a placebo, by around three years on some measures, though all were already ill.
Other startups are looking to reverse ageing altogether. They include Mr Altman’s Retro; Altos Labs; and NewLimit, co-founded by Brian Armstrong, a crypto entrepreneur, which in June announced $435m in fresh funding. Most are betting on “epigenetic reprogramming”, the idea that the chemical switches on DNA, which become muddled with age, can be reset.
Previous efforts by drugmakers to create longevity treatments have ended in disappointment. In 2008 Britain’s GSK bought Sirtris, a biotech developing drugs inspired by resveratrol, a compound in red wine. Five years later it shut the firm down. Calico, launched by Google in 2013 to tackle ageing, has achieved little. Unity Biotechnology, a startup focused on clearing out ageing cells, laid off its entire staff in May last year after disappointing trials.
The new wave of biotech founders and investors argue this time will be different, thanks in part to AI, which they hope will accelerate discoveries. The first human trials for a drug targeting epigenetic reprogramming—a liver treatment developed by NewLimit—may begin next year. While the results are gathered, consumers will keep seeking immortality elsewhere.
