epub_80.title: AI is turning protectionists into free traders
epub_80.text:
AI is turning protectionists into free traders
Finance & economics
| Globalisation strikes back
AI is turning protectionists into free traders
Barriers to commerce are rising—except in technology
Nov 5th 2026
A YEAR AND a half ago Donald Trump was riding high and bent on reversing globalisation. As Americans fretted about the cost of living, the self-proclaimed “Tariff Man” declared “chronic trade deficits” a “national emergency” and slapped hefty tariffs on imports. The protectionist mood spread. In August India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, urged his fellow citizens to embrace swadeshi (self-sufficiency), insisting that not “a single foreign thing” should enter their homes. The European Union moved to double tariffs on steel imports. Mexico approved steep levies on goods from China and other Asian economies. An index compiled by economists from the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and the IMF shows that restrictive trade measures rose by over 60% in 2025 alone.
Yet for all the protectionist fervour, global trade today is booming. Since the final quarter of 2024, just before Mr Trump returned to office, the dollar value of world trade has surged by more than 27%. The pace has accelerated this year. In the first eight months of 2026 it was up by 18% on the same period last year, a remarkable pace by historical standards. Even by volume, trade is expected to grow faster than the world economy for a second year running—a hallmark of globalisation’s heyday before the financial crisis of 2007-09.
Free traders can thank artificial intelligence. As firms race to build data centres, trade in the servers, chips and networking equipment that power them has soared. Governments, eager to build AI capabilities at home, have largely spared foreign hardware from tariffs. Using the WTO’s classification of AI-related goods, The Economist calculates that trade in such products exploded by 55% in the first eight months of 2026, compared with a year earlier. Strip out AI-related goods and world trade is still growing, but at a far less impressive pace (see chart 1, top panel). AI hardware accounts for about a quarter of world imports, up from 15% in 2023. Protectionists, it seems, have learned to love free trade when it suits them.
Nowhere is AI trade perkier than in America. Spending on computers, telecoms gear and data-centre construction now amounts to 2.5% of GDP. Almost all the kit comes from abroad: for every dollar America invests in high-tech equipment, it imports roughly 90 cents’ worth, according to the Federal Reserve. Imports of AI-related goods are on course to exceed an eye-watering $1trn this year.
The world’s largest importer, then, is not retreating from globalisation quite as planned. America’s goods imports have risen by 16% since late 2024, roughly in line with their trend from 2018 to 2024. But the AI boom has transformed what America buys from abroad. We calculate that imports of AI-related products surged by 69% in the first eight months of 2026, compared with the same period last year. Imports of everything else fell by 10% (see chart 1, bottom panel). Three years ago America imported more than five times as much in vehicles, oil, pharmaceuticals and metals as in servers, chips and networking kit. Now the latter group has edged ahead.
Since his “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025, Mr Trump has largely spared hardware powering the AI boom. Fully 97% of computing-hardware imports and 85% of networking-equipment imports fall into categories covered by tariff exemptions, according to a study by an economist at the Minneapolis Fed. In 2025 Uncle Sam collected tariffs equivalent to less than 2% of the value of imported computing and networking equipment, compared with nearly 10% on goods unrelated to AI.
Even the grandly named “semiconductor tariffs” imposed in January are full of holes. The 25% levy is aimed chiefly at advanced chips such as Nvidia’s H200, which must pass through America for inspection on their way from Taiwan to China. Exemptions for American data centres, startups, research and other domestic uses are so sweeping that the Congressional Research Service, a non-partisan beancounter, questions whether any of the affected imports of chips would pay the tariff at all.
The protectionist-in-chief’s embrace of free trade has complicated his ambition to shrink America’s trade deficit. In September the goods deficit reached $136bn, more than 70% wider than a year earlier, as total imports hit a record high. Appetite for foreign AI hardware is part of the explanation. America accounts for four in ten global imports of servers, computer parts and networking gear, against just one in six for other goods. Its exports of such equipment are nowhere near large enough to offset these purchases. The result is by far the largest AI-related trade deficit among major economies (see chart 2, top panel). Had imports of AI-related goods grown at the same pace as other imports in recent years, the goods deficit would have been 16%, or nearly $200bn, smaller in 2025.
All this shows the folly of judging economic success by trade deficits. A server assembled abroad worsens the goods balance when it enters the country. But installed in an American data centre, it becomes productive capital, generating computing power for years to come. Research by the Fed finds that previous technology-driven investment booms widened the current-account deficit even as they raised output. Free trade allows American firms to concentrate on what they do best, from chip design to AI research and software, while relying on specialised manufacturers abroad for the equipment.
AI’s labyrinthine supply chains, meanwhile, expose the limits of reshoring. Six economies—Taiwan, Mexico, Vietnam, Thailand, South Korea and Malaysia—account for more than four-fifths of America’s AI imports (see chart 2, bottom panel). Mexico and Taiwan alone supply 85% of its imports of AI servers and other computer-processing kit. Though this will include some rerouted goods, China’s observable share of such imports has plunged, as have those of other countries outside the sextet.
Consider an Nvidia GB300 AI server rack destined for an American data centre. Its chips are designed in America, fabricated in Taiwan using Dutch lithography machines fitted with precision mirrors made in Germany, and paired with high-bandwidth memory, a South Korean speciality. Eighteen compute trays, containing 72 powerful AI chips, then travel from Taiwan to Mexico, where workers combine them with cooling systems, power modules, network switches and components sourced from China and Vietnam. The completed racks then head north across the border. And that is the simplified version. Even Nvidia’s Blackwell AI chips, now being fabricated by Taiwan's biggest chipmaker in Arizona, must travel back to Asia to be packaged with high-bandwidth memory.
Mr Trump’s unlikely embrace of free trade has its limits, even in AI. His tariffs on steel, aluminium and copper are making data centres more expensive to build, raising the cost of everything from building materials to cooling systems. The Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a think-tank, estimates that existing metal tariffs could add $130bn to America’s planned data-centre buildout by 2030.
Worse could be coming. The president is considering broader tariffs on semiconductors and products containing them, potentially including the servers powering America’s AI boom. A blanket 25% levy could add $360bn to data-centre construction costs, CSIS reckons.
Perhaps the midterm elections  on November 3rd will make the administration think twice. Americans liked the idea of tariffs until their prices rose as a result. Now they are rediscovering their inner free traders. Roughly two-thirds of voters in the midterms believe Mr Trump’s levies have hurt the economy, according to election-night polling. Discontent over living costs helped Democrats make sweeping gains. Even if the president does not take the hint, though, globalisation is proving a stubborn thing to kill.

epub_81.title: Intensive parenting is no longer the preserve of the rich
epub_81.text:
Intensive parenting is no longer the preserve of the rich
Finance & economics
| Tiger mothers of the world, unite
Intensive parenting is no longer the preserve of the rich
But wealthy families still come out on top
Nov 5th 2026
RICH PARENTS are different. They have money. They also used to be different in spending pots of it on their offspring’s edification. Yet as competition for university places and well-paying jobs heats up, parents across income levels are bankrolling their children’s futures earlier and more aggressively. From piano lessons for toddlers to tennis for teenagers, intensive parenting is on the rise.
The sums are significant. More than half of American children take part in a sport after school or at weekends. In 2024 this cost the average family $1,016, just for one child’s main sport. That was a 46% jump from 2019, twice the cumulative rate of inflation. Between the logistics of chauffeuring children to several practices each week and conferring with coaches, American parents are dedicating more than 15 hours a week to their children’s sports—a commitment on a par with a part-time job.
As with young bodies, so with young minds. Private tutoring has long been an obsession in richer parts of Asia. Three in four school-age South Koreans took paid lessons in 2025, according to national surveys, including 57% in the lowest income quintile. So did four in five five-year-olds. The OECD, a club of mostly rich countries, estimates that average tutoring spending per pupil has reached roughly a tenth of average household disposable income.
Now other Asian parents are splashing out. Around 27% of pupils in India, and 31% of those in urban areas, receive private tuition. In China spending on education has grown fastest in the poorest regions.
The trend is not confined to Asia. One in three French pupils aged 15-18 is enrolled in private coaching. The share of state-educated British ones with access to tutoring is now nearly level for the poorest and richest households; 37% of those from the lowest quartile have them, just shy of the 39% among the richest quartile, according to the Sutton Trust, an education charity. In London the figure for state-school pupils rises to 45% (see chart 1). The gap has narrowed in part thanks to an expansion of state-funded tutoring schemes. Yet parents are paying, too: 30% of British youngsters aged 11-16 in state schools say they have had private tutoring, up from 18% in 2005, Sutton Trust’s data show.
Matthias Doepke of the London School of Economics and Fabrizio Zilibotti of Yale University find that, historically, the more unequal the country, the less attention parents pay to soft virtues like independence or imagination (see chart 2). Western populations believe inequality to be increasing, and a middle-class lifestyle is perceived to be less of a given, meaning parents have grown less relaxed. Their focus is shifting to qualities like hard work, which intensive parenting tries to instil.
High-pressure education comes at a growing cost, too. In 1990 private spending in America on schools and universities, plus tutoring, coaching and the like, worked out at 18% of total lifetime educational investment (including public spending), according to the National Transfer Accounts, an international research project. By 2020 (the latest figure available) the share was 24%, equivalent to $68,000. In 2023 private  spending accounted for 42% of lifetime educational investment per child in South Korea, an eye-watering $152,000 (also in 2020 dollars).
Yet these investments do not necessarily translate into social mobility. That may be because although the poor are spending more, the rich are not letting up. The likelihood that children do better than their parents has stagnated over the past decade in France and Spain, and collapsed in Singapore and South Korea. Getting into a top university is harder than ever. Harvard admits 3% of applicants, down from 30% in 1960. The share of rural students admitted to Peking University dropped from a third between 1978 and 1998 to around a sixth in 2021—faster than the relative decline in China’s rural population.
Even with a degree in hand, 30% of Americans from non-graduate family backgrounds reach the top fifth of earners, compared with 41% of those whose parents attended university, according to the Sutton Trust. Although the share of adults from non-graduate families earning a university degree has climbed by ten percentage points over the past decade, the college earnings premium such people could expect fell by 11 percentage points. In Britain graduates who grew up in poverty, defined by eligibility for free school meals, earned 7% less than their peers a decade after graduating from the same university and course, according to the Resolution Foundation, a think-tank. In a competition for their children’s future, rich parents still have the edge.

epub_82.title: America’s renters are in serious trouble
epub_82.text:
America’s renters are in serious trouble
Finance & economics
| Past due
America’s renters are in serious trouble
Several gauges of their financial health are flashing red
Nov 5th 2026
Jacob ramirez, a 31-year-old operations manager for a café chain, has long struggled to make ends meet. In college he used a credit card to buy textbooks; after graduating, he occasionally did so to pay rent and utility bills. By 2022 he, his wife and their dog were in a one-bedroom flat in Pomona, east of Los Angeles. But rising rent and other expenses—“like an anaconda snake choking me out”—pushed him deeper into debt. In 2023, owing $28,000 on five cards, Mr Ramirez turned to a non-profit debt-counselling service. He is on track to pay his debts by 2028.
America’s economy is growing steadily, thanks to an artificial-intelligence boom and robust consumer spending. But for three or four years a divide has been opening between homeowners and renters like Mr Ramirez, who make up a third of American households. An analysis by The Economist suggests that tenants are increasingly missing payments and turning to costly short-term credit, even as homeowners’ finances remain resilient. Is America experiencing a renters’ recession?
Their difficulties represent a turnaround. During the global financial crisis of 2007-09 it was homeowners who suffered. By 2010 one in 20 mortgages was in foreclosure and one in ten delinquent. House prices had fallen by nearly a quarter; nearly one in four homeowners owed more than their dwellings were worth.
Now it is the turn of renters to suffer more. The Federal Reserve’s latest Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF), published last month, shows that in the past year more than one in eight were at least 60 days late on a loan payment, the most since records began in 1989 (see chart 1). Another Fed survey, in late 2025, found that a quarter had not paid all their bills in full the previous month, compared with one in ten mortgage-holders (see chart 2). About one in six finds it “difficult to get by”, more than three times the rate among mortgage-holders.
Some of the divide reflects demography. Renters tend to be younger, poorer and less educated: their median household income in 2025 was $57,000, against $103,000 for homeowners. But these characteristics explain three-fifths of the gap between renters and mortgage-holders, we calculate. What about the rest?
Partly, the rent. Since 2019 rents in America have risen by 42%, according to the Census Bureau, a government agency, while renters’ household incomes have gone up by 34%. Mortgage-holders’ housing costs outpaced their incomes by a similar margin. But much of this reflects higher payments for new buyers, who have been screened by lenders for their ability to pay and whose mortgage payments are typically fixed for several years. Renters face higher payments when leases expire, whether they can afford them or not.
Next, a lack of savings to fall back on. The typical renter has $2,000 in liquid savings, according to the SCF, versus $12,000 for mortgage-holders. Homeowners also tend to have larger investment portfolios. “A lot of homeowners are supporting their spending by withdrawing from their brokerage funds,” says Ted Gayer of the JPMorgan Chase Institute, a think-tank within a bank. The resumption of student-loan repayments after the covid-19 pandemic added to the strain, accounting for about half of the recent rise in renters falling behind on their debts, but only about a quarter of that among mortgage-holders.
Renters are putting off paying other bills. They have gone from being less likely than mortgage-holders to incur late fees on credit cards to being more likely, after controlling for income, age and other demographic factors, according to our calculations using data from the FINRA Foundation. Some renters are turning to other forms of short-term borrowing. Another Fed survey finds that more than one in ten took out a payday loan or pay-cheque advance in 2025, nearly twice the share in 2019. Saving must wait: “As rents increase, the ability to save, whether it’s for a down-payment, for an emergency, for whatever, is really much harder,” says Whitney Airgood-Obrycki of Harvard University’s Joint Centre for Housing Studies.
And some, like Mr Ramirez, are seeking help. Once his debts are cleared, he hopes to start saving for his own home. Others have a much longer road ahead.

epub_83.title: What markets make of the midterms
epub_83.text:
What markets make of the midterms
Finance & economics
| Waves and ripples
What markets make of the midterms
Democrats triumph. Investors yawn
Nov 5th 2026
IN GEOLOGY, AN earthquake causes a tsunami. In American politics, a
blue tsunami
is causing an earthquake. In midterm elections on November 3rd the Democratic Party swept all before it. Ruby-red Texas elected a blue senator for the first time in decades and crimson Kansas for the first time in nearly a century. As we published this the Senate race in Mississippi, where Donald Trump last won by 23 percentage points, was too close to call.
In financial markets, the response to these seismic events was, for the most part, a shrug. The S&P 500 index of large American firms ticked up the morning after and ended the day 1.6% higher. Yields on ten-year Treasury bonds edged down. The dollar weakened by a touch.
Investors’ indifference is understandable. They like certainty, and the Democratic wave precluded the nightmare scenario of an endlessly contested election or even a constitutional crisis. After the scale of his Republican Party’s rout became clear on election night, Mr Trump told the New York Times that he would accept the results. Call it the “phew” effect.
Markets also like the inevitable stasis of divided government—at least in America, where the business environment is already favourable (political paralysis is more of a problem in places like Europe, where the underlying conditions are not pro-growth). If anything,
oversight from a reinvigorated Congress
will probably make it a bit harder for the president to raise tariffs, wage wars and gut the public sector. Fights over the budget are inevitable, but then they would have been anyway. And Democrats have tended to be less willing than Republicans to court sovereign default by blocking rises to the federal debt ceiling.
Still, placidity on the surface conceals more churn beneath, especially in equities (see chart). One loser is Elon Musk. The right-wing sometime trillionaire wasted nearly $500m trying to help elect Republicans in this year’s races. Democrats will return the favour by poring over the government’s contracts with his carmaker, Tesla, and his rocketry firm, SpaceX. Their share prices fell by 3% and 4%, respectively.
Other federal contractors do not inspire as much personal animus among Democrats. But they can still expect scrutiny now that the opposition party controls the purse strings, especially in industries that lefties find objectionable. Private-prison operators such as CoreCivic and GEO, both of which have assisted Mr Trump’s heartless mass-deportation effort, shed value on fears that the incoming Congress would squeeze the immigration budget. Democrats are also unlikely to accept Mr Trump’s request to spend $1.5trn on defence, hitting Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, RTX and other armsmakers.
The second group of losers comprises firms whose fortunes depend wholly on the buildout of artificial-intelligence data centres. These installations were supported by many Republicans—until they provoked a backlash which the Democrats ruthlessly exploited. Three of the four states which accounted for half of planned new capacity—Georgia, Ohio and Texas—have Republican governors. From next year all four will have Democratic ones. In Texas, the top destination for data centres, the governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, campaigned on a promise to impose an immediate moratorium on their construction.
The share price of CoreWeave, a big independent data-centre operator, duly slumped by 10%. Micron, which makes memory chips that go into AI servers, lost 7% of its value. Nvidia, the $5trn behemoth of AI-chipmaking, slipped by 3%. Manufacturers of electrical components—lots of which are needed in data centres and in power plants that supply them with electricity—have also taken a knock. Before the elections the two parties had reached a tentative deal on a bill that would make it easier for big energy projects, such as pipelines and wind farms, to secure the necessary permits. Democrats may now wish to drive a harder bargain. The shares of GE Vernova, Vistra and Vertiv each lost around a tenth of their value.
Conversely, the blue wave has lifted industries that can count on Trumpian budget cuts being unwound (health care and clean energy) and large spenders on data centres. Big tech’s “hyperscalers” may now spend less, preserving their margins, while facing less competition for their existing capacity from CoreWeave and the like. Amazon and Microsoft were up by more than 6%. Alphabet gained over 3%. Even Meta, led by the manospheric Mark Zuckerberg, edged up. The tech bosses can expect to be hauled before Congress for adversarial hearings, both about AI and their obsequiousness towards Mr Trump. But at least their next earnings calls may turn out to be more amicable.

epub_84.title: Indebted tycoons haunt China’s banking system
epub_84.text:
Indebted tycoons haunt China’s banking system
Finance & economics
| Collateral damage
Indebted tycoons haunt China’s banking system
Lenders are feeling the hangover from years of Wild East capitalism
Nov 5th 2026
ON OCTOBER 31ST Bank of Shanghai gave investors a nasty shock. It said its net profit had collapsed by 93% in the third quarter, year on year, to 350m yuan ($53m); its non-performing loans shot up by 75% in the first nine months of 2026; and the capital set aside to cover unexpected losses hit the lowest in a decade. Its share price plunged by over 10%. The main source of the lender’s troubles seems to be its relationship with one man, Yao Zhenhua.
Mr Yao has been stalking Chinese finance since 2015. That year his conglomerate, Baoneng, made a hostile bid for Vanke, a giant property developer. This was a triple surprise: such takeovers are almost unheard of in China; they are entirely unheard of when the target is, like Vanke, partly state-owned; and Baoneng financed the deal in an unconventional way, using premiums from several insurers it owned. This brazenness earned Mr Yao the nickname “barbarian”, in tribute to American corporate raiders of the late 1980s.
The takeover failed and Mr Yao’s use of premiums was found to be illegal (China tightly regulates how they can be invested). In 2017 he was banned from the insurance industry for ten years. But he expanded his empire in other areas. This included a 6.6bn yuan debt-fuelled investment in Qoros, a maker of electric cars. As Bank of Shanghai has disclosed, commercial conquest has not gone well for the barbarian.
As part of a long-running lawsuit against Mr Yao and Baoneng, the lender has sought to recover loans extended to his companies worth at least 12.9bn yuan. The loans were secured in 2020 with property and with personal guarantees from Mr Yao. This collateral took a hit when China’s property sector imploded. Qoros, meanwhile, sold too few cars and folded. In January this year Mr Yao, whose poor credit score bans him from commercial flights and luxury hotels, appeared in a social-media post claiming that local government officials had cheated him out of his investment in the car firm.
The most stunning revelation from Bank of Shanghai is that Mr Yao and his companies have “no executable assets” from which to recover those debts. This would explain photos posted to social media of someone looking remarkably like him riding the metro in Shenzhen, a big southern city, rather than taking a limo. More importantly for Bank of Shanghai’s investors, it explains what happened to the lender’s profits, which were eaten up by huge impairment losses. Many other Chinese banks that have done business with Mr Yao and Baoneng may be next.
Mr Yao is not the first tycoon to rattle the banking system. In 2019 another, Xiao Jianhua, caused a mini financial crisis. He is in prison. A fellow indebted plutocrat, Lai Xiaomin, was executed in 2021. Despite the Communist Party’s efforts to rid Chinese finance of such rogues, the Baoneng barbarian is probably not the last.

China’s AI stock-market struggles are a warning
Finance & economics
| Buttonwood
China’s AI stock-market struggles are a warning
What happens when the supply of new tech catches up with demand?
Nov 5th 2026
IN THE GOOD old days China appealed to investors as the world’s greatest convergence story. Its living standards would catch up with those in the West, its economy would multiply in size and the value of its stock market would grow in tandem. Or so the story went. Investors just needed to position themselves on the right side of history before everyone else arrived.
In more recent years China’s residual appeal to global investors has rested on the opposite logic—not convergence, but diversification. There is less talk of China’s destiny, more recognition of its idiosyncrasy. China, it has become clear, dances to the beat of the Communist Party’s own drum. That means it can defy global trends, good and bad.
One recent example is the stock market. Global equities have risen by 11% this year, according to the MSCI World index, despite recent jitters. Other East Asian economies like South Korea and Taiwan have ridden the artificial-intelligence boom to far greater heights. China is also tightly stitched into the AI supply chain and boasts several innovative model-makers of its own, including listed companies like Z.ai and MiniMax, which both trade in Hong Kong. But China’s tech shares have plummeted in the second half of the year, onshore and off. And its blue-chip index, the CSI 300, is down by more than 11% so far in 2026. Chinese equities have put the sync into idiosyncrasy.
China’s government seems fed up with this particular source of exceptionalism. The rout has prompted fresh buying from the “national team”, state-owned financial institutions that prop up the market when needed. China’s central bank has also lent a hand. On November 2nd it said it would dust off a scheme that helps institutional investors, such as insurers and brokers, obtain the liquid collateral they need to finance their equity purchases. It will also make it cheaper for companies to borrow to buy back their own shares.
Why is the stock market sagging? Some of it has to do with those Chinese characteristics. Take fiscal policy. Other big economies would benefit from budgetary restraint but will see little of it. In China, by contrast, the government is tightening its belt when it should be loosening it. Its fiscal deficit, broadly defined, will narrow this year by 1.4% of GDP, reckons Goldman Sachs, a bank.
An endless property slump is also still taking a toll. On October 29th Fitch, a credit-rating agency, said it might downgrade the bonds issued by Zhuhai Huafa Group, a state-owned conglomerate based in China’s Pearl River Delta. Known for a 72-storey tower overlooking the coastal cities of Zhuhai and Macau, the group also has lofty debts worth 413bn yuan ($62bn). According to Bloomberg, it recently delayed payment on two trust products (debt obligations that do not trade on exchanges) and asked for an extension on bank loans. The share price of its listed property unit fell by more than a fifth—never mind that the group’s main owner, the city of Zhuhai, is unlikely to let it default on a publicly traded bond.
Another explanation for China’s underperformance is more worrying. It may be an early victim of an investment trend that seems to be spreading around the world: the loss of enthusiasm for AI. In the West investors have begun to worry that AI models will eventually become commoditised. Pricing power will disappear as innovators struggle to maintain a durable lead over imitators. In China that grim end-game was more or less the industry’s starting-point.
Chinese AI labs openly shared the mathematical “weights” that make models clever. That encouraged adoption, and helped the labs attract brainiacs motivated by intellectual glory as well as financial success. But openness comes at a commercial cost. The AI-related revenues of China’s six leading firms together amount to about a tenth of the combined revenues of America’s top two, OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Epoch AI, a research firm.
China may also offer a foretaste of what happens when the supply of new tech shares finally catches up with demand. It has tested investors’ appetite with a crowded pipeline of initial public offerings. America may find that Anthropic’s highly anticipated listing provokes similar indigestion, even in its much bigger market.
China’s oddities deter many global investors. A bigger worry in tech circles is that China’s lean present becomes the rest of the world’s future. China may be less an outlier than an omen.

epub_86.title: William Nordhaus, favourite economist of the right and the left
epub_86.text:
William Nordhaus, favourite economist of the right and the left
Finance & economics
| Free Exchange
William Nordhaus, favourite economist of the right and the left
The Nobel-prizewinner was fascinated by what happens when markets fail
Nov 5th 2026
WILLIAM NORDHAUS had faith in the tools of his profession. For decades he helped run Yale University’s economics department, where he arrived in 1967, aged 26, and stayed until he died on October 30th. He edited “Economics”, a textbook still used by American undergraduates. And he was convinced that economic methods could be useful to other disciplines, leaving wonkish topics behind in pursuit of debates that consumed policymakers: the climate, technology and taxes.
His faith made him unflinching—and unafraid of a fight. No other economist of his generation worked across such a breadth of controversial topics. He pioneered carbon prices (which helped earn him a Nobel prize in 2018), pleasing America’s progressives and irking its conservatives. He also defended billionaires, with the opposite effect. As a result, he became a rare economist to win the respect of the left and right alike.
Economics relies on the price system. Mr Nordhaus spent his life calculating prices that are missing. His doctoral thesis examined such failures in the knowledge economy, and suggested the optimal patent life for inventions that minimises underinvestment in copyable ideas and maximises social welfare. In the 1970s he decided that building theoretical models of technological change was “too hard” (and left the task to Paul Romer, with whom he shared the Nobel). So he turned to climate change instead.
Although the practice of climate economics would in time become politically fraught, the theory was manageable. Economic growth depended on energy. Firms that produced and used energy were not bearing the cost of the resulting carbon pollution. The warming that would ensue could hurt growth. What to do? One research group at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology favoured abandoning growth altogether. Mr Nordhaus disagreed. The problem, he thought, was a lack of a model that brought together the scientific and economic equations to connect growth, emissions and the environment.
Mr Nordhaus spent the next two decades trying to construct one. In 1992 he published a paper outlining the “dynamic integrated climate economy” (DICE) model. Its more than 20 equations eventually ranged from basic economic ones he taught undergraduates to scientific predictions about the risk of catastrophes and forecasts about how humans would adapt to a hotter world. Throw in a discount rate, the value placed on the lives of future generations relative to the present, and the model churns out the path of emissions reductions that would not plunge millions into poverty today, as a result of insufficient energy production, or tomorrow, if global warming wrecked the economy. The carbon price which would set the world on that path equalises the cost of abating an extra tonne of CO2 and that of the damage this tonne would do in the future. As concerns about climate change mounted, so did interest in this work. By 2010 Barack Obama’s administration had incorporated DICE into American policy.
Mr Nordhaus’s climate economics had critics. He fought a long battle with Nicholas Stern, a British economist who favoured more weight on future lives. Some climate scientists thought he underestimated the probability of catastrophic events and contested the conclusion of his DICE paper that the economically optimal outcome was to allow average global temperature to rise by 3°C above pre-industrial levels. Yet even as they challenged some of his numerical assumptions, his detractors happily worked within his framework.
DICE made Mr Nordhaus a climate celebrity. But it was only the tip of a vast iceberg of academic output. A paper from 1975 suggested that politicians loosened monetary policy to bring down unemployment in the months before elections to win votes—and led to a proliferation of similar political-economy studies. In 1996 he compared the cost of generating the equivalent of an hour’s worth of light from a modern lightbulb over the ages. His conclusion, that it plummeted from 5.4 hours of a worker’s labour in 1800 to less than half a second in 1992, implied that conventional price indices vastly understate gains in living standards.
He eventually returned to the preoccupation of his doctoral days. In 2005 he used American records from 1948 to 2001 to calculate that inventors got just 4% of the value their inventions brought to society. The economic contributions of innovators, in other words, far exceeded their fortunes. The paper appeared as America was minting new tech billionaires, and its arguments were embraced by their defenders. If the self-made tycoons give so much to society, why tax them more? Even progressive Californians seem to agree: in midterm elections on November 3rd most of the state’s voters appear to have rejected a ballot measure to tax billionaires’ wealth.
Above all, Mr Nordhaus’s economics was a triumph of pragmatism. He believed in moulding messy problems into understandable frameworks—and embracing the implications, regardless of where they took you. Producing numbers that were useful, he thought, was sometimes more important than being precise. The best economic predictions, he argued in a paper in 1987, are the ones that incorporate the most information (his own informed projection made a decade before, that global temperatures would have risen by about 1°C by around now, was on the money).
He imparted openmindedness to his students at Yale, too, patiently taking their questions after lectures—often for hours given how packed these got. In another display of enlightened generosity, he presented the Nobel museum with the ancient Babylonian lamp he procured while investigating the cost of light. Beside his intellectual gifts to economics, this was but a flicker.

epub_88.title: Astronomers are mystified by little red dots in the sky
epub_88.text:
Astronomers are mystified by little red dots in the sky
Science & technology
| Connecting the dots
Astronomers are mystified by little red dots in the sky
They could be the universe’s first supermassive black holes
Nov 5th 2026
WHEN THE James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), a high-resolution camera orbiting the Sun, began sending images back to Earth in 2022, astronomers were greeted with something strange. Alongside the eclectic cast of cosmic characters they had been expecting—stars, galaxies, nebulae and the like—were a handful of small, red-tinted points of light, or, as the technical jargon has it, “little red dots”. Astronomers had no idea what they were.
In looking for answers they have turned to the most mysterious objects in the universe—black holes. For some astronomers, the dots are black holes caught in unprecedentedly violent growth spurts. For others, they are bizarre, star-like objects with black holes at their centre. Getting it right matters: these dots could reveal the origins of the supermassive black holes that sit at the centre of galaxies, and explain how they got so big so quickly. The debate is fierce, says Dale Kocevski, an astronomer at Colby College, in Maine. “I’ve never quite seen anything like this.”
What is known is that the little red dots are, unsurprisingly, little—typically with a width less than 0.5% of the Milky Way’s—and red, emitting bright light that is rich in longer, redder wavelengths. They are also old. The universe’s first little red dots were born in the cosmic dawn 13.4bn years ago, when the universe was around 500m years old—not long after the first galaxies appeared. Since the dots were first discovered more than 500 of them have been reported, and the number continues to rise. “In every single image you’re taking, you’re seeing one of these objects stare right back at you,” says Rohan Naidu, an astronomer at the University of Hawaii who was part of the team that coined the term. “So they have to be important.”
When astronomers first saw the little red dots, they thought the objects were the glow of very populous mature galaxies. But such well-developed galaxies would not have had enough time to form so soon after the Big Bang. That led some to dub the dots “universe breakers”, whose existence implied the universe might be older than previously thought.
Then, in early 2023, Dr Kocevski and his colleagues discovered a unique pattern in the spectrum of light the dots produce. It suggested that they were surrounded by a cloud of dense, rapidly moving hydrogen gas. To get gas moving at the necessary speeds, huge gravitational forces would be needed. That disfavoured universe-breaking galaxies, as the large distances between their stars would keep the forces relatively small. Instead, a huge amount of mass would need to be concentrated in a tiny volume. That is the perfect description of a black hole.
But this seems paradoxical. The gravity of black holes is so strong that not even light can escape their grasp: how, then, could they glow? The answer is that as matter falls into them, a process known as accretion, it emits radiation as it heats up. If a black hole is big enough, that radiation can be extraordinarily intense. For example, active galactic nuclei (AGNs)—accreting supermassive black holes at the centre of most galaxies—are among the universe’s brightest light sources.
Accreting black holes could thus be responsible for the brightness of the little red dots seen by the JWST. And although ordinary AGNs are surrounded by doughnuts of gas and dust, the heavy elements that make up the dust may not have had time to form so early in the universe’s history. “There may be so much gas that that doughnut becomes a cocoon,” says Dr Kocevski. “It completely envelops the thing.” Light interacting with the hydrogen gas would also come out reddened.
But there is a problem. AGNs also release X-rays as the matter falling into them heats up. Little red dots, however, emit almost none at all. To explain this, the AGN advocates propose that the central black holes are accreting at an unusually high rate. Just as it is hard to get off a train as a crowd is scrambling to get on, the build-up of infalling matter limits how many X-rays can break through. For Dr Kocevski the appeal of this explanation comes down to Occam’s razor: “These are things we already know about, just slightly modified.”
Dr Naidu, however, is in a more imaginative camp. “We just need to concede that this is a fundamentally new kind of astrophysical object,” he says. Dr Naidu and his colleagues propose that the little red dots are neither stars nor black holes, but something that shares features with both. Their imagination, however, does not extend to nomenclature: they call these novelties “black-hole stars”.
Like an AGN, a black-hole star is an accreting black hole wrapped in a gas cocoon. But this cocoon’s density is much greater. So great, in fact, that no radiation emitted by the black hole’s infalling matter—not light, not X-rays—can ever directly escape. Instead, the radiation is absorbed by the innermost layer of gas, causing it to emit new radiation, at longer wavelengths, which the next layer will absorb. After many such stages, say the idea’s proponents, the light would emerge from an outer layer similar to a star’s glowing surface, possessing a distinctive red tinge. Such objects would thus look like stars from the outside, but powered by growing black holes instead of nuclear fusion.
Although both proposals go some way to explaining the dots’ unique characteristics, neither does so satisfactorily. Critics of the AGN scenario contend that it requires a string of assumptions to explain their unusual appearance. But the advocates of black-hole stars have to explain why a handful of dots have displayed light leaking out of the gas cocoon, something their model forbids. Which side of the debate sounds more convincing can come down to taste. As Jenny Greene, an astronomer at Princeton University, puts it: “People see what they want to see.”
What could settle the matter? The answer may lie in the dots’ mass. The two proposals predict wildly different numbers from the same data: AGN-like objects can be several orders of magnitude heavier than black-hole stars. Writing in Nature, in May, a team led by Ignas Juodzbalis, then at the University of Cambridge, published the first mass measurement of a little red dot. They calculated the speeds with which different patches of the gas cocoon moved, and used them to infer the dot’s mass. The result, about 50m solar masses, was a point for team AGN.
But the work has proved controversial. Dr Juodzbalis himself points out that it provides only one data point. What’s more, “I think they can’t do what they said they did,” says Dr Greene. She contends that the authors’ technique works only when measuring the speeds of clearly defined objects, such as two stars, and not the motion within the messy gas cocoons that surround little red dots.
More than academic vindication is at stake. Astronomers do not know how the first supermassive black holes put on their weight, for example, nor how that shaped the galaxies in which they sit. The modest masses of black-hole stars would suggest that they started small and grew quickly by feeding on their gas cocoons. But if the AGN advocates are right, somehow the first black holes were massive at birth. On such questions, the little red dots punch far above their weight.

epub_89.title: AI models can tinker with one another’s brains
epub_89.text:
AI models can tinker with one another’s brains
Science & technology
| Weights and measures
AI models can tinker with one another’s brains
For now, the tweaks are relatively small-scale
Nov 5th 2026
Numbers such as -0.180, -0.080 and 0.191 do not mean very much to the untrained human eye. Even if a specialist were told that these were an AI model’s “weights”—as its internal parameters are called—they would struggle to reconstruct what sort of model it was, or what it was trained to do. But it seems that a cutting-edge large language model (LLM), such as OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, would have no such difficulty.
So said Rikiya Takehi, a PhD student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and his collaborators in a blog post published on November 2nd. They claimed that Astra figured out that a second AI model had been trained to play Pong, a basic video game, just by looking at its weights. More impressive still, it fixed a known bug in a small LLM by tweaking its weights, thereby sextupling its score on a popular maths test, and manually programmed the weights for an AI model capable of playing Go, a board game. If ordinary model design is akin to natural selection, in which external conditions are set to allow the right weights to emerge on their own, the tweaks Astra made were closer to genetic engineering.
These claims rapidly caught the attention of others in the field. Some observers speculated that a future AI could tweak its own weights, potentially releasing a runaway train of recursive self-improvement. Others hoped that AI systems could help them peer inside future models to catch possible misbehaviour early.
The blog post is no guarantee that either of these will materialise. It shows only relatively simple examples of models finding and fixing flaws in other models that are still thousands of times smaller than Astra itself. What’s more, says Fazl Barez, an AI researcher at Oxford University who was not involved in the work, it is likely that the model’s abilities emerged only because it had been trained on previous human-led experiments to do the same thing. A comprehensive understanding of frontier models remains a long way off. But if it happens, says Dr Barez, “It’ll be the happiest day of my life.”

epub_90.title: Drones don’t just blow up the enemy
epub_90.text:
Drones don’t just blow up the enemy
Science & technology
| Ears in the sky
Drones don’t just blow up the enemy
They can also pick up on radio transmissions to identify future targets
Nov 5th 2026
In the David and Goliath war between Ukraine and Russia,
drones
have proved a great equaliser. Ukraine’s short-range aircraft are cutting Russia’s supply lines to its occupying troops, while long-range versions attack oil refineries, airfields and warehouses as far afield as Siberia.
Not all military drones, however, carry
warheads
. Many are used instead for spying and target location. A lot of these gather their data at optical or infrared frequencies. But some, involved in the field of signals intelligence, or SIGINT, listen out for radio waves. And within that category are those which seek not to understand what is being broadcast, but merely to identify and locate its source, the better to attack it—a field of endeavour called electronic support measures (ESM).
According to Thomas Withington, an electronic-warfare expert at the Royal United Services Institute, a think-tank, the result has been an arms race in which the radio frequencies used to control drones have migrated ever further up and down the spectrum, in attempts to evade detection. Frequency-hopping radios, which skip from one wavelength to another thousands of times a second, are getting faster, so a transmitter may be visible only momentarily; signals are increasingly disguised to merge into background noise.
Dr Withington notes the advantages drones bring to ESM. A lorry-mounted system with a ten-metre antenna can detect transmitters roughly 13km away. The same receiver on a drone at an altitude of 1,000 metres can see for 130km. Having antennae on drones is also more useful when an attack may come from any direction. It avoids blind spots caused by topography.
The Ukrainians are reluctant to discuss what they are up to. But not all their research is being done in-house. At Eurosatory, a European defence exhibition held in June, Aaronia, a German manufacturer, unveiled a SIGINT electronics package that can be mounted on a drone. The developers say three such drones working in tandem can pinpoint transmitters to within 25 metres from up to 75km away.
At 5kg, Aaronia’s product is inconveniently heavy. Sky Spy, based in Delaware, recently demonstrated Agent 001, a 500-gram electronics package that can be mounted on a small Orqa quadcopter. This proved able to detect, identify and locate “hostile” radios as part of an exercise in Estonia. Agent 001 also has on-board processing, linked to the drone’s camera, so it can move towards a transmitter and capture video for its operator to confirm the identity of the source.
One limitation of small drones, says Dr Withington, is that the amount of processing capacity they can carry is restricted. Such capacity is essential for sifting through signal data. Drone-control signals may, for example, be hidden in Wi-Fi.
New processors and AI software are, however, making small drones vastly more capable. One bit of kit that can be mounted onto a drone, known as Barn Owl, has been developed by NxGenComm of North Carolina. David Gross, NxGenComm’s marketing director, says Barn Owl follows all traffic in the Wi-Fi range, analysing changes to pick out the signatures of concealed military signals. He claims the process is fast enough to keep up with the most nimble frequency-hopping radios, and powerful enough to scan and analyse an 800MHz-wide swathe of radio signals.
Intelligence can go to commanders, or directly to other units. In one proposed set-up, a parliament of Barn Owls would be linked directly to interceptor drones. When they detected an incoming drone, they would launch an interceptor and guide it to the target’s location until it was close enough for visual confirmation by the operator. NxGenComm hopes to deploy Barn Owl to Ukraine in the next few months, and is in discussion with American military customers.
As well as locating enemy drones, ESM can also help identify their control frequencies so that they can be jammed. Both sides get round this by flying some drones via fibre-optic control cables, which unspool as they fly. Such drones, which can carry 50km of fibre, emit no radio signals. Similarly, some AI-enabled drones can operate incommunicado, flying and striking targets without operator input.
In the meantime, however, the vast majority of drones still rely on radio, and the electronic-warfare arms race continues. Falling behind can be disastrous: if an enemy can jam communications and knock drones out of the sky while remaining invisible, heavy losses are sure to result.

epub_91.title: OpenAI’s approach to mathematics does not add up
epub_91.text:
OpenAI’s approach to mathematics does not add up
Science & technology
| Show your working
OpenAI’s approach to mathematics does not add up
Two months after the firm’s initial advances, its lack of transparency is still causing problems
Nov 5th 2026
On October 29th leading mathematicians gathered at the Royal Society in London to discuss the future of their field. There was plenty of excitement at the progress artificial intelligence is making, leavened with nostalgia for the good old days of early 2026 when human-led mathematics was the only game in town.
Many attendees were also critical of how AI labs have been handling their models’ breakthroughs. In recent months labs have flooded the field with papers that are almost impenetrable to human minds, and kept the details of new results under wraps. Such secrecy, say mathematicians, increases the chance of needless errors and risks creating an illusion of progress. They do not feel the labs are keeping their promises to be more transparent.
Take the announcement by OpenAI, an American lab, on October 26th, of solutions to three more long-standing problems. The first is a proof of the Kakeya conjecture, related to how to rotate an infinitely thin needle while sweeping out as little area as possible. Thus far the conjecture had been found to hold in up to three dimensions. OpenAI said its proof extends it to any number.
The second is a disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), which sets an upper limit on how fast any algorithm can solve a specific problem. The hypothesis had long been assumed to be true, with implications for disciplines ranging from computational biology to database management. A proof that it is false “re-opens questions” about how quickly such tasks could be performed, said OpenAI. For both ETH and the Kakeya conjecture, the lab released the AI’s output so experts can begin working out what these results mean.
When it came to the third of the results, however, a cloak of secrecy descended. It is related to the Yang-Mills existence and mass-gap problem, one of seven landmark riddles known as the Millennium Prize problems. It asks whether a mathematical framework called Yang-Mills theory, which underpins physicists’ understanding of the universe, stands on firm mathematical footing (or, in mathematical jargon, “exists”). For many physicists, the question is of little relevance—the theory already makes predictions that match real-world data, so its truth is assumed. Mathematicians, though, are more pernickety.
OpenAI says its model has proved that Yang-Mills theory exists. But the firm has said little else. Instead, it has chosen to keep the AI’s 1,147-page proof under wraps while a “shepherding committee” of five physicists decides what to do with it. The committee has said that before they release it they “would like to be convinced that it is correct”. Until then, and until those outside the committee are similarly satisfied, there are question marks about how seriously to take their claim.
These worries are not theoretical. Ever since OpenAI released a
solution to the Navier-Stokes problem
—another of the Millennium Prize problems—on September 8th, mathematicians have been trying to follow its working. They know the proof is worth understanding because it was accompanied by a certificate of logical watertightness known as a Lean formalisation. If a proof translated into Lean code runs without errors, it verifies that the proof contains no inconsistencies.
In a study published online on October 6th, a team led by Anders Hansen, of the University of Cambridge, showed that the proof’s Lean verification does not, in fact, correspond to what is written in the paper. The problem is unlikely to be fatal. Dr Hansen reckons that the Lean code accurately reflects a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, but that its contents differ from those of the accompanying paper. OpenAI, for its part, says it is possible its models came up with two distinct proofs.
Anyone who has spent time navigating a foreign country will know that dodgy translations can cause misunderstandings. The same is true for mathematics. If AI labs do not check that a proof’s Lean code matches the ideas behind it, they risk creating unnecessary confusion. As Kevin Buzzard, a Lean whiz at Imperial College London, put it during his presentation at the Royal Society, the AI labs are doing only one part of the job.

epub_92.title: Is brown rice really healthier than white rice?

Is brown rice really healthier than white rice?
Science & technology
| Well Informed
Is brown rice really healthier than white rice?
The scientific evidence goes against the grain
Nov 5th 2026
RICE SUPPLIES nearly a fifth of the world’s calories. Which sort, though, is healthiest? Brown rice becomes white when milling removes its fibrous outer layer (known as the bran), and nutrient-rich seed embryo (the germ), so nutritional lore naturally favours the former. Indeed, some striking findings seem to support that preference. Look closer, though, and the colour of rice may not be what matters most.
Rice is rich in starch, which digestion turns into glucose, or blood sugar. If the body struggles to regulate it, type-2 diabetes can eventually develop. Consider a review of eight observational studies that tracked the diets and health of 577,426 people. Writing in BMJ Open in 2022, the researchers calculated that once daily consumption exceeded about two 158-gram servings of cooked white rice, each additional serving was linked to a 13% higher risk of the disease.
Brown rice, meanwhile, appears to offer some protection. Fibre in the bran slows the breakdown of starch, so glucose enters the bloodstream more gradually. The bran and germ also contain magnesium, B vitamins and other nutrients that may help the body regulate blood sugar. A paper in Archives of Internal Medicine in 2010, included in the 2022 review, analysed three studies that followed 197,228 Americans for 14 to 22 years. Modelling suggested that replacing 50 grams of cooked white rice a day with brown rice was linked to a 16% lower risk of type-2 diabetes.
Correlation, though, is not causation. People who prefer brown rice tend to smoke less, exercise more and eat healthier food overall. Although the authors of the papers from 2022 and 2010 attempted to account for such confounding lifestyle differences, they acknowledged that their findings could still be skewed. So what happens when researchers actually instruct people to eat brown rather than white rice?
Not much. The 2022 review also examined 11 randomised controlled trials involving 1,034 participants. Those assigned to eat brown rice showed no statistically significant improvements in their short- or longer-term control of blood sugar. There was also no clear evidence of improved sensitivity to insulin, which helps cells absorb glucose. Nor did the trials consistently find improved blood pressure.
What matters more for blood sugar than rice’s colour, it turns out, is how much of a starch called amylose it contains. Amylose resists rapid digestion, so it limits spikes in blood sugar. A review of 32 randomised controlled trials published in 2015 identified amylose content—which is largely a function of a rice’s variety—as “the most consistently important” determinant of how sharply rice raises blood sugar.
Processing matters, too. Parboiling—soaking and steaming rice before milling—moves B vitamins from the bran into the grain while making its starch more resistant to digestion. An experiment reported in Nutrition in 2018 found that, among people without diabetes, eating parboiled rather than ordinary white rice reduced the cumulative rise in blood sugar over the following two hours by 38%. It also appeared to have an edge over ordinary brown rice.
A similar trick can be performed at home. Refrigerating cooked rice, whether brown or white, alters some of its starch so that it is digested more slowly. Care, though, is needed: to limit bacterial growth, rice should be cooled within an hour and reheated only once, until steaming hot, within a day.

epub_94.title: Is childlessness contagious?
epub_94.text:
Is childlessness contagious?
Culture
| (Don’t) be my baby
Is childlessness contagious?
A new book offers some surprising reasons people aren’t having children
Nov 5th 2026
IT’S ALL gone to the
dogs
. In South Korea sales of buggies for pets have overtaken those for children. Shrines in Japan sometimes bless more canines than babies. Conventional wisdom once held that when a couple got a puppy, they would start to conceive of parenthood—and then start trying to conceive. But a growing number of pet “parents” see four-legged creatures as a permanent substitute for two-legged offspring. Some firms have begun to offer “pawternity” leave, so employees can bond with a new pet or tend to it when it is sick.
Some find nothing cute or cuddly about the trend.
Pope Francis
warned about a “demographic winter” and frostily decried the choice not to have children as “selfish”.
Elon Musk
has said falling birth rates are the “biggest danger civilisation faces by far”. The largest 15 countries by GDP are now all below the population replacement rate, including America, China and India.
Declining birth rates
could cause the world’s population to shrink later this century for the first time since the Black Death killed tens of millions in the 14th century.
Baroness Camilla Cavendish, a columnist for the Financial Times, gives those delaying or forgoing children a name: Generation Maybe. In a fascinating new book, she examines why “what we once thought of as the most profound human instinct, to continue the line, is on the wane.”
The consequences of the baby bust are intuitive: ageing societies will have to rely on a smaller group of youngsters to fuel growth and
fund pensions
and public services. They are also enormous. Falling birth rates will reshape culture, society and geopolitics. By 2050 Nigeria will overtake America as the third-most-populous country, according to some projections (though such estimates are hotly debated). Low-growth nations could invade one another to expand their numbers and distract from tensions and anxiety at home, Lady Cavendish suggests. She predicts the world will become less peaceful and probably more religious, as “a greater proportion of the planet will live in countries with predominantly Islamic or Christian populations.”
And as more people choose to have just one child, it has sparked a “kin crash” of fewer siblings and other relatives. Fifty years ago the average Canadian 35-year-old would have had 20 living cousins. Today she has about ten, and in 2095 she may have only five. By the end of the century there will be a 38% global drop in the number of living relatives for people aged 65 compared with 1950, according to a study published by America’s National Academy of Sciences. The Beatles’ sombre chorus about “all the lonely people” may be what the future has in store.
What is behind this reverse baby fever? Affordability and housing costs get a lot of attention. Fewer people want to have a baby when they feel like a grown-up child, stuck living with their own parents. One study by Benjamin Couillard at the University of Toronto estimates that about half the recent decline in birth rates in America may be due to
housing prices
, and that around 13m more children would have been born from 1990 to 2020 if those costs had remained stable. Yet fertility has fallen sharply even in countries where housing is not especially expensive, including Japan.
Opportunity costs may be a bigger factor. Children demand a huge amount of time. As countries grow richer, the alternative uses for that time grow more attractive. And many parents think they have a better shot at winning the educational arms race if they shower Mandarin and violin lessons on one or two kids, rather than stretching their resources over three or four. Academics call this “intensive” parenting; others invoke analogies to helicopters and tigers.
“Social contagion” influences people’s opinions about whether to bear children and how many to have, Lady Cavendish intriguingly argues. TikTok videos exalt the gloriously #Childfree life, which apparently includes mid-afternoon naps, bucket-list travel, big savings and early retirement. (Sorry, exhausted parents, but it’s too late for second thoughts.) Research has shown TV shows, including MTV’s “16 and Pregnant” and Brazil’s telenovelas that feature small (albeit dysfunctional) families, have contributed to falling fertility rates. A growing body of “misery memoirs”, which complain about how hard parenthood and marriage are, acts as a prophylactic, too.
Friends and siblings can strongly influence how many children someone wants. Polish women who move to Britain, for instance, have more babies than their peers back home, “mirroring the household average of their new country, even though it often costs more to raise a child in London than in Warsaw”, Lady Cavendish writes.
Those who think they may like children but are waiting—for the right partner, the right moment, the right bank balance—may be wrongly guided. Lady Cavendish is searing about
IVF
and egg-freezing; clinics give women a rosier view of their prospect of parenthood than data support. The success rate for frozen embryos varies widely and depends on a woman’s age, but the national average in Britain is under 30%.
Men also face little-discussed problems as they get older. A “spermapocalypse” is quietly occurring, with
men’s sperm count
having fallen precipitously in many countries, possibly because of exposure to household products. Age degrades sperm quality, too, though even those alert to a ticking biological clock do not always factor in males’ fertility decline.
What can be done to baby-proof the baby bust? Immigration can help, but is often unpopular, and many countries are becoming less welcoming. Efforts to persuade people to have more babies have met little or no success. Campaigns are more likely to vitiate than titillate. Take the “Do it for Denmark” TV adverts (encouraging couples to go on holiday and send proof of conception to win prizes) or a rap in Singapore (“I’m a patriotic husband, you’re my patriotic wife, let’s do our civic duty and manufacture life!”).
Lady Cavendish runs through 11 less cringe-inducing ideas to boost baby-making, which span the sensible (teach both sexes more about the biological clock) to the improbable (rethink the whole education system so people can start families sooner). Some are no-brainers, like trying to make procreation less political and polarising. Other suggestions are brainteasers: for example, should families with children be entitled to more votes? Paul Demeny, a late demographer and economist, proposed that parents should be given a proxy vote for each of their children. This could help counteract
older voters’ obvious self-interest
in investing more in health care and less in education. But it seems like an unlikely political mantle.
Ultimately child-bearing is a personal choice with public consequences. The pressing question is whether Generation Maybe will become Generation No. For that, demographers and authors will have to wait for the next chapter.

epub_95.title: What is it like to be a newborn?
epub_95.text:
What is it like to be a newborn?
Culture
| Born wild
What is it like to be a newborn?
Nobody can quite say. But a new book tries to figure it out
Nov 5th 2026
The naked creature in the incubator measures perhaps 50 centimetres and weighs some 900 grams. It scowls and twitches but cannot smile. Its skin is almost transparent, and its veins close to invisible; it will take a doctor several minutes first to find one and then to draw a few drops of blood. It is probably intubated to help breathing; another tube trickles milk directly to the stomach. If you put tape on this fragile being, you will tear its skin. But if you leave it, it will cry.
Clémentine Goldszal, a French journalist, is consumed by this image and by a single imperative: to find out what birth is like for newborns, and how they experience the multiple medical interventions that may, in a worst case, immediately follow. She would interview them if she could. But of course there is no communication. When her own son Lucien was born, what she took as sweet kittenish sounds turned out to be signs of acute respiratory distress. An apparently lively baby may, in fact, be having convulsions.
She decided to “construct a phenomenology of the newborn” by spending many months as an observer in the neonatal unit of the Necker in Paris. This is a superb hospital, especially for its care of premature babies, rated seventh in the world. Sick babies are rushed there from all over France. Standing in a corner of the incubator rooms, out of the way, she sees nurses ceaselessly watching the beeping monitors, checking on breathing and feeding. In other rooms she watches operations so delicate, performed with miniature instruments, that a margin of error of a millimetre would be a catastrophe.
What she wanted to decipher was the attitude of medical staff to the newborn: whether or not they considered them fully human, individual and even having personalities. She had viewed Lucien as merely “a generic entity” for some weeks, and found it hard to say his name. But at Necker newborn patients were all called by their names and treated tenderly. They were assumed to have agency, if only to close their eyes or poo in their nappies. When those nappies were changed, blankets were put over the incubators to shield their privacy. After all, in French law, they were individuals as soon as they drew breath and no longer occupied their mother’s womb.
And yet without their consent, these babies were invaded. They were injected, intubated, placed among noisy machines and blinded by harsh lights. Tiny catheters were sent in to deliver fluids. In France 94% of babies born between 27 and 31 weeks left the hospital in perfect health. (At 25 weeks, though, the figure fell to 60%.)
These numbers were improving steadily, and had been doing so ever since the days when the only treatment for a struggling newborn was to dangle it by its heels or, in the case of Louis XIII of France, dose it with red wine. Nonetheless, Ms Goldszal worries about the long-term effects of brutal modern procedures, even wondering whether her disabled or confused friends were damaged by them, long before they knew how to complain.
She paints a gripping, vivid picture of life at Necker, especially the nurses, permanently exhausted but perceptive enough to lay a gentle hand on a newborn, turn down the lighting, or rock them. It is the medical setting, among people in scrubs and the tang of sanitiser, that thrills her: she  finds herself surrounded at staff meetings by “an entire continent” of words she can’t understand: oesophageal atresia, hypocalcaemia, exomphalos.
Ms Goldszal goes only sketchily into the philosophy of personhood and the difficult legal line between the full-term fetus inside the womb and the newborn outside it. For ideas of ensoulment she has even less time. She envies religious Jews their belief that God breathes life into the fetus at the moment of birth, but she is a modern woman; this is really just “magical thinking”.
All she needs to know she has seen at Necker, and it is “fundamentally prosaic”: new life appears where before there was nothing, and medical ingenuity does its best to ensure that life does not swiftly return to nothing again.
Yet a mystery remains. The last epigram that opens the book comes from
J.G. Ballard
, an English writer, recording the birth of his daughter: “For the first few seconds I had the sense she was immensely old. She looked like something from Egyptian sculpture, streamlined by time. Within a few seconds she was suddenly very young.” Newborns may seem able to tell us nothing. But perhaps sometimes, for a moment, their eyes and their parents can.

epub_96.title: What goes on behind the doors of Claridge’s?
epub_96.text:
What goes on behind the doors of Claridge’s?
Culture
| Fit for a king
What goes on behind the doors of Claridge’s?
A new book gives readers a key card to the storied hotel’s past
Nov 5th 2026
THINGS CHANGE all the time inside hotels. Guests check in and out; towels and bed sheets are regularly laundered (or so you would hope). Hotels are also forced to accommodate upheavals that take place outside their doors. Two recent books, “
The Finest Hotel in Kabul
” and “
Hotel Exile
”, explored the turmoil of the 20th century from the front desks of hotels in Afghanistan and France. Now readers can journey to Claridge’s, one of London’s most prestigious hotels.
Martin Williams, a historian, traces how the hotel has witnessed all manner of political and cultural shifts since 1812. This is a top-down view of history, for Claridge’s clients have always been exceptionally posh. Princes and empresses slept there on visits to Britain; the future George IV, then prince regent, was thought to have slept there with lovers.
In periods of turmoil, such as the revolutions of 1848 and the
second world war
, European royals and aristocrats ousted from their countries took refuge in Mayfair. Alexander, the crown prince of Yugoslavia, was born in one of its suites in 1945. (Dirt was rumoured to have been spread under the bed so he could say he was born “on Yugoslavian soil”.) Legend holds that a diplomat once telephoned the hotel and asked to speak to the king. “Certainly, sir,” the operator said. “But which one?”
The war years are invariably the most fascinating. Soldiers back from Dunkirk—their uniforms still covered in “salt, sand and sweat”—lunched in the restaurant alongside women in hats. (Like the best hotels, this book pays attention to the details.) American officials moved in to be close to the embassy and were charmed by the hotel’s old-world grandeur. Though
Dwight Eisenhower
, then commander of American forces in Europe, was not among them: he took offence to his room’s “whorehouse pink” decor.
In the decades since, many notable people have strolled through the lobby. Audrey Hepburn first met William Wyler, the director of “Roman Holiday” (1953), in the hotel; the movie would make her a star and an Oscar winner. In 1974
Agatha Christie
made one of her last public appearances at a dinner there, when she celebrated the premiere of the film adaptation of “Murder on the Orient Express”. In 1970 Jackie Kennedy Onassis prompted the hotel to overturn its long-standing policy banning women from wearing trousers.
The trousers tussle notwithstanding, Claridge’s has managed a difficult balance of tradition and innovation over the course of its two centuries. Mr Williams shows how it has adapted time and again to changing social mores and expectations of high-end hospitality. Today it lures foodies and fashionistas. Gordon Ramsay and
Noma
have had stints in the restaurant; since 2009 the hotel has invited a fashion designer to create its Christmas tree. (This year’s will be unveiled on November 25th, though the designer has yet to be announced.) If you do not feel like shelling out between £1,500 and £60,000 ($2,000-80,000) for a suite, “Claridge’s” offers a sweet (and cheap) escape.

epub_97.title: Is it time to end the era of remote work?
epub_97.text:
Is it time to end the era of remote work?
Culture
| In praise of watercoolers
Is it time to end the era of remote work?
A new book makes a case for getting out of your tracksuit and into your officewear
Nov 5th 2026
Those mulling the current AI boom should look back to a kitchen in Google’s office in the early 2000s. Two employees, Noam Shazeer and Georges Harik, began to chat about how computers differentiated between essential and superfluous information. This chance encounter windingly led to the mechanism that underpins
large language models
.
Had Google allowed remote work, Mr Shazeer and Mr Harik might never have spoken. In-person spitballing has led to ideas ranging from the hugely consequential (IBM’s personal computer) to the hugely entertaining (
“Finding Nemo”
). That is one reason why bosses often lament the rise of remote work, notes a new book by Natalia Emanuel and Emma Harrington, two economists. In 2019 American workers spent 7% of their paid days working at home. Now it is about a quarter.
Studies suggest that remote work may increase the quantity of output while decreasing its quality. In 2025 a review of return-to-office mandates at large banks found that when firms called analysts back to the office for a few days each week, the accuracy of their earnings forecasts leaped 15% compared with peers at banks that remained fully remote.
What is more, remote work tends to dent the sort of tasks that rarely show up in measures of output. Senior software engineers write more code from the comfort of their homes, but they review junior employees’ work less comprehensively. Lost mentorship and undiscovered ideas can affect the future of a firm.
Such losses may be why the shift has stung new graduates in particular. A new study by Peter John Lambert of the London School of Economics and Yannick Schindler of the University of Oxford suggests remote work, not AI, is to blame for
young jobseekers’ woes
of late. Jobs done entirely online tend to be susceptible to being done remotely. Firms that are reluctant to let untested employees work away from their boss’s watchful eye may be choosing not to hire them at all.
So why not cancel the corporate Zoom subscription and squeeze back into the cubicle? The authors note that some employees are well-served by remote work: for example, parents and people with disabilities. For most companies a mix is best. To help bosses settle on the right number of days in-office, “In Person” features a “calculator” that asks them to add and subtract days based on the firm’s characteristics. But what executive would not say the stakes of their business are high (add two days), or that innovation is crucial to their firm’s future (add three days)? When it comes to such decisions, psychologists may be more helpful than economists.
Still, many of the book’s points are well-taken. How many days employees spend at the office may be less important than whether they overlap with key colleagues.
Hot-desking
is a scourge, as would-be collaborators sit together only occasionally. And if bosses want to reap the benefits of in-person culture, they also need to show face. “In Person” should contribute to an ongoing conversation about why remote work has remained so persistent if it comes with so many drawbacks. Watercooler-chat lovers, rejoice.
